スネルの法則.desc: The relation n₁ sinθ₁ = n₂ sinθ₂ that gives how much light bends at a boundary between media of different refractive index. Angles are measured from the normal to the surface.

about.p: When light crosses a boundary between media of different refractive index, the angle of incidence θ₁ and the angle of refraction θ₂ obey n₁ sinθ₁ = n₂ sinθ₂. Inside a medium the speed of light drops to c/n while the frequency stays the same, so the wavelength shrinks to λ₀/n. The equation follows from requiring the crests and troughs of the wavefronts to match up along the boundary. It is easy to remember as the product n sinθ being equal on both sides. Snell found it around 1621, and Descartes published it in 1637, which is why French speakers often call it Descartes' law.

about.h: Typical angles and the critical angle
about.p: Light entering glass of index 1.5 from air at 45° has sinθ₂ = sin45°/1.5 ≈ 0.471, so it refracts at about 28.1°; for water (n = 1.33) the angle is about 32.1°. Light moving into the higher-index side bends toward the normal, and light moving into the lower-index side bends away from it. In the second case, once n₁ sinθ₁/n₂ exceeds 1 there is no solution for the refraction angle and total internal reflection occurs; the boundary between the two cases is the critical angle. Because n sinθ is conserved through any stack of parallel surfaces, the final exit angle depends only on the first and last media, and the layers in between merely shift the beam sideways.

about.h: Color dependence and where it does not apply
about.p: The refractive index varies with wavelength (dispersion), so different colors refract at different angles even for the same angle of incidence. The optical glass BK7 has n = 1.5224 at 486 nm and 1.5143 at 656 nm, and at 45° incidence the blue and red refraction angles differ by about 0.16°. This is why a prism splits white light and why lenses show chromatic aberration. The extraordinary ray in an anisotropic crystal such as calcite, on the other hand, travels in a direction that this simple formula does not predict. Note also that measuring angles from the surface rather than from the normal swaps sine and cosine and gives wrong answers.

about.h: How it is used in design
about.p: Ray tracing in lens design calculates the refraction at every surface exactly with Snell's law. The paraxial approximation, sinθ ≈ θ, shows no aberrations, and the difference between the exact calculation and the paraxial one is precisely the aberration. The numerical aperture of an optical fiber, NA = √(n₁² − n₂²), is also derived by applying Snell's law to the total-internal-reflection condition at the core–cladding boundary and to the refraction at the fiber end. More recently, metasurfaces, which add a phase gradient along the boundary with arrays of fine structures to bend light in unusual directions, have been studied; their behavior is described by a generalized Snell's law.

faq.q: Where are the angles in Snell's law measured from?
faq.a: From the normal to the boundary surface. Using angles measured from the surface itself swaps sine and cosine and gives the wrong result. Normal incidence corresponds to 0°, and then light is not bent regardless of the refractive indices.

faq.q: How do I calculate refraction when light leaves a higher-index medium?
faq.a: Use the same equation, n₁ sinθ₁ = n₂ sinθ₂, with n₁ as the index of the side the light comes from. The refraction angle is larger than the angle of incidence, and at angles where sinθ₂ would exceed 1 (beyond the critical angle) there is no refracted light and total internal reflection occurs.

faq.q: Why does the refraction angle depend on color?
faq.a: Because of dispersion, the variation of refractive index with wavelength. Ordinary glass has a higher index at shorter wavelengths, so blue light is bent more strongly. The same effect makes a prism spread light into a rainbow and gives a single lens chromatic aberration.

全反射.desc: The phenomenon in which light traveling from a higher-index medium toward a lower-index one at an angle of incidence beyond the critical angle has no transmitted beam and is reflected completely.

about.p: In Snell's law, n₁ sinθ₁ = n₂ sinθ₂, when n₁ > n₂ the refraction angle reaches 90° before the angle of incidence θ₁ does. The angle of incidence at that point is the critical angle θc, with sinθc = n₂/n₁. It is about 41.8° from glass (n = 1.5) to air, and about 24° from silicon (n ≈ 3.48) to oxide (n ≈ 1.44). At angles of incidence larger than θc there is no solution for a refracted ray, and all the energy is reflected. Conversely, for light incident from the lower-index side, total internal reflection never occurs at any angle.

about.h: The evanescent wave and the phase shift
about.p: Even under total internal reflection, the field outside the boundary is not exactly zero. An evanescent wave extends beyond the boundary, decaying exponentially, with a penetration depth on the order of a wavelength. It carries no energy away, but if another medium is brought close, light can tunnel across (frustrated total internal reflection). Directional couplers and prism couplers exploit this effect. Total internal reflection also shifts the phase of s- and p-polarized light by different amounts, and this phase difference can be used to make broadband wave plates such as the Fresnel rhomb.

about.h: Devices that use total internal reflection
about.p: Optical fibers and waveguides confine light by total internal reflection, making the core index higher than the cladding's. Ideal total internal reflection is lossless, which makes kilometer-scale transmission possible. Right-angle prisms fold light paths by 90° or 180° with total internal reflection at the hypotenuse; they reflect better than metal mirrors and degrade less, so they are used in binoculars and laser beam paths. Total internal reflection fluorescence (TIRF) microscopy illuminates only the region near the sample surface with the evanescent wave. Fingerprint sensors and rain sensors also use the way objects touching a surface disturb total internal reflection.

faq.q: How is the critical angle for total internal reflection calculated?
faq.a: With n₁ the higher index and n₂ the lower, use sinθc = n₂/n₁. From glass (1.5) to air (1.0), sinθc ≈ 0.667, so the critical angle is about 41.8°. The angle is measured from the normal, not from the surface.

faq.q: Does total internal reflection really reflect 100%?
faq.a: At an ideal boundary with no absorption or scattering, yes. An evanescent wave extends beyond the boundary but carries no energy. However, light can leak out if another medium is nearby, and dirt or roughness on the surface causes loss.

faq.q: Why is there no total internal reflection for light entering from the lower-index side?
faq.a: Light going from a lower-index medium into a higher-index one bends toward the normal, so the refraction angle is always smaller than the angle of incidence. It never reaches 90°, so a refracted ray always exists and total internal reflection does not occur.

開口数.desc: The quantity NA = n sinθ that describes the range of angles a lens or fiber accepts. A larger NA means a brighter image and higher resolution.

about.p: Numerical aperture (NA) is defined as NA = n sinθ, using the refractive index n of the medium on the object (or image) side and the half-angle θ between the optical axis and the marginal ray. In air it cannot exceed 1, but with oil immersion of index about 1.5 it can reach about 1.4. Because n sinθ is conserved across boundaries (Snell's law), NA has the same value in whichever medium it is measured, making it a common measure of an optical system's light-gathering power. For a system that satisfies the sine condition, it is related to the f-number used for camera lenses by F ≈ 1/(2NA).

In a microscope, the smallest separation at which two points can be distinguished is about 0.61λ/NA (the Rayleigh criterion), so a larger NA reveals finer detail. The resolution of semiconductor lithography tools is likewise written k₁λ/NA, and immersion has raised NA to 1.35. The diameter of a focused spot is also roughly proportional to λ/NA. The depth of focus, however, shrinks in proportion to λ/NA², so raising NA sharply narrows the range that stays in focus. A larger NA also makes aberrations harder to correct, so high-NA lenses are built from many elements.

For an optical fiber, NA is found from the core and cladding indices n₁ and n₂ as NA = √(n₁² − n₂²), and the maximum angle of incidence θ from air for light to be guided in the core is given by sinθ = NA. Standard single-mode fiber has an NA of about 0.12, an acceptance half-angle of about 7°; multimode fiber has 0.2–0.3. When coupling from a source or another fiber, choose lenses so that the spread of incoming angles stays within this NA. For single-mode fiber, matching the mode field diameter matters more than NA in determining coupling efficiency.

faq.q: How do numerical aperture and f-number convert?
faq.a: For imaging an object at infinity in air, F ≈ 1/(2NA). For example, NA 0.25 corresponds to f/2. The f-number is used in photography as a measure of brightness, while NA is common in microscopy and fiber optics.

faq.q: Can the numerical aperture exceed 1?
faq.a: Yes. Since NA = n sinθ, immersion lenses that fill the space between sample and lens with high-index oil or water can exceed 1. Oil-immersion microscope objectives reach about 1.4, and semiconductor immersion lithography about 1.35.

faq.q: Is a larger NA always better?
faq.a: Resolution and brightness improve, but the depth of focus becomes shallower in proportion to λ/NA² and aberrations become harder to correct. The working distance also tends to shrink, so NA must be chosen to suit the application.

収差.desc: A departure from ideal imaging. There are monochromatic aberrations such as spherical aberration, coma and astigmatism, and chromatic aberration caused by the wavelength dependence of the refractive index.

about.p: In an ideal optical system, light leaving one point of an object comes together at one point in the image. In real lenses, the spherical shape of the surfaces and the dispersion of the material prevent the rays from meeting at a single point, so the image is blurred or distorted. These departures are aberrations. Monochromatic aberrations, which occur even with a single wavelength, include the five Seidel aberrations: spherical aberration, coma, astigmatism, field curvature, and distortion. On top of these come axial and lateral chromatic aberration, caused by the wavelength dependence of the refractive index. How small the aberrations are determines image quality in cameras, microscopes, and lithography tools.

Aberrations arise as departures from the paraxial approximation sinθ ≈ θ, and the first terms to matter are the third-order ones (Seidel aberrations). The transverse ray error in the image grows with the pupil height ρ and the image height y as ρ³ for spherical aberration, ρ²y for coma, ρy² for astigmatism and field curvature, and y³ for distortion. So making a lens faster (smaller F-number) rapidly increases spherical aberration and coma, while widening the field of view increases astigmatism and distortion. This is why it is hard to combine a bright lens with a wide field.

about.h: Aberrations versus diffraction, and common misconceptions
about.p: Even with every aberration removed, the image of a point is not a point: diffraction spreads it to roughly the size of the Airy disk. Aberrations are errors that design and manufacturing can reduce, whereas diffraction is a fundamental limit set by the aperture size, and the two are different things. Stopping down reduces spherical aberration but increases diffraction blur, so the sharpest image occurs at some intermediate F-number. Distortion changes only the shape of the image without blurring it. Mirrors do not rely on refraction, so they have no chromatic aberration and are used in telescopes and spectrometers covering wide wavelength ranges.

Aberrations are cancelled against each other by combining several lenses with different curvatures and materials. An achromatic doublet, which cements a positive and a negative lens with different Abbe numbers, corrects chromatic aberration, and aspheric lenses are effective against spherical aberration. A finished system is evaluated by measuring its transmitted wavefront with an interferometer and decomposing it into Zernike polynomial terms, or by measuring the MTF. By the Maréchal criterion, an RMS wavefront error of about λ/14 or less gives a Strehl ratio of about 0.8 or more, a common benchmark for being diffraction-limited. Adaptive optics in astronomy corrects aberrations from atmospheric turbulence in real time with a deformable mirror.

faq.q: What is the difference between monochromatic and chromatic aberration?
faq.a: Monochromatic aberrations are imaging errors caused by the shape and arrangement of lenses, and they occur even at a single wavelength (spherical aberration, coma, and so on). Chromatic aberration arises because the refractive index differs with wavelength, so the focus position or image size shifts with color; it matters for white light.

faq.q: What happens to aberrations when you stop down a lens?
faq.a: Aberrations that depend strongly on aperture, such as spherical aberration and coma, become smaller. However, diffraction blur grows as the aperture shrinks, so stopping down too far makes the image softer again. Distortion does not change with the stop size.

faq.q: If aberrations are zero, is the image a perfect point?
faq.a: No. Even an ideal lens without aberrations spreads the image of a point into a finite Airy disk because of diffraction. This is called the diffraction limit, and better resolution requires a larger numerical aperture or a shorter wavelength.

ABCD行列.desc: A method that represents changes in the height and angle of a paraxial ray with a 2×2 matrix. Multiplying element matrices analyzes a whole system, and it also applies to Gaussian-beam propagation.

about.h: Describing a ray with two numbers
about.p: In the paraxial approximation, the state of a ray at a given plane can be described by two numbers: its height y above the optical axis and its angle θ to the axis. After an optical element, the output (y, θ) is a linear function of the input values, so the element can be represented by a 2×2 matrix [[A, B], [C, D]]. Free space of length d is [[1, d], [0, 1]], and a thin lens of focal length f is [[1, 0], [−1/f, 1]]. Multiplying the matrices from right to left in the order the light passes through reduces a system of any number of lenses to a single matrix, whose four numbers summarize the whole system.

The C element of the system matrix is −1/f and gives the effective focal length. For example, lenses with focal lengths of 100 mm and 200 mm separated by 50 mm give C = −1/80 mm⁻¹ after multiplying the matrices, so the effective focal length is 80 mm. When B = 0, the output height does not depend on the input angle, so the input and output planes are conjugate (an imaging relation), and A is then the lateral magnification. When A = 0, light entering parallel to the axis comes to a single point at the output. If the input and output are in media of the same index, the determinant AD − BC is always 1, which is handy for checking calculations.

ABCD matrices rest on the paraxial approximation, so they cannot describe aberrations. Large angles or the effects of aspheric surfaces require ray tracing that applies Snell's law exactly at each surface. Textbooks also define the angle differently: in the convention that uses nθ, the angle multiplied by the refractive index, the determinant is always 1 even between media of different index. The matrix for refraction at a curved surface and the sign convention for concave mirrors also vary from book to book, so when combining matrices from different sources it is important to make the definitions consistent. Multiplying in the wrong order is another common mistake.

about.h: Applications to Gaussian beams and resonators
about.p: ABCD matrices apply not only to rays but directly to the propagation of Gaussian beams. The complex beam parameter q, which combines the beam radius and wavefront curvature, transforms as q₂ = (Aq₁ + B)/(Cq₁ + D), so the position and size of the waist after focusing by a lens can be calculated. In a laser resonator, when the round-trip matrix satisfies −1 ≤ (A + D)/2 ≤ 1, rays do not walk away from the axis however many round trips they make, and the resonator is stable. This is the same condition as 0 ≤ g₁g₂ ≤ 1 written with the g parameters of the two mirrors.

faq.q: In what order are ABCD matrices multiplied?
faq.a: Place the matrix of the first element the light meets on the far right, and multiply leftward in the order the light passes. This is because the first element's matrix acts on the input ray vector first. Reversing the order generally gives a different result.

faq.q: When is the determinant of an ABCD matrix not 1?
faq.a: In the convention that uses the plain angle θ, when the input and output media have different refractive indices. The determinant is then n₁/n₂. Using the angle multiplied by the index, nθ, makes it always equal to 1.

faq.q: Can ABCD matrices calculate aberrations?
faq.a: No. ABCD matrices are a first-order relation based on the paraxial approximation sinθ ≈ θ, so they describe ideal imaging without aberrations. To study aberrations, use ray tracing that calculates each surface exactly with Snell's law.

コヒーレンス長.desc: A rough measure of the path difference over which light can interfere, about λ²/Δλ. The narrower the spectrum, the longer it is: kilometers for narrow-linewidth lasers, around a micrometer for white light.

about.p: Two beams split from the same source interfere when recombined, but as their path difference increases the fringes fade and eventually vanish. The coherence length is the path difference up to which fringes are visible. Because light has a finite spectral width Δν, its phase stays well defined only for about the coherence time τc ≈ 1/Δν. The distance light travels in that time is lc = cτc ≈ c/Δν, or λ²/Δλ in terms of the wavelength width. Depending on the spectral shape and the convention used, the prefactor can be smaller than 1, so the coherence length is only an estimate.

Written in frequency, lc ≈ c/Δν does not depend on wavelength: about 300 m for a laser with a 1 MHz linewidth and about 3 km for 100 kHz. At 1550 nm, 1 MHz corresponds to a wavelength width of only about 8 fm, so long coherence lengths require extremely narrow linewidths. Broadband sources have short coherence lengths: about 14 µm for an SLD centered at 850 nm with a 50 nm width, and about 1 µm for visible white light (centered at 550 nm, about 300 nm wide). In a laser oscillating on many longitudinal modes, the overall spectral width sets the visibility range, and the fringes revive at path differences equal to multiples of twice the optical length of the cavity.

about.h: How it differs from spatial coherence
about.p: The coherence length describes temporal coherence, along the direction of propagation. Separately, spatial coherence describes whether light at two points across the beam can interfere, and it is set by the apparent size of the source. A small point source or a single-transverse-mode laser has high spatial coherence, which has nothing to do with spectral width. Also, the coherence length is not how far light can travel; it is the tolerance on the path difference between the two arms being made to interfere. In a medium, the allowed difference in geometric length is lc divided by the group index.

about.h: When longer is better, and when shorter is better
about.p: Holography, interferometers with large path differences, FMCW lidar, and fiber sensors need sources whose coherence length is much longer than the path difference to be measured, so they use narrow-linewidth lasers. Optical coherence tomography (OCT), by contrast, uses a broadband source with a short coherence length and exploits the narrow range of path differences over which interference occurs to locate depth. The broader the bandwidth, the finer the depth resolution. In microscope illumination and image-based measurement, too much coherence produces speckle and unwanted fringes, so coherence is sometimes deliberately reduced.

faq.q: How do you calculate coherence length?
faq.a: Estimate it as lc ≈ λ²/Δλ from the center wavelength λ and spectral width Δλ, or as lc ≈ c/Δν from the frequency linewidth Δν. For example, a 1 MHz linewidth gives about 300 m. The prefactor changes slightly with spectral shape, so treat it as an estimate.

faq.q: How is coherence length related to linewidth?
faq.a: They are inversely proportional. The narrower the linewidth (spectral width), the longer the coherence length; cutting the linewidth to one tenth makes it ten times longer. Narrow-linewidth lasers oscillating on a single longitudinal mode reach kilometers, while LEDs and SLDs are in the range of micrometers to tens of micrometers.

faq.q: What is the difference from spatial coherence?
faq.a: Coherence length (temporal coherence) describes how readily light interferes with itself for path differences along the propagation direction, and it is set by the spectral width. Spatial coherence describes how readily light at two points across the beam interferes, and it is set by the size of the source.

反射防止膜.desc: A thin film that cancels surface reflection by interference. For a single layer, the ideal is an optical thickness of λ/4 and an index of √(n₀ns). Multilayer coatings work over a broad band.

about.p: At normal incidence, about 4% of light reflects from the surface of glass with an index of 1.5. That may seem small for one surface, but in a lens system with 10 surfaces, reflection alone lowers transmission to about 66%, and the reflected light becomes stray light that forms ghosts and flare. For silicon, with an index of 3.48, reflection reaches about 31% per surface. An anti-reflection coating is a thin film on the surface that makes the reflections from its top and bottom interfaces cancel by interference. The cancelled reflection is not absorbed; it continues forward as transmitted light, raising the transmittance.

about.h: Conditions for a single layer and practical values
about.p: A single layer gives zero reflection at the design wavelength when its optical thickness (index × thickness) is λ/4, making the two reflections opposite in phase, and its index is √(n₀ns), making their amplitudes equal. Few dense materials come close to the ideal of about 1.22 for glass, and MgF₂ (n = 1.38) on BK7 (n = 1.52) leaves a reflectance of about 1.3%. The physical thickness of an MgF₂ layer for 1064 nm is about 193 nm. For silicon (3.48) the ideal index is about 1.87, and a silicon nitride film with n ≈ 2.0 lowers the reflectance to about 0.5%.

about.h: Multilayers, and dependence on wavelength and angle
about.p: A single layer suppresses reflection well only near its design wavelength. Combining several high- and low-index layers produces broadband coatings that keep reflectance at about 0.5% or less across the whole visible range. Coatings with a V-shaped response, minimizing reflection at a single wavelength, are common in laser optics. At larger angles of incidence the layers behave as if they were thinner, shifting the response toward shorter wavelengths, and s- and p-polarized light behave differently. The purple or green tint of a coated lens is the residual reflection at wavelengths that are not fully cancelled.

Anti-reflection coatings are used widely on camera and microscope lenses, eyeglasses, display surfaces, and solar cells. Solar cells combine light trapping by surface texture with a silicon nitride film to reduce reflection losses. For laser optics, a damage threshold high enough to withstand high power is another criterion in choosing a coating. Where even tiny reflections are a problem, such as the facets of semiconductor optical amplifiers, coatings are combined with angled facets. Moth-eye structures, arrays of protrusions finer than the wavelength that grade the refractive index smoothly, are also used in place of thin films.

faq.q: How is the thickness of an anti-reflection coating chosen?
faq.a: For a single layer, make it a quarter of the wavelength inside the film, that is, a physical thickness d = λ/(4n). For MgF₂ (n = 1.38) designed for 1064 nm, that is about 193 nm. Setting the thickness to λ/4 without dividing by the index gives a coating that works at the wrong wavelength.

faq.q: Where does the light cancelled by an anti-reflection coating go?
faq.a: In a film without absorption or scattering, transmitted light increases by exactly the amount reflection decreases. Interference does not destroy light energy; it only changes the split between reflection and transmission. That is why an anti-reflection coating increases the light passing through a lens.

faq.q: Why do coated lenses look tinted?
faq.a: Reflection is cancelled well only near the design wavelength, so a little reflection remains at other wavelengths. A single-layer coating optimized for the middle of the visible range leaves some violet-blue and red reflection at the two ends, so it often looks purplish.

マイケルソン干渉計.desc: An interferometer that splits light in two, reflects each part from a mirror and recombines them. Each λ/2 of mirror movement shifts the fringes by one, enabling precise measurement of length and refractive index.

about.h: How it works and its history
about.p: A Michelson interferometer splits light into two arms with a beam splitter, reflects each beam from a mirror at the end of its arm, and recombines them at the same beam splitter. When the path difference between the arms is a whole number of wavelengths the beams reinforce, and when it is off by half a wavelength they cancel. Because the light travels to each mirror and back, moving a mirror by d changes the path difference by 2d, and the fringes shift by one for every λ/2 of mirror travel. Michelson devised it in the late 19th century, and the failure of the 1887 Michelson–Morley experiment to detect Earth's motion through the ether became part of the background to special relativity.

about.h: Counting fringes to measure length and refractive index
about.p: With a 632.8 nm He-Ne laser, moving a mirror by 1 mm sends about 3160 fringes past the detector. Simply counting fringes measures length with the wavelength as the ruler. To measure refractive index, a cell of length L is placed in one arm and the gas inside is pumped out or let in; counting the number of fringes N that pass gives the index change as Δn = Nλ/(2L). Changing a 10 cm cell from vacuum to air (n − 1 ≈ 2.7×10⁻⁴ at room temperature and 1 atm) gives about 85 fringes. Because the index of air changes with temperature, pressure, and humidity, precision length measurement must correct for it.

about.h: How it differs from other interferometers
about.p: A Mach–Zehnder interferometer sends the split beams along separate paths and recombines them at a second beam splitter, so the light does not double back and passes a sample only once. It suits waveguide modulators and the observation of index variations in transparent objects. A Fabry–Perot resonator superimposes many reflections in multiple-beam interference and can produce sharp transmission peaks. The Michelson interferometer uses two-beam interference, so its fringes are sinusoidal. Its output is split between two ports: when the detector port is dark, the light returning toward the source is bright, so total energy is conserved.

The Michelson layout remains the basis of many instruments in use today. Laser interferometers for displacement measure the positions of machine tools and stages with nanometer-level resolution, and Fourier transform infrared (FTIR) spectrometers compute spectra from the interferogram recorded while scanning a mirror. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) is the same arrangement with the mirror in one arm replaced by the sample. The gravitational-wave detector LIGO has 4 km arms with Fabry–Perot resonators built into each arm; by measuring tiny changes in arm length, it made the first direct detection of gravitational waves in 2015.

faq.q: How far does the mirror move when one fringe passes in a Michelson interferometer?
faq.a: Half a wavelength (λ/2). The light travels to the mirror and back, so the path difference changes by twice the mirror displacement d, and one fringe passes each time 2d changes by one wavelength. At 1550 nm, one fringe corresponds to 775 nm.

faq.q: What is the difference between Michelson and Mach–Zehnder interferometers?
faq.a: A Michelson interferometer folds the light back with mirrors and recombines it at the same beam splitter, so the light travels each arm twice. A Mach–Zehnder interferometer uses two beam splitters, and the light passes each path only once. They are chosen according to the application and ease of setup.

faq.q: Why is the fringe contrast poor in my Michelson interferometer?
faq.a: The main causes are unequal power in the two arms, mismatched polarization, a path difference exceeding the coherence length, and wavefront mismatch from tilted mirrors. Balancing the arm powers and polarizations and keeping the path difference well below the coherence length improves contrast.

ファブリ・ペロー共振器.desc: A resonator in which light bounces back and forth between two parallel mirrors. It transmits sharply when the round-trip optical path is an integer number of wavelengths, with an FSR of c/(2nL).

about.h: Resonance condition and free spectral range
about.p: When light travels back and forth between two mirrors with spacing L in a medium of index n, at wavelengths where the round-trip optical path 2nL is an integer number of wavelengths, all the multiply reflected beams add in phase and reinforce. The transmission then shows a sharp peak, and the frequency spacing to the next peak is called the free spectral range (FSR): FSR = c/(2nL). It is 15 GHz for a 10 mm air gap, and about 139 GHz for a 300 µm semiconductor laser chip with an index of 3.6. In wavelength, Δλ = λ²/(2nL) (strictly, the group index including dispersion is used).

The higher the mirror reflectance R, the more round trips light makes before leaving, and the sharper the transmission peaks. Sharpness is expressed by the finesse F = FSR/δν (δν is the full width at half maximum); for lossless mirrors, F ≈ π√R/(1 − R). It is about 61 for R = 0.95 and about 310 for R = 0.99. The resonator's Q is the resonance frequency divided by the linewidth and is proportional to the time photons stay in the resonator. For a symmetric resonator with no absorption or scattering, the transmission on resonance is 100% regardless of the reflectance, but mirror absorption, imperfect parallelism and beam spreading lower the peak and broaden the linewidth.

Fabry–Perot resonators are used as laser resonators themselves and as wavelength filters with narrow passbands. The cleaved facets of a semiconductor laser also form a Fabry–Perot resonator, and its longitudinal mode spacing sets the wavelength spacing of multimode lasing. A scanning Fabry–Perot interferometer, whose spacing is varied with a piezo, acts as a spectrometer for observing a laser's modes. High-finesse resonators are also used for laser frequency stabilization (the PDH method) and in gravitational-wave detectors. Conversely, unintended reflections, for example at chip facets, form parasitic resonances that make transmission ripple periodically; they are suppressed with anti-reflection coatings.

faq.q: How is the FSR of a Fabry–Perot resonator found?
faq.a: In frequency, FSR = c/(2nL); in wavelength, λ²/(2nL). Here n is the refractive index of the medium between the mirrors (the group index if there is dispersion), and L is the mirror spacing. A shorter spacing gives a wider FSR.

faq.q: What is finesse?
faq.a: It is the ratio of the transmission-peak spacing (FSR) to the full width at half maximum of a peak, and expresses how sharp the resonance is. Without loss, it follows from the mirror reflectance R as F ≈ π√R/(1 − R), increasing with reflectance.

faq.q: Why can the transmission reach 100% with mirrors that reflect 99%?
faq.a: At resonance, light that has made many round trips builds up a large field inside the resonator, and the light leaking out of it cancels the reflection at the input side. As a result, without loss, all the incident light is transmitted. Off resonance, almost nothing is transmitted.

回折格子.desc: An element with periodic grooves that diffracts light in directions given by d sinθ = mλ, separating it by wavelength. Used in spectrometers and for wavelength selection in lasers.

about.p: A diffraction grating is an element with grooves or steps arranged with period d. Light from the grooves reinforces only in directions where the path difference between neighboring grooves is a whole number of wavelengths. At normal incidence this gives d sinθ = mλ (m is the diffraction order), and for oblique incidence a term for the angle of incidence is added. A grating with 1200 lines per millimeter has a period of about 833 nm. Within a given order, each wavelength diffracts at a different angle, so the grating separates light by wavelength. The zeroth order (m = 0) simply reflects like a mirror (or passes straight through) and does not separate wavelengths.

The change in angle with wavelength (angular dispersion) is dθ/dλ = m/(d cosθ), larger for finer grooves and higher orders. For example, 500 nm light at normal incidence on a grating with 600 lines per millimeter leaves in first order at about 17.5°. The resolving power for distinguishing two close wavelengths is λ/Δλ = mN, where N is the number of illuminated grooves; illuminating 50 mm of a 1200 lines/mm grating gives 60000 in first order, separating wavelengths about 0.008 nm apart at 500 nm. However, light of order m and light of another wavelength in order m+1 can leave at the same angle, so filters are used to separate the orders.

about.h: Differences from a prism, and efficiency
about.p: A prism bends short wavelengths more, whereas a grating diffracts long wavelengths to larger angles. Grating dispersion depends almost only on the period and not on material dispersion, so the relation between wavelength and angle is easy to calculate. Diffraction is possible only when mλ/d is at most 2 (at most 1 at normal incidence), so if the grooves are too fine, long wavelengths do not diffract at all. A blazed grating, whose grooves have a sawtooth profile, concentrates light into a particular order and wavelength to raise efficiency. Diffraction efficiency also depends on polarization.

In a spectrometer, light dispersed by the grating is collected by a concave mirror and measured by wavelength at an exit slit or a detector array. In external-cavity semiconductor lasers, the Littrow configuration 2d sinθ = mλ sends the first order back along the incident beam, and rotating the grating selects the lasing wavelength. For a 1200 lines/mm grating at 1550 nm, the angle is about 68°. In chirped-pulse amplification of ultrashort pulses, pairs of gratings make the path length depend on wavelength to stretch or compress pulses. Fiber Bragg gratings, periodic structures written into a fiber, rely on the same diffraction principle.

faq.q: How is the number of lines per millimeter related to the period?
faq.a: The period d is 1 mm divided by the number of lines: about 833 nm for 1200 lines/mm and about 1667 nm for 600 lines/mm. More lines give larger angular dispersion but lower the maximum wavelength that can be diffracted (λ < d/m at normal incidence).

faq.q: When does a grating produce no second-order light?
faq.a: When sinθ in d sinθ = 2λ would exceed 1. At normal incidence, there is no second order if the wavelength is longer than half the period. Conversely, a grating whose period is much larger than the wavelength produces many orders at once.

faq.q: What determines the resolving power of a grating?
faq.a: The resolving power λ/Δλ is the product mN of the diffraction order m and the number of illuminated grooves N. It increases not only with groove density but also by illuminating a wider area. In real spectrometers, the slit width and detector pixels also limit it.

エアリーディスク.desc: The bright central disk formed when light is focused through a circular aperture. The first dark ring lies at an angle of 1.22λ/D, which sets the resolution limit of a lens.

about.h: The diffraction pattern of a circular aperture
about.p: When light passing through a uniformly illuminated circular aperture is focused by a lens and viewed in the focal plane, the image is a bright central spot surrounded by alternating dark and bright rings. The central spot is the Airy disk, named after Airy, who calculated this pattern in 1835. The intensity is [2J₁(x)/x]², written with the first-order Bessel function, and the first dark ring appears at the angle sinθ ≈ 1.22λ/D, where D is the aperture diameter. About 84% of the total energy falls inside the central disk, and the rest is shared among the outer rings.

In the focal plane, the radius of the first dark ring is r ≈ 1.22λf/D = 1.22λN, where N is the F-number. At 550 nm and F8 it is about 5.4 µm, a diameter of about 11 µm, which shows why a camera with a pixel pitch of a few micrometers blurs from diffraction when stopped down too far. For microscope objectives it is written r ≈ 0.61λ/NA, about 0.22 µm for NA 1.4 at 500 nm. The angular resolution of a telescope is also set by 1.22λ/D: for the Hubble Space Telescope, with its 2.4 m aperture, it is about 0.05 arcseconds at 500 nm.

Spot size has several definitions, so care is needed. The angular radius of the first dark ring is 1.22λ/D, but the full width at half maximum is about 1.03λ/D, less than half the diameter of the dark ring. The Rayleigh criterion takes the resolution limit as the separation at which the center of one point image falls on the first dark ring of the other. A focused Gaussian laser beam has almost no outer rings and is described by the 1/e² intensity radius, so its formula has a different coefficient from the Airy disk. A central obstruction, such as a telescope's secondary mirror, sends more energy into the rings.

Even an ideal optical system without aberrations cannot image a point smaller than the Airy disk. This condition is called diffraction-limited, and comparing a real image with the Airy disk tells you how good an optical system is. Aberrations lower the central intensity and push energy into the rings, and the ratio of the central intensities is the Strehl ratio. The star test, which looks at a star image defocused on either side of focus, identifies the type of aberration from distortions of the ring pattern. In camera design, comparing the Airy disk diameter with the pixel size gives a guide to the smallest usable aperture.

faq.q: How do you calculate the size of the Airy disk?
faq.a: The first dark ring is at the angle sinθ ≈ 1.22λ/D (D is the aperture diameter), and its radius in the focal plane is 1.22λ × the F-number. In microscopy it is written 0.61λ/NA. It gets smaller with shorter wavelengths and larger apertures.

faq.q: How is the Airy disk related to Rayleigh resolution?
faq.a: The Rayleigh criterion takes the limit for distinguishing two points as the separation at which the center of one point image lies on the first dark ring of the other. The resolvable angle is therefore 1.22λ/D, the same as the Airy disk radius.

faq.q: How does the Airy disk change when you stop down?
faq.a: A smaller aperture makes the Airy disk larger. Its radius is proportional to the F-number, so going from F8 to F16 doubles it. Even though aberrations decrease, diffraction blur increases, so stopping down too far makes the image softer.

偏光.desc: The direction in which light's electric field oscillates and how it changes. Depending on the amplitudes and phase difference of two orthogonal components, light is linearly, circularly or elliptically polarized.

about.p: Light is a transverse wave whose electric field oscillates perpendicular to the direction of travel, and that field is considered as orthogonal x and y components. If the phase difference between the two is 0 or π, the field oscillates in a fixed direction: linear polarization. If the amplitudes are equal and the phase difference is π/2, the tip of the field traces a circle: circular polarization. Any other case is generally elliptical polarization. Light whose polarization changes randomly over short times, like sunlight or light from a bulb, is called unpolarized (natural) light, and a mixture of polarized and unpolarized components is partially polarized. Much laser light is linearly polarized because of Brewster windows in the resonator or the properties of the crystal.

A polarizer passes only the field component in a particular direction, and the transmitted intensity follows Malus's law, I = I₀cos²θ. A wave plate is a birefringent crystal that creates a phase difference between its two axes: a quarter-wave plate turns linear polarization into circular, and a half-wave plate rotates the direction of linear polarization by twice the axis angle. A polarizing beam splitter separates light in two, transmitting p and reflecting s polarization. A Faraday rotator, which rotates polarization with a magnetic field, is a nonreciprocal element whose rotation does not cancel on a round trip, and combined with polarizers it forms an optical isolator. The action of elements is calculated with Jones matrices, or with Mueller matrices when partial polarization is included.

Polarization plays an important role in many optical technologies. Reflectance differs for s and p polarization, and at Brewster's angle the p reflection vanishes, which is used for laser windows and for sorting polarizations. Silicon waveguides guide TE and TM very differently, so handling light of undefined polarization arriving from a fiber requires polarization splitting and rotating elements. Coherent optical communication doubles capacity with polarization multiplexing, carrying separate signals on two orthogonal polarizations, and tracks polarization fluctuations with signal processing at the receiver. Polarization is also used in liquid-crystal displays, 3D movies, stress visualization (photoelasticity) and polarization cameras.

faq.q: What is the difference between linear and circular polarization?
faq.a: In linear polarization the field oscillates in a fixed direction, and the two orthogonal components have a phase difference of 0 or π. In circular polarization, two components of equal amplitude are superposed with a π/2 offset, and the field direction rotates at a constant rate. A quarter-wave plate converts one into the other.

faq.q: Is natural light unpolarized?
faq.a: Sunlight and light from bulbs change their polarization randomly over very short times and, on average, have no particular polarization: they are unpolarized. Passed through a polarizer, their intensity is cut exactly in half regardless of the polarizer's orientation.

faq.q: How is polarization represented?
faq.a: Fully polarized light is represented by a Jones vector listing the complex amplitudes of the x and y components, and the action of elements is calculated with 2×2 Jones matrices. When partial polarization is included, Stokes parameters and Mueller matrices are used, and states can be plotted on the Poincaré sphere.

ブリュースター角.desc: The angle of incidence at which the reflectance for p-polarized light is zero, with tanθB = n₂/n₁. About 56° from air into glass (1.5). The reflected light is purely s-polarized.

about.h: The angle at which p-polarized reflection vanishes
about.p: When light strikes a boundary obliquely, the angle of incidence at which the reflectance of p-polarized light, which oscillates in the plane of incidence, becomes exactly zero is Brewster's angle θB, with tanθB = n₂/n₁. At this angle the reflected and refracted rays are exactly perpendicular to each other. The electrons in the second medium oscillate along exactly the direction the reflected ray would travel, and since an oscillating dipole radiates nothing along its axis, no p-polarized reflected light is produced at all. The angle is named after Brewster, who found the relation around 1815.

Brewster's angle is about 56.3° from air into glass (n = 1.5), about 53.1° into water (n = 1.33), and about 74° into silicon at 1550 nm (n ≈ 3.48). Going the other way, from glass into air, it is about 33.7°, smaller than the critical angle of about 41.8°; Brewster's angle always comes before the critical angle. At Brewster's angle from air into glass, s-polarized reflectance is not zero but about 15%. So for unpolarized input the reflected light is purely s-polarized, while the transmitted light is only partially polarized, with plenty of s-polarized light remaining.

Brewster's angle is a different angle from the critical angle for total internal reflection. Total internal reflection occurs only for light incident from the higher-index side, but Brewster's angle exists for incidence from either side. Also, only p-polarized reflection vanishes; for ordinary dielectrics there is no angle at which s-polarized reflectance is zero. In strongly absorbing materials such as metals, p-polarized reflectance becomes small but never reaches zero, and the angle of the minimum is called the pseudo-Brewster angle. The statement that all light is transmitted at Brewster's angle is correct only for p-polarized light.

Tilting the windows of a gas laser's discharge tube to Brewster's angle lets p-polarized light make round trips without loss, while s-polarized light loses some power to reflection at every window, so the output is linearly polarized. Crystals such as titanium sapphire are cut with Brewster-angle end faces for the same reason: to keep losses low without anti-reflection coatings. Glare from water and roads is mostly s-polarized (horizontal oscillation), so polarizing sunglasses with a vertical transmission axis reduce it. Stacking several glass plates at Brewster's angle makes a simple polarizer that increases the degree of polarization of the transmitted light.

faq.q: How do you calculate Brewster's angle?
faq.a: With n₁ the index on the incident side and n₂ on the other side, use tanθB = n₂/n₁. From air into glass (1.5), tanθB = 1.5, giving about 56.3°. The angle is measured from the normal, not from the surface.

faq.q: What is the difference between Brewster's angle and the critical angle?
faq.a: Brewster's angle is where p-polarized reflectance becomes zero, tanθB = n₂/n₁; the critical angle is where total internal reflection begins, sinθc = n₂/n₁. The critical angle exists only for incidence from the higher-index side, whereas Brewster's angle exists for incidence from either side.

faq.q: What is the polarization of light reflected at Brewster's angle?
faq.a: Since p-polarized reflection vanishes, only s-polarized light, oscillating perpendicular to the plane of incidence, is reflected. The transmitted light, however, is partially polarized and still contains s-polarized light, so getting highly polarized transmitted light requires a stack of many plates.

波長板.desc: A plate that uses birefringence to create a phase difference between two orthogonal polarizations. A quarter-wave plate turns linear polarization into circular, and a half-wave plate rotates the polarization direction.

about.h: How a phase difference is produced
about.p: A wave plate is a birefringent plate in which the polarization components along two orthogonal axes (the slow and fast axes) see different refractive indices, so they emerge with a phase difference. A plate of thickness d and birefringence Δn produces a retardance Γ = 2πΔn·d/λ. Γ = π/2 makes a quarter-wave plate and π makes a half-wave plate, corresponding to path differences of one quarter and one half of a wavelength between the two components. Materials include quartz, mica, MgF₂, and stretched polymer films. Ideally a wave plate absorbs no light and changes only the polarization state.

about.h: What quarter- and half-wave plates do
about.p: A half-wave plate turns linear polarization at angle θ from its axis into linear polarization at θ on the opposite side of the axis, rotating the polarization by 2θ. Because the polarization direction can be set freely just by rotating the plate, it is indispensable for adjusting power in combination with a polarizing beam splitter. A quarter-wave plate turns linear polarization at 45° to its axis into circular polarization, and circular polarization into linear. At angles other than 45° the output is elliptical, and polarization parallel to an axis passes unchanged. Passing a quarter-wave plate twice acts like a half-wave plate and rotates the polarization of a round-trip beam by 90°.

about.h: Zero-order versus multi-order plates, and wavelength dependence
about.p: Retardance is inversely proportional to wavelength, so a plate acts as a quarter- or half-wave plate only near its design wavelength. Multi-order plates, thick plates with several extra waves of retardance, are easy to make but sensitive to changes in wavelength and temperature. Ignoring dispersion, a plate with about 10 waves of retardance changes its retardance by about 36° for a 1% wavelength shift, whereas a zero-order quarter-wave plate changes by only about 0.9°. Broad wavelength ranges call for achromatic wave plates that combine two materials, or Fresnel rhombs that use the phase difference of total internal reflection.

In optical disc pickups, a polarizing beam splitter and a quarter-wave plate rotate the polarization of light reflected from the disc by 90° over the round trip, directing it to the detector rather than back to the laser. Polarization controllers for fiber use loops of coiled fiber as wave plates. Circular-polarization glasses for 3D cinema and the compensation films that improve the viewing angle of liquid-crystal displays are also applications of retarders. The axis orientation can be checked by rotating the plate between two crossed polarizers and finding the angle where the transmitted light is darkest.

faq.q: What is the difference between a quarter-wave plate and a half-wave plate?
faq.a: They impose different retardances. A quarter-wave plate gives a quarter wave (π/2) and turns linear polarization at 45° into circular polarization. A half-wave plate gives a half wave (π) and rotates linear polarization while keeping it linear; rotating the plate by θ rotates the polarization by 2θ.

faq.q: How do zero-order and multi-order wave plates differ?
faq.a: A zero-order plate has exactly the design retardance (exactly a quarter wave for a quarter-wave plate), so its retardance shifts little with changes in wavelength, temperature, or angle of incidence. A multi-order plate is thicker, with several extra waves of retardance; it is cheaper but more sensitive to these changes.

faq.q: Can a wave plate be used at any wavelength?
faq.a: No. The retardance Γ = 2πΔn·d/λ is inversely proportional to wavelength, so away from the design wavelength it no longer gives the intended phase difference. For broad wavelength ranges, choose an achromatic wave plate or a Fresnel rhomb.

複屈折.desc: The property of having a refractive index that depends on the direction of polarization. Shown by crystals such as calcite and quartz, it splits light into ordinary and extraordinary rays and is the principle of wave plates.

about.h: Refractive index that depends on polarization
about.p: Birefringence is the property of a material whose refractive index depends on the polarization of the light passing through it; it appears in crystals whose atomic arrangement has a preferred direction. In the simplest case, a uniaxial crystal, the ordinary ray, oscillating perpendicular to the optic axis, sees index no, while the extraordinary ray, oscillating in a plane containing the optic axis, sees an index between no and ne depending on its direction of travel. The birefringence is written Δn = ne − no; crystals with ne > no are positive uniaxial and those with ne < no are negative uniaxial. Crystals with two optic axes are biaxial.

At 589 nm, calcite has no ≈ 1.658 and ne ≈ 1.486, a very large Δn ≈ −0.17, while quartz has no ≈ 1.544 and ne ≈ 1.553, Δn ≈ +0.009. When light enters calcite at an oblique angle to the optic axis, the energy flow of the extraordinary ray deviates from the ordinary ray (walk-off) by up to about 6°. A crystal 10 mm long therefore produces two beams about 1 mm apart, which is used in beam displacers that separate polarizations spatially. Quartz, with its small birefringence, is suited to wave plates whose retardance must be set precisely.

about.h: How it differs from similar effects
about.p: Birefringence is a difference in refractive index and is distinct from dichroism, a difference in absorption. Dichroism is used in polarizers such as polarizing films. No birefringence appears for light traveling along the optic axis or in isotropic media such as glass. Even isotropic materials, however, become birefringent under stress (photoelasticity), which disturbs polarization in molded lenses and clamped windows. Optical fibers also have weak birefringence from slight core ellipticity and bending. A difference in index between left- and right-circular polarization is called circular birefringence, which underlies optical activity and Faraday rotation.

Wave plates, polarizing prisms such as Glan–Taylor and Wollaston prisms, and beam displacers use birefringence directly. In nonlinear optics, birefringence is used for phase matching, equalizing the refractive indices of the fundamental and the harmonic. Liquid-crystal displays switch brightness by using voltage to reorient the liquid-crystal molecules and so control the phase difference from birefringence. Polarization-maintaining fibers hold polarization by building in a large birefringence, on the order of 10⁻⁴, with stress-applying parts. Viewing a transparent molded part between polarizers reveals birefringence from residual stress as colored fringes, which is also used for quality inspection.

faq.q: What is the difference between the ordinary and extraordinary rays?
faq.a: The ordinary ray is the component oscillating perpendicular to the optic axis; it sees the same index no in every direction and obeys Snell's law. The extraordinary ray oscillates in a plane containing the optic axis; its index depends on direction, and it can travel in a direction that departs from Snell's law.

faq.q: What is the difference between positive and negative uniaxial crystals?
faq.a: A crystal is positive if the extraordinary index ne is larger than the ordinary index no, and negative if it is smaller. Quartz is positive (Δn ≈ +0.009) and calcite is negative (Δn ≈ −0.17). The distinction matters in wave plate design because it determines which axis is the slow axis.

faq.q: How is the size of birefringence expressed?
faq.a: As the index difference Δn, a dimensionless number. After a plate of thickness d the path difference is Δn·d, and dividing by the wavelength gives the retardance in waves. For stress birefringence in glass, the path difference is sometimes given in nm/cm.

ジョーンズ行列.desc: A method that represents polarization by the complex amplitudes of the x and y components (the Jones vector) and calculates the action of polarizing elements with 2×2 matrices. It handles fully polarized light.

about.p: Jones calculus is a method for calculating polarization proposed by R. C. Jones in 1941. The x and y components of the electric field are represented as a pair of complex numbers carrying amplitude and phase (the Jones vector), and elements such as polarizers and wave plates are represented by 2×2 complex matrices. For example, horizontal linear polarization is (1, 0) and linear polarization at 45° is (1, 1)/√2. Multiplying the matrices from right to left in the order the light passes through the elements gives the output polarization. The intensity is the sum of the squared magnitudes of the two components.

about.h: Common matrices and a worked example
about.p: A horizontal polarizer is [[1, 0], [0, 0]], and a polarizer with its transmission axis at angle θ is [[cos²θ, sinθcosθ], [sinθcosθ, sin²θ]]. Passing horizontal polarization (1, 0) through a polarizer at 30° gives an intensity of cos²30° = 0.75, in agreement with Malus's law for polarizers. A quarter-wave plate with a horizontal fast axis is [[1, 0], [0, i]], ignoring an overall phase factor, and applying it twice gives [[1, 0], [0, −1]], a half-wave plate. The matrix of an element rotated by θ is obtained by sandwiching its matrix between rotation matrices as R(−θ)·M·R(θ).

about.h: How it differs from Mueller matrices
about.p: Jones calculus, however, can handle only fully polarized light with a fixed phase relationship. Unpolarized or partially polarized light requires Stokes parameters, defined by averaged intensities, and 4×4 real Mueller matrices. Conversely, because Jones calculus keeps the phase of the field, it can handle calculations such as superposing two beams inside an interferometer. One thing to watch out for is differing conventions: writing the wave's phase as exp(i(kz − ωt)) or as exp(i(ωt − kz)) flips the sign of i, and this swaps the identification of right- and left-handed circular polarization.

about.h: Uses in optical communications and optical design
about.p: Polarization changes in an optical fiber can be represented as the product of many matrices for short sections whose birefringence axis and magnitude vary randomly, and this is used to analyze polarization mode dispersion. One measurement method, Jones matrix eigenanalysis, derives the differential group delay from the eigenvalues of Jones matrices measured at two closely spaced wavelengths. Digital coherent receivers separate polarization-multiplexed signals, which send independent data on two polarizations, by estimating the inverse of the fiber's Jones matrix at the receiver. Jones calculus is also used to trace polarization in the design of liquid-crystal displays and polarization cameras.

faq.q: What is the difference between Jones and Mueller matrices?
faq.a: Jones matrices are 2×2 complex matrices that act on the electric field of fully polarized light with a fixed phase relationship. Mueller matrices are 4×4 real matrices that act on Stokes parameters; they can handle unpolarized and partially polarized light but carry no information on the phase of the field.

faq.q: In what order are Jones matrices multiplied?
faq.a: Place the matrix of the first element the light meets immediately to the left of the Jones vector, and multiply leftward in the order the light passes. The matrices of polarization elements generally do not commute, so changing the order changes the result.

faq.q: How do you find the matrix of a rotated wave plate or polarizer?
faq.a: Sandwich its matrix M for an axis along x between rotation matrices R(θ), as R(−θ)·M·R(θ). This means rotating the coordinates to align with the element's axis, applying it, and rotating back. The sign convention for rotation differs between sources, so check it.

ファラデー回転子.desc: An element that rotates polarization in a magneto-optic material inside a magnetic field. It is nonreciprocal: the sense of rotation does not depend on the direction of travel, so the rotation doubles over a round trip.

about.p: The Faraday effect, discovered by Faraday in 1845, is the rotation of the direction of linearly polarized light traveling parallel to a magnetic field through a material. The magnetic field makes the refractive indices for right- and left-circular polarization slightly different, so the linear polarization formed by combining them rotates. The sense of rotation is set by the direction of the magnetic field, not by the direction of travel of the light. Light reflected back by a mirror is therefore rotated further in the same sense as on the way out, and the rotation doubles over the round trip. This nonreciprocity is the defining feature of a Faraday rotator.

The rotation angle is θ = VBL, where V is the Verdet constant, B is the magnetic flux density along the direction of travel, and L is the length of the material. The Verdet constant varies greatly with material and wavelength and is generally larger at shorter wavelengths. When V is given in rad/(T·m), convert 45° to about 0.785 rad for the calculation. From the visible to the 1 µm band, crystals of terbium gallium garnet (TGG), which has a large Verdet constant, are used in the strong field of permanent magnets. In the 1.3 to 1.55 µm telecom bands, bismuth-substituted magnetic garnet films reach 45° of rotation at a thickness of a few hundred micrometers with their magnetization saturated.

about.h: How it differs from optical activity and wave plates
about.p: Optical activity in quartz or sugar solution also rotates polarization, but it is reciprocal: light reflected back through the material has its rotation undone and returns to the original polarization. Rotation of polarization by a half-wave plate is likewise reciprocal. Only a Faraday rotator adds the rotations of the two passes, so it can tell the forward and backward directions apart. A common mistake is to think of the rotation as, say, clockwise relative to the direction of travel; in fact the sense of Faraday rotation is fixed relative to the magnetic field in the laboratory frame. Reversing the field reverses the rotation.

The main applications of Faraday rotators are optical isolators, combined with polarizers, and optical circulators, which route light entering each port to a designated output port. A Faraday rotator mirror, combining a 45° rotator with a mirror, returns light with polarization orthogonal to the input, cancelling the effect of birefringence in the fiber traversed in both directions; it is used in fiber sensors and interferometers. Fiber-optic current sensors, which wind fiber around a conductor and measure the Faraday rotation caused by the current's magnetic field, are used for measurements in electrical substations.

faq.q: What is the difference between Faraday rotation and optical activity?
faq.a: Faraday rotation is caused by a magnetic field and is nonreciprocal, with its sense set by the field, so the rotation doubles over a round trip. Optical activity comes from the structure of the material itself and is reciprocal, so a round trip undoes the rotation and restores the original polarization.

faq.q: How do you calculate the rotation angle of a Faraday rotator?
faq.a: Use θ = VBL (Verdet constant V, flux density B, length L). When V is in rad/(T·m), work in radians, not degrees; 45°, for example, is about 0.785 rad. The Verdet constant changes strongly with wavelength, so use its value at the operating wavelength.

faq.q: What is a Faraday rotator mirror?
faq.a: A device with a mirror placed behind a 45° Faraday rotator. The polarization rotates by 90° over the round trip, so the returning light is polarized orthogonally to the input. The birefringence of the fiber in between cancels between the outward and return paths, allowing interferometers that stay stable even when polarization fluctuates.

光アイソレータ.desc: An element that passes light in only one direction. Combining polarizers with a 45° Faraday rotator, it blocks back-reflected light and keeps lasers stable.

about.p: An optical isolator passes light in one direction only and blocks light traveling in the opposite direction. When part of a laser's output reflects from a fiber end or a lens back into the cavity, lasing becomes unstable in several ways, causing intensity noise, linewidth broadening, and mode hopping. Semiconductor lasers are especially sensitive to back-reflection, and even a slight reflection can affect their output. In optical amplifiers, they also prevent amplified back-reflections from causing unwanted oscillation. For these reasons, isolators are built into narrow-linewidth lasers, telecom transmitters, fiber lasers, and EDFAs.

about.h: How it works and how much it blocks
about.p: The basic configuration is an input polarizer, a Faraday rotator that rotates polarization by 45°, and an output polarizer tilted at 45°. Forward light is rotated and passes straight through the output polarizer. Backward light passes the output polarizer and is then rotated another 45° in the same sense by the Faraday rotator, so at the input it is orthogonal to the polarizer and is blocked. Isolation is given in dB; 30 dB reduces back-reflected light to 1/1000. If the rotation is off from 45° by just 1°, isolation is limited to about 35 dB, so changes in rotation with temperature and wavelength set the performance limit, and two stages are cascaded when higher isolation is needed.

The configuration above is the polarization-dependent type, for input light with a known linear polarization, and is used with free-space lasers. Because the polarization of light in a fiber is not fixed, fiber isolators use the polarization-independent type. Instead of polarizers, birefringent wedges or displacer plates split the light into two polarizations, each is rotated by the Faraday rotator, and the two are recombined; backward light is directed away from the core of the input fiber and does not couple into it. A quarter-wave plate with a polarizing beam splitter can also separate return light, but it cannot block reflections that scramble polarization and is not a true isolator.

A device that sends blocked return light to another output port instead of discarding it is an optical circulator, used to separate transmission and reception on a single fiber or to extract the light reflected by a fiber Bragg grating. The performance of an isolator is described by its isolation together with its forward insertion loss, usable wavelength range, and power handling. On silicon photonics chips, magneto-optic materials are hard to build onto the same substrate, so integrating isolators remains a major challenge, and approaches such as bonding magnetic garnet are being studied.

faq.q: Why do lasers need optical isolators?
faq.a: Because back-reflected light entering a laser disturbs the cavity conditions and causes intensity noise, linewidth broadening, and wavelength hops. Semiconductor lasers and narrow-linewidth lasers are especially sensitive, so an isolator is placed right after the output to block return light.

faq.q: What does 30 dB of isolation mean?
faq.a: It means light entering in the reverse direction is reduced to 1/1000 of its power; 40 dB means 1/10000. When higher isolation is needed, two isolators are cascaded. Low forward insertion loss is required at the same time.

faq.q: What is the difference between an optical isolator and a circulator?
faq.a: An isolator blocks and discards light traveling in the reverse direction, whereas a circulator routes that light to another port where it can be used. Both rely on the nonreciprocity of a Faraday rotator, and circulators are used for tasks such as separating transmitted and received signals.

誘導放出.desc: The process in which a photon arriving at an excited atom causes it to emit a photon with the same frequency, phase, direction and polarization. It is the amplification principle of lasers.

about.h: The origin of the word laser
about.p: Stimulated emission occurs when a photon whose energy equals the difference between two levels meets an atom or molecule in the upper level: prompted by that photon, the atom drops to the lower level and emits a photon with the same frequency, phase, direction, and polarization as the incoming one. Einstein predicted its existence in 1917 from the conditions for matter to be in equilibrium with thermal radiation. Since one photon becomes two, the light is amplified, and this is the origin of the name laser (Light Amplification by Stimulated Emission of Radiation).

about.h: Relation to absorption and spontaneous emission
about.p: The probability of stimulated emission is proportional to the intensity of the incident light and is described by the Einstein B coefficient. Ignoring degeneracy, the coefficients for absorption and stimulated emission are equal, so which wins is decided by the populations of the upper and lower levels. Meanwhile, the ratio of the spontaneous emission coefficient A to B is proportional to the cube of frequency. In thermal-equilibrium radiation, the ratio of stimulated to spontaneous emission is 1/(exp(hν/kT) − 1): about 10⁻²¹ at 300 K for 1 µm light, but about 6000 for 1 GHz microwaves. Spontaneous emission becoming stronger at shorter wavelengths is one reason the maser was realized before the laser.

In stimulated emission, the incoming photon is not absorbed and split in two; it stays as it is, and one more photon in the same state is added. Nor does stimulated emission always increase the light. Atoms in the lower level absorb light with the same probability, so net amplification occurs only with a population inversion, where more atoms are in the upper level. Spontaneous emission continues even with an inversion. This spontaneous emission seeds laser oscillation, but when amplified it becomes noise (ASE) and sets the noise figure of optical amplifiers.

about.h: Gain design and uses beyond lasers
about.p: The amount of amplification is expressed by the gain coefficient g = σΔN, the product of the stimulated emission cross section σ and the population inversion ΔN. This relation is fundamental to the design of solid-state lasers, fiber amplifiers, and semiconductor optical amplifiers. Stimulated emission is also used in microscopy: in STED microscopy, a doughnut-shaped beam drives excited fluorescent molecules at the edge of the focus back down by stimulated emission, switching off their fluorescence so that only a region smaller than the diffraction limit glows. EDFAs in optical communications also amplify signals by stimulated emission from erbium ions.

faq.q: What is the difference between stimulated and spontaneous emission?
faq.a: Spontaneous emission is the emission of a photon by an atom in the upper level without any trigger, with random direction and phase. Stimulated emission is triggered by an incoming photon, and the emitted photon has the same frequency, phase, direction, and polarization as the incoming one. LED light comes mainly from spontaneous emission.

faq.q: Does stimulated emission alone amplify light?
faq.a: No. Absorption by atoms in the lower level occurs with the same probability, so a population inversion, with more atoms in the upper level than the lower, is required. In thermal equilibrium the lower level is more populated, so the inversion is created by pumping.

faq.q: Who predicted stimulated emission?
faq.a: Einstein predicted it in 1917 by considering the equilibrium between matter and thermal radiation. Absorption and spontaneous emission alone could not reproduce Planck's radiation law, so stimulated emission had to be added. The laser was realized in 1960.

反転分布.desc: A state in which more atoms occupy the upper level than the lower. It does not occur in thermal equilibrium and is created by pumping. It is the condition for light to be amplified by stimulated emission rather than absorbed.

about.p: A population inversion is a state in which the number of atoms N₂ in the upper of two levels exceeds the number N₁ in the lower level (N₂/g₂ > N₁/g₁ when degeneracy is included). In thermal equilibrium, populations follow the Boltzmann distribution N₂/N₁ = exp(−ΔE/kT), so the lower level is always more populated and light is absorbed as it passes. With an inversion, stimulated emission outweighs absorption and passing light is amplified. Formally it corresponds to a Boltzmann distribution with a negative temperature, so it is sometimes called a negative-temperature state.

In a system with only two levels, optical excitation balances absorption against stimulated emission and only brings N₂ toward N₁. Lasers therefore use three- or four-level systems, in which atoms excited to a higher level drop quickly to the upper laser level. In a three-level system such as ruby, the ground state is the lower laser level, so more than half the atoms must be pumped up. In a four-level system such as Nd:YAG, the lower level empties quickly, so an inversion forms with only slight excitation. Materials with a long upper-level lifetime store energy more easily: about 230 µs for Nd:YAG and about 10 ms for erbium in silica.

Having an inversion alone does not make a laser oscillate. The gain over one round trip of the cavity must exceed the losses from mirror transmission and internal loss, and the inversion at that point is called the threshold inversion. Even if pumping increases above threshold, in steady state the inversion stays nearly fixed at the threshold value (gain clamping), and the extra pumping is converted into output light. Q-switching keeps the loss high to prevent oscillation, stores an inversion far above threshold, and then releases it all at once.

about.h: Inversion in semiconductors and optical amplifiers
about.p: In semiconductor lasers, what is inverted is not atomic levels but electrons in the conduction band and holes in the valence band. When injected current makes the separation of the electron and hole quasi-Fermi levels larger than the band gap, light with energies between them is amplified (the Bernard–Duraffourg condition). In optical amplifiers, incomplete inversion affects the amount of noise; an EDFA's noise figure approaches the quantum limit of about 3 dB only when the inversion is nearly complete. Pumping methods include flash lamps, semiconductor lasers, electrical discharges, and current injection.

faq.q: Why can't a population inversion occur in thermal equilibrium?
faq.a: Because in thermal equilibrium populations follow the Boltzmann distribution N₂/N₁ = exp(−ΔE/kT), so higher-energy levels are always less populated. However high the temperature, N₂ only approaches N₁; the upper level never becomes more populated.

faq.q: What is the difference between three-level and four-level lasers?
faq.a: In a three-level system, the lower laser level is the ground state, so more than half the atoms must be excited to reach inversion. In a four-level system, the lower level lies above the ground state and empties quickly, so inversion forms with little excitation and the threshold is easier to keep low.

faq.q: How is a population inversion created in a semiconductor laser?
faq.a: Forward current through the pn junction injects electrons and holes into the active layer. When the quasi-Fermi level separation exceeds the band gap, the medium has gain for light, and the current at which that gain exceeds the cavity loss is the threshold current.

縦モード.desc: An oscillation frequency at which the round-trip optical path of a resonator is an integer number of wavelengths. The spacing is c/(2nL), wider for shorter resonators.

about.p: In a laser resonator, only light for which the round-trip optical path 2nL is a whole number of wavelengths returns in phase on every round trip and builds up. The frequencies that satisfy this condition, νq = qc/(2nL) with q an integer, are the longitudinal modes. The integer q is very large: about 950,000 for a 30 cm He-Ne laser at 632.8 nm. The spacing between adjacent longitudinal modes is c/(2nL), which becomes narrower as the cavity gets longer. When the medium is dispersive, the group index is used in place of n.

The number of longitudinal modes that actually lase depends on how many fit inside the gain bandwidth. A 30 cm He-Ne laser has a mode spacing of about 500 MHz, so around three modes fit within the neon gain width (about 1.5 GHz). A 10 m fiber laser (n = 1.45) has a spacing of only about 10 MHz, so a very large number of modes can lase. Conversely, in a vertical-cavity surface-emitting laser (VCSEL), with a cavity only a few micrometers long, the mode spacing exceeds the gain width and there is a single longitudinal mode.

about.h: How they differ from transverse modes
about.p: Longitudinal modes are standing waves along the direction of propagation and set the lasing frequencies. Transverse modes (TEMmn), by contrast, describe the shape and pattern of the intensity profile across the beam. The phrase single-mode laser is used both for one transverse mode (TEM00) and for one longitudinal mode (single frequency), so care is needed about which is meant. With several longitudinal modes, a detector sees beat notes at the mode spacing, mode hops occur when temperature suddenly switches the lasing mode, and the coherence length of the light becomes shorter.

about.h: Achieving a single longitudinal mode, and using many
about.p: Applications that need a single frequency restrict lasing to a single longitudinal mode. Common methods include DFB and DBR lasers with gratings built into the cavity, an intracavity etalon that transmits only a particular mode, and ring resonators that avoid spatial hole burning. The longitudinal-mode content can be examined with a scanning Fabry–Perot interferometer or by the beat frequencies seen on a fast photodetector. Conversely, locking the phases of many longitudinal modes produces ultrashort pulses by mode locking, and the resulting spectrum then forms an evenly spaced optical frequency comb.

faq.q: How do you calculate longitudinal mode spacing?
faq.a: The frequency spacing is Δν = c/(2nL), where L is the cavity length and n is the refractive index (the group index if the medium is dispersive). To convert to wavelength spacing, use Δλ = λ²Δν/c. For a 30 cm cavity in air, for example, the spacing is about 500 MHz.

faq.q: What is the difference between longitudinal and transverse modes?
faq.a: Longitudinal modes are standing waves along the cavity axis and set the lasing frequencies and their spacing. Transverse modes are the shapes of the intensity profile across the beam (TEM00, TEM01, and so on) and set how the beam spreads and how well it focuses. The two must be selected separately.

faq.q: How do you make a laser oscillate on a single longitudinal mode?
faq.a: Methods include shortening the cavity so the mode spacing exceeds the gain width, selecting the wavelength with a grating as in DFB and DBR lasers, and inserting an etalon that passes only one mode. Such lasers are used in measurement and communications that need a narrow linewidth and a long coherence length.

ガウシアンビーム.desc: The basic form of laser light, whose cross-sectional intensity follows a Gaussian distribution. Its propagation is set by the waist radius w₀ and the Rayleigh range πw₀²/λ.

about.h: The shape of a Gaussian beam
about.p: The fundamental transverse mode (TEM00) of many lasers has a Gaussian intensity profile, I(r) = I₀ exp(−2r²/w²). Here w is the beam radius, at which the intensity falls to 1/e² (about 13.5%) of its center value. The radius changes with propagation as w(z) = w₀√(1 + (z/zR)²), and the narrowest point is called the beam waist (radius w₀). zR = πw₀²/λ is the Rayleigh range; at a distance zR from the waist, the radius has grown by √2. A Gaussian beam is a special solution that spreads by diffraction without changing shape, and after passing through a lens it remains a Gaussian beam with a different waist.

Far enough from the waist, the beam radius grows in proportion to distance, with a half-angle θ = λ/(πw₀). The narrower the waist, the greater the divergence, so that w₀θ = λ/π stays constant.
