faq.a: From the round-trip time t, using z = ct/(2n_g). With a group index of 1.468, a signal after 10 µs comes from about 1.02 km away. If the group index setting is off, the displayed distance is off by the same ratio.

faq.q: What is an OTDR dead zone?
faq.a: The stretch just after a strong reflection, such as a connector, where the receiver is saturated or recovering and the trace cannot be measured correctly. Shorter pulses narrow it. To measure near the start of a fiber, a launch (dummy) fiber is inserted in between.

faq.q: Why does the trace sometimes rise at a splice?
faq.a: If the fiber after the splice backscatters more strongly (for example because its mode field diameter is smaller), the scattered light increases and looks like a gain. Measuring from both directions and averaging gives the true splice loss.

LiDAR.desc: A technique that illuminates objects with laser light and measures their distance and shape from the reflections. Methods include ToF, which times pulse round trips, and FMCW, which uses frequency sweeps.

about.p: The ToF method sends a short pulse and finds the distance from the time t until the reflection returns, using d = ct/2. For an object 200 m away the round trip takes about 1.33 µs, and a time resolution of 0.1 ns corresponds to about 1.5 cm of distance. The FMCW method emits light whose frequency is swept linearly and finds the distance from the beat frequency between the returning light and the transmitted light. Its range resolution is set by the sweep bandwidth B as c/(2B), about 7.5 cm for 2 GHz. FMCW also gives velocity at the same time from the Doppler shift.

When a diffuse target with reflectance ρ is larger than the beam, the received light is roughly the transmitted power times ρA/(πR²), where A is the receiving aperture area and R the distance. For ρ = 0.1, a 25 mm aperture and 100 m, this is about 1.6×10⁻⁹, about 88 dB weaker. Doubling the distance cuts the received light to a quarter (−6 dB). To detect this weak light against sunlight, ToF systems use sensitive detectors such as APDs or SPADs with narrow wavelength filters, while FMCW systems use amplification by the local oscillator (coherent detection).

about.h: Choosing the wavelength, and eye safety
about.p: The 905 nm region has the advantage of inexpensive silicon detectors and SPADs, but because this wavelength reaches the retina, eye-safety limits strictly restrict the power that can be emitted. Light near 1550 nm is absorbed by water in the cornea and lens and hardly reaches the retina, so the allowed exposure is much larger and longer ranges are easier. It needs detectors such as InGaAs, however, and absorption by water in rain and fog is greater. At either wavelength, products are usually designed to stay within Class 1 (safe under normal use).

Measuring the distance to a single point does not reveal shape, so the beam is scanned to build a point cloud. The direction can be changed by rotating mechanical heads, MEMS mirrors or optical phased arrays (OPAs), or a flash system can illuminate a wide area and measure it all at once with a detector array. LiDAR is used in automated driving and driver assistance, robots, surveying and terrain mapping, and 3D measurement of buildings, and smartphones carry short-range ToF sensors. Its wavelength is much shorter than radar's, so it resolves finer shapes, but it tends to suffer more in rain and fog.

faq.q: What is the difference between ToF and FMCW LiDAR?
faq.a: ToF finds distance from the round-trip time of a pulse; FMCW finds it from the beat frequency of frequency-swept light. FMCW resists background light and can measure velocity, but needs a narrow-linewidth laser that sweeps linearly and more signal processing.

faq.q: What determines LiDAR range resolution?
faq.a: For ToF it is the time resolution or pulse width, cΔt/2 (about 1.5 cm for 0.1 ns). For FMCW it is the frequency sweep width B, c/(2B) (about 15 cm for 1 GHz). Averaging many measurements can make the precision finer than the resolution.

faq.q: Should LiDAR use 905 nm or 1550 nm?
faq.a: 905 nm works with inexpensive silicon detectors, but its output is limited by eye safety. 1550 nm hardly reaches the retina, so higher power and longer range are possible, but the detectors cost more and absorption by water is larger.

OCT.desc: Optical coherence tomography: interferometry using the short coherence length of broadband light to image the depth structure of tissue with micrometer-level resolution.

about.p: OCT splits broadband light into a reference arm and a sample arm, and interferes the light returning from each depth of the sample with the reference to line up reflection strength along the depth direction. Broadband light has a short coherence length, so only reflections whose path difference falls within it interfere, letting depth be resolved finely. A depth difference of 1 µm gives a round-trip time difference of only about 7 fs, too short to separate by timing pulses electronically, so OCT measures path difference by interference. It resembles ultrasound imaging but uses light instead of sound.

For a Gaussian spectrum, the axial resolution in air is Δz = (2 ln2/π)λ²/Δλ ≈ 0.44λ²/Δλ, finer for broader bandwidth and shorter center wavelength. A center of 1050 nm with 100 nm width gives about 4.9 µm, and 1310 nm with 50 nm gives about 15 µm; in tissue these are divided by the refractive index (about 1.35 to 1.4). Because scattering is strong, the depth that can be imaged in tissue is roughly 1 to 2 mm. Lateral resolution is set by the focusing of the objective lens, independently of the axial resolution.

Early time-domain OCT scanned depth by moving the reference mirror. Today's mainstream Fourier-domain OCT keeps the reference fixed and divides into SD-OCT, which measures the spectrum of the interference light with a spectrometer, and SS-OCT, which uses a rapidly wavelength-swept source and a single detector. Fourier transforming the fringes in the spectrum gives all depths at once, which greatly improved speed and sensitivity. The maximum depth is set by the spectral resolution δλ as about λ²/(4δλ); at 1310 nm with δλ = 0.1 nm it is about 4.3 mm in air.

OCT is most widespread in ophthalmology, where it images retinal layer thickness and macular disease without contact at a resolution of a few micrometers. The retina is imaged in the 800 nm and 1050 nm bands, where water absorption is low, and strongly scattering skin and blood vessels in the 1310 nm band, which penetrates deeper. Intravascular OCT, with an optical fiber in a catheter, views the inner wall of coronary arteries, and OCT angiography visualizes blood flow. In industry, OCT is used for non-destructive internal measurements such as the thickness of coatings and multilayer films, and semiconductor inspection.

faq.q: What determines the axial resolution of OCT?
faq.a: The spectral width of the source: for a Gaussian spectrum, Δz ≈ 0.44λ²/Δλ in air. Broader bandwidth and shorter center wavelength give finer resolution, and in tissue the value is further divided by the refractive index. The objective's numerical aperture sets the lateral, not the axial, resolution.

faq.q: How does OCT differ from ultrasound imaging?
faq.a: OCT uses optical interference, and its resolution of a few to about fifteen micrometers is more than ten times finer than common diagnostic ultrasound, but scattering limits the imaging depth in tissue to about 1 to 2 mm. Ultrasound reaches depths of several centimeters or more.

faq.q: What is the difference between SD-OCT and SS-OCT?
faq.a: Both are Fourier-domain OCT. SD-OCT measures the whole spectrum at once with a broadband source and a spectrometer; SS-OCT measures it in time sequence with a rapidly swept source and a single detector. SS-OCT suits longer wavelengths and deeper ranges.

第2高調波発生.desc: The second-order nonlinear optical process that produces light at twice the frequency, 2ω (half the wavelength), from light at frequency ω. Abbreviated SHG.

about.p: A material's polarization is proportional to the field for weak light, but for intense light higher-order terms appear: P = ε₀(χ⁽¹⁾E + χ⁽²⁾E² + …). The square E² of a field at frequency ω contains a component oscillating at 2ω, which radiates new light: the second harmonic. In terms of photons, two photons at ω produce one photon at 2ω. Because χ⁽²⁾ exists only in crystals lacking inversion symmetry, nonlinear optical crystals such as LiNbO₃, KTP, BBO and LBO are used. In centrosymmetric materials such as glass and silicon, it does not occur in the bulk.

For the second harmonic generated at each point in the crystal to add up, the polarization driven by the fundamental and the generated second harmonic must stay in phase through the crystal. Because of dispersion, generally n(2ω) ≠ n(ω), so on its own the SH builds up and cancels repeatedly over each coherence length (a few to tens of micrometers). Achieving Δk = 0, by birefringent phase matching, which uses birefringence to equalize the indices of waves with different polarizations, or by quasi-phase matching, which periodically reverses the crystal's spontaneous polarization (domain orientation), makes the conversion efficiency grow with the square of crystal length and with fundamental power.

A typical application is the green laser, which makes 532 nm light from a 1064 nm Nd:YAG or fiber laser. Combined with sum-frequency generation, it also yields ultraviolet light at 355 nm or 266 nm, used for fine laser machining and inspection. Its dependence on the square of power is exploited in autocorrelators that measure the width of ultrashort pulses, and in SHG microscopes, which produce signal only near the focus. Because inversion symmetry is broken at surfaces, it also serves as a spectroscopic method that selectively probes interfaces.

faq.q: How is the SHG wavelength calculated?
faq.a: The frequency doubles, so the wavelength is half the fundamental's: 532 nm for 1064 nm, 775 nm for 1550 nm. It follows from energy conservation, ħω + ħω = ħ(2ω).

faq.q: Why does SHG not occur in glass?
faq.a: Because glass is an isotropic material with inversion symmetry, its second-order susceptibility χ⁽²⁾ is zero. It does have a third-order χ⁽³⁾, so the Kerr effect and third-harmonic generation do occur.

faq.q: How can SHG efficiency be raised?
faq.a: With phase matching in place, choose a crystal with a large nonlinear coefficient, use pulses with high peak power, focus the beam, or lengthen the crystal. The efficiency rises in proportion to the fundamental power, and the SH output in proportion to its square.

位相整合.desc: In nonlinear wavelength conversion, making the wavenumber mismatch Δk = 0 so that the generated light and the driving polarization stay in phase through the crystal.

about.h: Why the phases must be kept aligned
about.p: In a nonlinear crystal, the input light creates polarization at every point, from which light at the new frequency is generated bit by bit. For the light generated at each point to add up at the exit, the phase of the driving polarization and that of the light already generated must not drift apart through the crystal. For second-harmonic generation the wavenumber mismatch is Δk = k(2ω) − 2k(ω), which in general is not zero because of dispersion. With Δk ≠ 0, the signal alternately builds up and cancels every coherence length Lc = π/Δk, and a longer crystal gives no more output.

about.h: How phase mismatch affects the output
about.p: Second-harmonic output is proportional to L² sinc²(ΔkL/2), and keeps growing as the square of the crystal length L only when Δk = 0. The output falls to half at |ΔkL| ≈ 2.78, so the longer the crystal, the narrower the allowed deviation (acceptance) in wavelength, angle and temperature, in inverse proportion to L. The coherence length is Lc = λ/(4Δn), where λ is the fundamental wavelength and Δn the index difference between the two waves; at 1064 nm with Δn = 0.01 it is only about 27 µm, so phase matching is essential to use crystals several millimeters long.

The standard method is birefringent phase matching, which uses birefringence to equalize the indices of two waves of different polarization. It can be done by angle, choosing the crystal orientation relative to the optic axis, or by temperature, adjusting the indices thermally, and depending on the polarization combination it is called type I (such as o + o → e) or type II. Angle tuning causes walk-off, in which the energy direction departs from the light's direction, reducing the overlap in long crystals. Noncritical phase matching, tuned by temperature at a 90° orientation, has no walk-off and a wide angular acceptance.

about.h: Other methods and when to use them
about.p: For crystals with small birefringence, or when the polarizations should be the same, quasi-phase matching, which periodically reverses the crystal's spontaneous polarization, is used. In waveguides, modal phase matching adjusts effective indices through mode order and waveguide dimensions. In four-wave mixing, a third-order process, the light's own index change also enters Δk along with dispersion, so efficiency in fiber rises near the zero-dispersion wavelength. In an optical parametric oscillator, selecting the wavelength pair that is phase-matched by changing angle, temperature or period is itself the tuning mechanism.

faq.q: What happens without phase matching?
faq.a: The generated light alternately builds up and cancels every coherence length Lc = π/Δk, so a longer crystal gives no more output. Lc is usually a few to a few tens of micrometers, so the conversion efficiency stays tiny.

faq.q: What is the difference between type I and type II phase matching?
faq.a: In type I the two fundamental photons have the same polarization (for example o + o → e); in type II they have orthogonal polarizations (for example o + e → e). Depending on crystal and wavelength, the phase-matching angle, acceptance and nonlinear coefficient differ.

faq.q: How is phase matching adjusted?
faq.a: In birefringent phase matching, the crystal angle or temperature is set; in quasi-phase matching, the poling period and temperature. In practice, the crystal sits on a rotation or temperature-controlled mount and the point of maximum output is found.

擬似位相整合.desc: A method that reverses the direction of a nonlinear crystal's spontaneous polarization (its ferroelectric domains, and with them the sign of χ⁽²⁾) every coherence length, canceling the phase slip so that conversion continues. Used in PPLN and similar materials.

about.h: Canceling the phase slip by flipping the sign
about.p: Even in a crystal that is not phase-matched, the second harmonic grows up to the coherence length Lc and then starts to fall. Quasi-phase matching reverses the crystal's spontaneous polarization (the sign of χ⁽²⁾) exactly where the decline would begin, putting the phase of the generated light back by π so that growth continues. One period is Λ = 2Lc; in terms of wavenumbers, the grating wavenumber 2π/Λ fills the mismatch, Δk = 2π/Λ. The output grows in steps, rising nearly as the square of the crystal length.

Because the sign alternates, the effective nonlinear coefficient for first-order quasi-phase matching is 2/π times that of true phase matching, and the efficiency (2/π)² ≈ 0.41 times. Third-order quasi-phase matching reduces the efficiency further, to about 0.045 times. Even so, in LiNbO₃ all polarizations can be extraordinary, using the largest coefficient, d₃₃. Since d₃₃ is about five to six times the d₃₁ used in birefringent phase matching, the efficiency advantage is roughly tenfold or more. Typical periods are about 20 µm for second-harmonic generation of 1550 nm and about 7 µm for 1064 nm.

about.h: How PPLN is made, and cautions
about.p: Periodic poling is done by patterning periodic electrodes on a ferroelectric such as LiNbO₃ (PPLN), LiTaO₃ (PPLT) or KTP (PPKTP) and applying a strong electric field to reverse the polarization in aligned domains. A strength of the method is that the period, from a few micrometers to a little over 30 µm, can be chosen freely through the mask design. LiNbO₃ is prone to photorefractive damage, in which visible light changes the refractive index, so MgO-doped crystals operated at elevated temperature are common. Changing the temperature changes the indices and fine-tunes the phase-matched wavelength.

Because it does not rely on birefringence, quasi-phase matching can use the crystal orientation that gives the largest nonlinear coefficient, has no walk-off, and achieves high efficiency in long crystals and waveguides. It is widely used for wavelength conversion in green and other visible lasers, generation of mid-infrared light by optical parametric oscillators, wavelength conversion in the telecom band, and generation of entangled photon pairs in quantum optics. Placing regions of different periods in one crystal, or gradually varying the period (chirping), allows wavelength switching or a broader conversion bandwidth. Combined with thin-film LN waveguides, conversion needs even less power.

faq.q: How is the quasi-phase-matching period chosen?
faq.a: It is twice the coherence length, Λ = 2Lc = 2π/Δk. For second-harmonic generation, Λ = λ/(2Δn), with λ the fundamental wavelength. For second-harmonic generation of 1550 nm in PPLN, about 20 µm is typical, fine-tuned by temperature.

faq.q: Is quasi-phase matching less efficient than true phase matching?
faq.a: For the same nonlinear coefficient, even first order lowers the efficiency to (2/π)² ≈ 0.41 times. In practice, however, it can use the largest coefficient, d₃₃, without walk-off, so it often outperforms birefringent phase matching.

faq.q: What is PPLN?
faq.a: Periodically poled lithium niobate: a LiNbO₃ crystal whose spontaneous polarization (domain orientation) has been periodically reversed by a strong electric field. It is used for wavelength conversion by quasi-phase matching. MgO-doped material is common, to prevent photorefractive damage.

光パラメトリック発振器.desc: A tunable light source that splits pump photons into signal and idler photons in a χ⁽²⁾ crystal and oscillates in a resonator. Abbreviated OPO.

about.h: Splitting photons in two and amplifying
about.p: In the optical parametric process, one pump photon in a χ⁽²⁾ crystal splits into two photons, a signal and an idler. Only pairs that satisfy both energy conservation, ωp = ωs + ωi, and phase matching, kp = ks + ki, are amplified. Pumping at 1064 nm with a 1550 nm signal gives an idler of about 3390 nm, from 1/λi = 1/1064 − 1/1550. At the degenerate point, where signal and idler are equal, both are at twice the pump wavelength, 2128 nm. An OPO places this amplification in a resonator so that it oscillates.

about.h: How it differs from a laser
about.p: The gain of an OPO comes not from a population inversion stored in atomic or molecular levels but from a nonlinear amplification that exists only while pump light is present. The output wavelength is therefore not fixed by energy levels, and it can be tuned continuously, while keeping energy conservation, by changing the crystal angle, temperature or quasi-phase-matching period. The signal and idler are always longer in wavelength than the pump. Each pump photon's energy is divided between the two outputs: pumping at 1064 nm with a 1550 nm signal, about 69% of the photon energy goes to the signal and the rest to the idler.

A singly resonant OPO (SRO), which resonates only the signal or only the idler, runs stably, but in continuous-wave operation its oscillation threshold is high, around a few watts, so pulsed pumping is common. A doubly resonant OPO (DRO), resonating both, has a lower threshold but must satisfy two resonance conditions at once, so its output wavelength and power tend to be unstable. A device without a resonator, amplifying in a single pass with an intense pump, is called an optical parametric amplifier (OPA) and is widely used for wavelength conversion of ultrashort pulses.

OPOs excel in the near- to mid-infrared around 1.5 to 5 µm, where good laser media are scarce. In PPLN, crystal absorption puts the practical limit at about 4 to 5 µm, and longer wavelengths use crystals such as ZGP or quasi-phase-matched GaAs. Applications include mid-infrared spectroscopy, rich in molecular absorption lines, gas detection, medicine and materials processing, and tunable light sources. Even a crystal without a resonator, weakly pumped, yields spontaneously split photon pairs (spontaneous parametric down-conversion), a basic tool of quantum optics as a source of entangled and single photons.

faq.q: How is the idler wavelength of an OPO found?
faq.a: From energy conservation, 1/λi = 1/λp − 1/λs. Pumping at 1064 nm with a 1550 nm signal gives about 3390 nm. Subtracting the wavelengths themselves is wrong; the calculation uses frequencies, the reciprocals of wavelength.

faq.q: How does an OPO differ from a laser?
faq.a: A laser amplifies with a population inversion stored in a medium's levels, and its wavelength is set by those levels. An OPO amplifies nonlinearly without storing energy, and its wavelength is set by phase matching, so changing angle, temperature or period tunes it widely.

faq.q: What wavelength range can an OPO produce?
faq.a: The outputs are always longer in wavelength than the pump. From the visible to the mid-infrared, the range is chosen by the crystal and pump. In PPLN the practical limit is about 4 to 5 µm, and longer mid-infrared wavelengths use crystals such as ZGP.

光カー効果.desc: The third-order nonlinear optical effect in which the refractive index changes in proportion to light intensity, n = n₀ + n₂I. It causes self-phase modulation and self-focusing.

about.h: An index that changes with intensity
about.p: The optical Kerr effect is the change in refractive index in proportion to light intensity, n = n₀ + n₂I, caused by the third-order susceptibility χ⁽³⁾. Because χ⁽³⁾ exists in every material regardless of inversion symmetry, the effect occurs in glass and even in air. In fused silica n₂ is about 2.6×10⁻²⁰ m²/W, so even at 10 GW/cm² (10¹⁴ W/m²) Δn is only about 2.6×10⁻⁶. Still, in light traveling through long fibers or in tightly focused intense pulses, the phase changes accumulate into large effects.

about.h: n₂ in different materials, and response speed
about.p: n₂ is around 5×10⁻¹⁸ m²/W in silicon, more than 100 times silica's, about 10 times silica's in silicon nitride, and about a thousandth of it in air. In fiber, its strength is expressed by the nonlinear coefficient γ = 2πn₂/(λA_eff), about 1.3 /(W·km) at 1550 nm for standard fiber with an 80 µm² effective area. The main part of the Kerr effect is an electronic response faster than a femtosecond, but in silica a Raman response from molecular vibrations adds roughly 20% with a delay, affecting the behavior of ultrashort pulses.

If the intensity is higher at the center of a beam, the index rises there and the medium acts like a convex lens, so the beam narrows itself: self-focusing. Above a critical power (a few megawatts in silica at 800 nm), diffraction can no longer stop it, causing material damage or filaments. In time, the intensity variation turns directly into a phase variation in self-phase modulation; another beam's intensity changes the phase in cross-phase modulation; and light at different frequencies mixes in four-wave mixing. All of these come from the same n₂.

about.h: Difference from the electro-optic Kerr effect, and uses
about.p: The electro-optic Kerr effect, in which the index changes with the square of an applied DC or low-frequency field, also comes from χ⁽³⁾; the one caused by the light's own field is called the optical Kerr effect to distinguish it. It differs from the Pockels effect (χ⁽²⁾), which is proportional to the field, in both its proportionality and the materials in which it occurs. The optical Kerr effect is used in Kerr-lens mode locking of Ti:sapphire lasers, optical solitons in fiber, microresonator frequency combs and supercontinuum generation, while in optical communication it distorts waveforms and sets the upper limit on transmitted power.

faq.q: What are the units and size of the nonlinear index n₂?
faq.a: It is the index change per unit intensity, so it is expressed in m²/W (or cm²/W). Fused silica has about 2.6×10⁻²⁰ m²/W, and silicon more than 100 times that. Values in esu units in older literature must be converted.

faq.q: What is the difference between the optical Kerr effect and the Pockels effect?
faq.a: The optical Kerr effect comes from χ⁽³⁾, is proportional to intensity (the square of the field) and occurs in every material. The Pockels effect comes from χ⁽²⁾, is proportional to the applied field and occurs only in crystals lacking inversion symmetry.

faq.q: Why does self-focusing occur?
faq.a: Intensity is highest at the beam center, where the Kerr effect raises the index, so the medium acts like a convex lens. Above a critical power the focusing overcomes diffraction spreading and continues, causing damage or filaments.

自己位相変調.desc: The phenomenon in which an optical pulse is phase-modulated through the Kerr effect by the time variation of its own intensity, producing a frequency chirp and broadening its spectrum. SPM.

about.h: Phase changed by its own intensity
about.p: When an intense light pulse passes through a medium, the optical Kerr effect makes the index n₀ + n₂I(t) follow the pulse intensity in time, and the phase changes in proportion. In fiber the maximum phase shift is φNL = γP₀L_eff, where P₀ is the peak power. Because of loss, the effective length L_eff is shorter than the actual length; in 0.2 dB/km fiber it can never exceed about 21.7 km. Sending 1 W of peak power through 1 km of fiber with γ = 1.3 /(W·km) gives a φNL of about 1.3 rad.

about.h: Direction and size of spectral broadening
about.p: The instantaneous frequency shift is the time derivative of the phase with its sign reversed, so with n₂ > 0 the front half of the pulse shifts to longer wavelengths and the back half to shorter ones. Because new frequency components are created, the spectrum broadens roughly in proportion to φNL. For a Gaussian pulse, when the maximum phase shift reaches about 1.5π the center of the spectrum dips and it splits into two peaks, and the number of peaks then grows as roughly φNL/π + 1/2. Without dispersion, the temporal intensity profile itself does not change.

The temporal waveform changes only when the chirp from self-phase modulation combines with dispersion. In normal dispersion, the long-wavelength front moves further ahead, so the pulse broadens while acquiring a nearly linear chirp; compressing it with a grating pair or chirped mirrors yields a pulse shorter than the original. In anomalous dispersion, dispersion cancels the chirp, and when the two balance the result is an optical soliton that keeps its shape. Cross-phase modulation, in which another channel's intensity changes the phase, is a further source of degradation in wavelength-division multiplexed transmission.

Self-phase modulation is a basic tool of ultrashort-pulse optics: it broadens the spectrum of ultrashort pulses for compression, produces even broader supercontinuum light, and enables mode locking of fiber lasers. In optical communication, by contrast, raising the power per channel makes the phase change combine with dispersion and distort the waveform, which puts an upper limit on launch power. Power should be raised to lower the impact of noise, but too much power increases nonlinear degradation, and this trade-off determines the optimum launch power.

faq.q: Does self-phase modulation change the pulse shape in time?
faq.a: Not without dispersion. Only the phase and instantaneous frequency change, and the spectrum broadens. In a dispersive fiber, this chirp combines with dispersion so that the pulse broadens or is compressed.

faq.q: What is the difference between self-phase and cross-phase modulation?
faq.a: In self-phase modulation a pulse's own intensity changes its phase; in cross-phase modulation the intensity of another beam traveling through the same medium does. Both come from the optical Kerr effect, and both degrade wavelength-division multiplexed transmission.

faq.q: How is the size of self-phase modulation estimated?
faq.a: In fiber, from the maximum nonlinear phase φNL = γP₀L_eff. With γ = 1.3 /(W·km), 500 mW of peak power and a 3 km effective length, it is about 2.0 rad. Spectral broadening becomes noticeable once φNL exceeds about 1 rad.

ポッケルス効果.desc: The linear electro-optic effect, in which the refractive index of a crystal lacking inversion symmetry changes in proportion to an applied field. Used in LN modulators and electro-optic Q-switches.

about.h: An index that changes in proportion to the field
about.p: The Pockels effect (linear electro-optic effect) is a change in refractive index proportional to an applied electric field E, written Δn = (1/2)n³rE, where r is the electro-optic coefficient. It arises from the second-order susceptibility χ⁽²⁾, so it occurs only in crystals lacking inversion symmetry. In LiNbO₃, r₃₃ is about 31 pm/V and the extraordinary index is about 2.14 at 1550 nm, so a field of 1 V/µm gives Δn ≈ 1.5×10⁻⁴. For 1550 nm light passing through 1 cm, this works out to a phase change of about 6.1 rad.

The voltage needed to change the phase by π is the half-wave voltage Vπ. In the longitudinal geometry, with the field along the light's direction, Vπ does not depend on crystal length, and a KD*P Pockels cell needs several kilovolts at 1064 nm. In the transverse geometry, with the field applied from the side, Vπ falls as the electrode gap narrows and the length grows. Waveguide modulators use this transverse geometry, with electrode gaps narrowed to a few micrometers and lengths of a few millimeters to a few centimeters, so that they run on a few volts. Performance is often compared through the product VπL.

Silicon is a centrosymmetric crystal with no χ⁽²⁾, so normally it cannot use the Pockels effect. Silicon modulators therefore use the carrier dispersion effect, which changes the index through carrier concentration, but the loss changes at the same time and Vπ tends to be large. Research is therefore combining materials that do have a strong Pockels effect, such as thin-film LiNbO₃, barium titanate or electro-optic polymers, with silicon circuits. The Kerr effect (χ⁽³⁾), which is proportional to the square of the field and occurs in silicon too, is a different effect from the Pockels effect and should not be confused with it.

The Pockels effect is an electronic response and extremely fast, so a modulator's bandwidth is set not by the crystal but by electrode loss and the velocity matching between light and microwave. LN modulators for optical communication apply opposite phases to the two arms of a Mach-Zehnder interferometer to modulate intensity or phase, and thin-film LN has achieved bandwidths of several tens of gigahertz and beyond. Pockels cells, which rotate polarization, serve as electro-optic Q-switches in pulsed lasers, as pulse pickers, and for switching light in and out of regenerative amplifiers. Electro-optic sampling, which measures terahertz electric fields, also uses this effect.

faq.q: What is the difference between the Pockels effect and the Kerr effect?
faq.a: The Pockels effect comes from χ⁽²⁾; its index change is proportional to the field, and it occurs only in crystals lacking inversion symmetry. The Kerr effect comes from χ⁽³⁾; it is proportional to the square of the field and occurs in all materials, including glasses and liquids.

faq.q: What is the half-wave voltage Vπ?
faq.a: The voltage needed to change the optical phase by π (half a wavelength). In a Mach-Zehnder modulator it is the voltage that swings the transmission from maximum to minimum. In transverse devices it falls with longer electrodes and narrower gaps.

faq.q: Why can't silicon use the Pockels effect?
faq.a: Silicon crystals have inversion symmetry, so the second-order susceptibility χ⁽²⁾ is zero. Silicon modulators use the carrier dispersion effect instead, and stronger modulation is obtained by combining materials such as LiNbO₃.

光ソリトン.desc: A wave packet of light that travels through an optical fiber keeping its pulse shape, because broadening from anomalous dispersion balances the chirp from self-phase modulation.

about.h: A balance of dispersion and nonlinearity
about.p: A pulse in optical fiber broadens through dispersion and acquires a chirp through self-phase modulation that shifts its front to longer and its back to shorter wavelengths. In anomalous dispersion (standard single-mode fiber in the 1550 nm band), shorter-wavelength components travel faster, so the short-wavelength back moves forward and the long-wavelength front falls back, canceling the SPM chirp. When the two effects balance exactly, the pulse travels keeping its shape and spectrum. This is the fundamental soliton, with a sech²-shaped intensity profile.

about.h: Rule of thumb for the required power
about.p: The peak power of a fundamental soliton is P₀ = |β₂|/(γT₀²), where T₀ is the pulse width, about 1/1.763 of the full width at half maximum. In fiber with D = 17 ps/(nm·km) (β₂ ≈ −21.7 ps²/km) and γ = 1.3 /(W·km), a 10 ps pulse needs about 0.52 W. Halving the pulse width quadruples the required power, so 1 ps needs about 52 W. Higher-order solitons, with soliton order N² = γP₀T₀²/|β₂| greater than 1, change shape periodically as they travel, returning to their original form after about 2.3 km for a 10 ps width.

about.h: Conditions and how solitons break up
about.p: Bright solitons exist only in anomalous dispersion; in normal dispersion the pulse just keeps spreading. In normal dispersion, dark solitons exist instead: dark dips in continuous light that travel keeping their shape. A soliton is an ideal solution for lossless fiber, so loss gradually widens it and breaks it up, and even when amplifiers make up the loss, noise-induced arrival-time jitter (the Gordon-Haus effect) remains. With ultrashort pulses, Raman scattering also shifts the center wavelength steadily to longer wavelengths, the soliton self-frequency shift.

Optical solitons in fiber were proposed theoretically by Hasegawa and Tappert in 1973 and observed experimentally by Mollenauer and colleagues at Bell Laboratories in 1980. Their shape-preserving property made them a strong candidate for long-distance communication, but they are not the mainstream in today's wavelength-division multiplexed and coherent transmission. They do, however, play important roles in the fields of ultrashort pulses and precision measurement: soliton mode-locked fiber lasers, supercontinuum generation through the fission of higher-order solitons, and optical frequency combs from dissipative Kerr solitons in microresonators.

faq.q: What are the conditions for an optical soliton?
faq.a: A medium with anomalous dispersion (D > 0, β₂ < 0), and a peak power and pulse width that satisfy P₀ = |β₂|/(γT₀²). Then the broadening from dispersion and the chirp from self-phase modulation balance, and the pulse keeps its shape.

faq.q: How does the required soliton peak power depend on pulse width?
faq.a: P₀ is inversely proportional to the square of the pulse width. In standard fiber at 1550 nm, about 0.5 W is typical for a 10 ps pulse and about 50 W for 1 ps. The shorter the pulse, the more steeply the required power rises.

faq.q: What is a dark soliton?
faq.a: A dark dip in light of constant intensity that travels through a normal-dispersion medium keeping its shape. It requires the opposite sign of dispersion from a bright soliton, in which a bright pulse keeps its shape.

F値.desc: The focal length divided by the entrance-pupil diameter, N = f/D. Image-plane irradiance is inversely proportional to N², so each full stop (a factor of √2 in N) halves the light.

about.p: The F-number is N = f/D, where f is the focal length and D the entrance-pupil diameter, and it expresses how bright a lens is. For distant objects, image-plane illuminance is proportional to the pupil area and inversely proportional to the square of the focal length, which sets the image size, so it scales as 1/N². Lenses of different focal length give the same image brightness at the same F-number. The sequence 1.4, 2, 2.8, 4, 5.6, 8 steps by √2, so each stop halves the light. Stopping down from f/1.4 to f/4 cuts the light to about 1/8 (three stops).

about.h: Larger numbers mean darker images and more diffraction
about.p: Because the aperture is in the denominator, a larger F-number means a smaller aperture and a darker image. Conversely, stopping down makes diffraction matter more: the diameter of the point image (Airy disk), 2.44λN, at 550 nm is about 3.8 µm at f/2.8 and about 21.5 µm at f/16. With sensors whose pixels are a few micrometers, stopping down too far makes the diffraction blur larger than a pixel and fine detail softer (diffraction softening). Aberrations, on the other hand, are largest near full aperture, so many lenses are said to perform best about two or three stops down from wide open.

about.h: Numerical aperture, working F-number and T-stops
about.p: For a lens satisfying the sine condition imaging an object at infinity, the image-side numerical aperture is related by N ≈ 1/(2NA), so f/2.8 is NA ≈ 0.18. In air NA cannot exceed 1, so f/0.5 is the theoretical limit. When a near object is imaged at magnification m, the image distance grows and the working F-number rises to about N(1 + m), so at 1:1 an f/4 lens is about as dark as f/8. T-stops, used for cinema lenses, include the lens transmittance τ, T = N/√τ; an f/2 lens with 80% transmittance is about T2.24.

In photography, F-number, shutter speed and sensitivity together set the exposure. Raising the F-number by one stop can be offset by doubling the exposure time. The F-number also sets depth of field, which deepens as the lens is stopped down. In optical design, a smaller F-number means steeper focusing angles and harder correction of spherical aberration and coma, so faster lenses need more elements and become larger and heavier. In spectrometers, telescopes and fiber coupling, matching F-numbers (numerical apertures) is also important to reduce losses when light is handed from one part to another.

faq.q: Why does a larger F-number make the image darker?
faq.a: The F-number is the focal length divided by the entrance-pupil diameter, so for the same focal length a larger value means a smaller aperture. Image-plane illuminance scales as 1/N², and each √2 increase (one stop) halves the light.

faq.q: How are the F-number and numerical aperture related?
faq.a: For a system satisfying the sine condition imaging an object at infinity, N ≈ 1/(2NA). f/2 is NA ≈ 0.25 and f/1 is 0.5. For near objects, convert using the working F-number.

faq.q: What is the difference between an F-number and a T-stop?
faq.a: The F-number is the geometric brightness set only by focal length and pupil diameter; the T-stop is the actual brightness including the lens transmittance τ, T = N/√τ. Because transmittance is below 100%, the T-stop is slightly larger than the F-number.

開口絞り.desc: The stop in an optical system that sets the width of the light bundle from an on-axis object point. Its image seen from the object side is the entrance pupil, and from the image side the exit pupil.

about.h: The stop that sets the bundle width
about.p: An optical system contains many things that limit light: lens rims, barrels, diaphragm blades. The aperture stop is the one that actually sets the width of the light bundle from an on-axis object point. Its image seen from the object side is the entrance pupil and from the image side the exit pupil, and the ray from the on-axis object point to the edge of the entrance pupil (the marginal ray) sets the numerical aperture and F-number. The ray from an off-axis object point through the center of the aperture stop is the chief ray, and image position, distortion and telecentricity are determined by its path.

about.h: How to tell which aperture is the stop
about.p: Which aperture is the stop cannot be judged from physical size alone. Image every aperture in the system into object space through the lenses in front of it; the image that appears under the smallest angle from the on-axis object point is the entrance pupil, and the aperture it came from is the aperture stop. When the object distance or zoom position changes, a different aperture can take over as the stop. The rim of the front element is the stop only when it appears smallest; in most camera lenses the diaphragm blades in the middle are the aperture stop.

about.h: Difference from field stops and vignetting
about.p: The extent of the image (the field) is set not by the aperture stop but by a field stop placed near the image plane, or by the sensor's frame. When part of the light bundle from an off-axis point is clipped by lens rims and the image corners darken, this is vignetting, distinct from the bundle limitation by the aperture stop. Changing the aperture stop's size changes image brightness, depth of field and aberrations, but not what is in the frame. Stopping down reduces vignetting and lightens the darkened corners because the stop narrows the bundle, so less of it is clipped at the rims.

Moving the stop changes the path of the chief rays, which changes the amounts of coma, astigmatism and distortion. Spherical aberration, set by the on-axis bundle, does not depend on stop position. Placing the stop at the lens's rear focal point puts the entrance pupil at infinity, giving an object-space telecentric system in which chief rays in object space are parallel to the axis. Because image size does not change when the object distance shifts slightly, such systems are used for dimensional machine-vision measurement. Placing it at the front focal point puts the exit pupil at infinity, giving image-space telecentricity.

faq.q: What is the difference between an aperture stop and a field stop?
faq.a: The aperture stop sets the width of the bundle from an on-axis object point and affects brightness, resolution and depth of field. The field stop sets the extent of the image and sits near the image plane or an intermediate image. Both are physical openings, but their roles are completely different.

faq.q: How are the entrance and exit pupils found?
faq.a: The entrance pupil is the image of the aperture stop seen from the object side through the lenses in front of it; the exit pupil is its image seen from the image side through the lenses behind it. Their positions and sizes are found with paraxial imaging equations.

faq.q: What is a telecentric optical system?
faq.a: A system with the aperture stop at a focal point, putting the pupil at infinity. In object-space telecentric systems, chief rays are parallel to the axis, so magnification stays the same even if the object distance changes somewhat; they are used for dimensional measurement.

ザイデル収差.desc: The third-order monochromatic aberrations caused by departures from the paraxial approximation: spherical aberration, coma, astigmatism, field curvature and distortion.

about.p: The paraxial approximation computes imaging with sinθ ≈ θ, but at larger apertures and field angles the next term in the expansion of sinθ shifts the image. Arranging this first deviation according to its dependence on pupil coordinate and image height splits it into five: spherical aberration, coma, astigmatism, field curvature and distortion. They are called Seidel aberrations after Seidel, who organized them systematically in the 19th century. Because they are third-order terms in the ray deviation (transverse aberration), they are also called third-order aberrations; in wavefront aberration they correspond to fourth-order terms. All are monochromatic aberrations.

With pupil radius y and image height h, the transverse aberrations scale as y³ for spherical aberration, y²h for coma, yh² for astigmatism and field curvature, and h³ for distortion. Fast lenses with large apertures therefore struggle mainly with spherical aberration, wide-angle lenses with distortion, and fast wide-angle lenses with all of them. The same dependence also shows that stopping down (making y smaller) greatly reduces spherical aberration but leaves distortion completely unchanged. As the field angle grows, astigmatism and field curvature quickly become prominent.

about.h: Relation to chromatic and higher-order aberrations
about.p: Seidel aberrations are monochromatic; axial and lateral chromatic aberration, caused by the index varying with wavelength, are treated separately. Third-order theory describes systems with small aberrations well, but in fast lenses with small F-numbers and at large field angles, fifth- and higher-order aberrations cannot be ignored, and third-order aberrations are sometimes deliberately left to balance them. The part of field curvature set only by lens powers and indices is expressed by the Petzval sum, which is reduced by combining separated positive and negative lenses.

Seidel aberrations can be computed as surface-by-surface contributions (Seidel sums) from paraxial ray tracing alone, showing at a glance which surface produces which aberration, so they are used to decide the initial configuration of a design. Lens bending, stop position and glass choice redistribute the aberrations so that they cancel. In configurations symmetric about the stop, odd aberrations such as coma, distortion and lateral color cancel (completely at unit magnification). The final performance of the design is then evaluated and optimized with real ray tracing and measures such as MTF.

faq.q: What are Seidel's five aberrations?
faq.a: Spherical aberration, coma, astigmatism, field curvature and distortion: the third-order monochromatic aberrations caused by departures from the paraxial approximation. Chromatic aberrations arise from the wavelength dependence of the index and are not among the five.

faq.q: Why are they called third-order aberrations?
faq.a: Expanding the ray's position error in the image plane (transverse aberration) in pupil coordinate and image height, the first error terms are third order. Expressed as wavefront error, the same aberrations are fourth-order terms. They come from the θ³ term in the expansion of sinθ.

faq.q: Does stopping down reduce Seidel aberrations?
faq.a: It depends on the aberration. With pupil radius y, spherical aberration falls as y³, coma as y², and astigmatism and field curvature as y. Distortion does not depend on y, so stopping down does not reduce it.

コマ収差.desc: An aberration in which the image of an off-axis point trails like a comet because each annular zone of the pupil images at a different magnification. Proportional to the square of the aperture and to the field angle.

about.h: Why the image looks like a comet
about.p: Coma arises because, for light from an off-axis object point, rays through the pupil center and rays through outer annular zones of the pupil image at different magnifications. Each zone forms a small circle in the image plane, larger and farther from the center for outer zones, so the overlapping image has a bright head and a spreading tail like a comet. These circles fit within a 60° wedge, and the tail's length in the radial (meridional) direction is 1.5 times its width in the perpendicular (sagittal) direction (tangential coma is three times sagittal coma).

about.h: Size and how to reduce it
about.p: The transverse aberration of coma is proportional to the square of the pupil radius and to the image height (field angle). Raising the F-number by √2 so that the pupil diameter becomes 1/√2 halves the coma. If spherical aberration is corrected and the sine condition is also satisfied, coma disappears as well; a system free of both is called an aplanat. In a single lens, bending changes the coma: for index 1.5 and an object at infinity, the shape with minimum spherical aberration and the shape with zero coma are close, and in both the more strongly curved convex surface faces the collimated light.

about.h: Difference from spherical aberration and decentering
about.p: Spherical aberration occurs even on axis and blurs symmetrically about the axis, while coma is zero on axis and produces a one-sided asymmetric blur in off-axis images. If a lens is tilted or shifted off the axis (decentered), however, coma-like blur appears even on axis. If star images in a telescope trail to one side, suspect a collimation error first. Distortion, for its part, only shifts image positions without blurring the point image itself, so it can easily be distinguished from coma.

about.h: Handling coma in telescopes and microscopes
about.p: A paraboloidal mirror has no spherical aberration on axis but large coma off axis, and the faster the mirror, the more star images streak at the edge of the field. The Ritchey-Chrétien design, a refined Cassegrain whose two mirrors also correct coma, is used in many large telescopes, including the Hubble Space Telescope. Microscope objectives are designed to satisfy the sine condition so that images stay intact across the field even at high numerical aperture. Lenses focusing laser beams also produce coma if tilted relative to the beam, so care is needed.

faq.q: How can coma be reduced?
faq.a: Stopping down reduces it as the square of the pupil radius. In design, use an aplanatic configuration that satisfies the sine condition, and choose lens bending and stop position. In assembly, eliminating decentering is also important.

faq.q: What is the difference between coma and spherical aberration?
faq.a: Spherical aberration occurs even on axis and blurs the image symmetrically about the axis. Coma occurs for off-axis points and gives an asymmetric blur that trails one way like a comet. Their dependences also differ: aperture cubed versus aperture squared times field angle.

faq.q: Why does coma-like blur appear even at the image center?
faq.a: Usually because a lens or mirror is tilted or shifted off the axis (decentered). In an ideally assembled system coma is zero on axis, so a trailing image at the center points to an assembly or alignment error.

色消しレンズ.desc: A lens that combines a convex and a concave element of crown and flint glass with different Abbe numbers, bringing two wavelengths to the same focal position.

about.p: Glass has a higher index at shorter wavelengths, so a single lens has axial chromatic aberration: blue light focuses nearer and red farther. An achromatic lens (achromat) combines a convex lens of low-dispersion crown glass with a concave lens of high-dispersion flint glass, canceling only the color shift while keeping overall power. For thin lenses in contact, the condition for two wavelengths (usually the C line, 656.3 nm, and the F line, 486.1 nm) to share a focus is φ₁/V₁ + φ₂/V₂ = 0, where φ is power and V the Abbe number.

about.h: An example of the power split
about.p: With total power φ, the elements need φ₁ = φV₁/(V₁ − V₂) and φ₂ = −φV₂/(V₁ − V₂). For a 100 mm focal length with a crown of Abbe number 60 and a flint of 30, the convex lens is 50 mm and the concave lens −100 mm. The smaller the difference in Abbe number, the stronger each element must be, so the surfaces curve more steeply and other aberrations grow; glass pairs with a large difference are therefore chosen. Most achromats are cemented doublets whose surface curvatures are also chosen to reduce spherical aberration and coma at the same time.

An achromat brings only two wavelengths to a common focus; other wavelengths, such as the green e line (546.1 nm), remain slightly displaced. This is the secondary spectrum, roughly 1/2000 of the focal length for ordinary glass pairs. For a telescope with a 1000 mm focal length that is about 0.5 mm, visible as color fringes around bright stars. An apochromat uses ED glass with anomalous partial dispersion or fluorite (CaF₂) to bring three wavelengths to focus, and is used in high-performance telescopes and microscope objectives.

Newton thought chromatic aberration in refracting telescopes unavoidable and built a reflecting telescope, but in the 18th century achromatic lenses combining crown and flint were devised, and Dollond put them into practical use, greatly advancing refracting telescopes. Today, besides glass combinations, diffractive surfaces can also be used. A diffractive surface disperses in the opposite direction to glass, with an equivalent Abbe number of about −3.45, so adding a weak diffractive surface to a refractive lens corrects chromatic aberration; this is used in lightweight telephoto lenses.

faq.q: Why does an achromat combine a convex and a concave lens?
faq.a: To cancel the convex lens's color shift in the opposite direction with a weak concave lens of high-dispersion glass. Satisfying φ₁/V₁ + φ₂/V₂ = 0 brings two wavelengths to the same focus while the pair still acts as a positive lens overall.

faq.q: What is the difference between an achromat and an apochromat?
faq.a: An achromat brings two wavelengths to a common focus and leaves a residual shift for others (the secondary spectrum). An apochromat uses ED glass or fluorite to bring three wavelengths to focus, greatly reducing the remaining color fringing.

faq.q: What is secondary spectrum?
faq.a: The focal shift that remains for other wavelengths in an achromat corrected at two wavelengths. For ordinary crown and flint pairs it is about 1/2000 of the focal length, and in long-focal-length telescopes it shows as color fringing.

MTF.desc: The modulation transfer function: a measure of imaging performance that expresses, as a function of spatial frequency, how much of the contrast of a sinusoidal light-dark pattern is preserved in the image.

about.p: When an object whose brightness varies sinusoidally is imaged, the image is a sinusoid with the same period, but its contrast (Imax − Imin)/(Imax + Imin) is lower than the object's. This ratio, expressed as a function of spatial frequency (cycles per millimeter), is the MTF. In incoherent imaging the image is the convolution of the object with the point spread function (PSF), so the magnitude of the optical transfer function (OTF), the Fourier transform of the PSF, is the MTF, and its phase is the phase transfer function (PTF). It is 1 at zero frequency and normally decreases for finer patterns.

about.h: The diffraction limit and the cutoff frequency
about.p: Even for an aberration-free system with a circular aperture, diffraction makes the MTF fall smoothly with frequency, reaching zero at the cutoff frequency fc = 1/(λN) = 2NA/λ. At 0.55 µm and f/4, that is about 455 cycles/mm. Because the incoherent MTF is set by the autocorrelation of the pupil function, its cutoff is twice that for coherent illumination (NA/λ). Aberrations push the MTF below the diffraction-limited curve, especially lowering contrast at intermediate frequencies. Comparing MTFs through focus and at each off-axis image height reveals performance across the whole image plane.

about.h: MTF combined with an image sensor
about.p: The MTF of a whole camera is normally estimated as the product of the MTFs of the lens, optical low-pass filter, pixel aperture, image processing and so on. The Nyquist frequency of an image sensor with pixel pitch p is 1/(2p), about 167 cycles/mm for 3 µm pixels. If the lens MTF remains at frequencies above this, aliasing produces moiré. Lens evaluations often use the MTF at around half the Nyquist frequency, or graphs showing the MTF in two directions, radial and tangential, at each image height.

faq.q: What does MTF express?
faq.a: It expresses, for each spatial frequency, how much contrast remains in the image when stripes of different fineness are imaged. A lens whose MTF stays high up to high frequencies renders fine detail clearly.

faq.q: Is the MTF of an aberration-free lens equal to 1?
faq.a: No. Because of diffraction, the MTF falls with frequency even without aberrations, reaching zero at the cutoff frequency 1/(λN). The larger the f-number, the lower the cutoff.

faq.q: Does MTF reveal distortion?
faq.a: No. Distortion only shifts image positions and does not reduce contrast, so it does not appear in the MTF. It is evaluated separately as a distortion percentage.

被写界深度.desc: The range of object distances in front of and behind the focus distance over which image blur stays within the acceptable circle of confusion. It increases with stopping down and, at the same distance, with shorter focal length.

about.h: The range that looks in focus
about.p: A lens focuses precisely at only one distance, but in front of and behind it the image still looks sharp to the viewer as long as the blur stays within the diameter c of the acceptable circle of confusion. This range of object distances is the depth of field. The circle of confusion is a convention set by how large the photograph is viewed and from how far; for 35 mm format about 0.03 mm is often used. Smaller sensors are enlarged more for viewing, so a smaller c is used. Since blur grows continuously, the boundary is not a sharp one.

Using the hyperfocal distance H ≈ f²/(Nc), focusing at distance s gives a near limit of sH/(H + s) and a far limit of sH/(H − s). With 50 mm, f/2.8 and c = 0.03 mm focused at 3 m, H is about 29.8 m and the range is about 2.73 to 3.34 m, a depth of about 0.61 m. The range extends further behind the focus than in front, by about 1.2 times in this example. When s is much shorter than H, the depth is about 2Ncs²/f², proportional to the F-number and to the square of the distance and inversely proportional to the square of the focal length.

about.h: At equal image size, focal length hardly matters
about.p: "Shorter focal lengths give deeper depth of field" applies to shooting from the same distance. Shooting with a 100 mm lens from 6 m, the same framing as 50 mm from 3 m, the depth is again about 0.61 m, almost unchanged. When a subject is imaged at the same magnification, depth of field is set mainly by the F-number and magnification. How the background blurs does change with focal length, though. The tolerable focus error on the image side is called depth of focus, roughly ±Nc, or ±0.24 mm at f/8 with c = 0.03 mm.

about.h: Use in photography and optical instruments
about.p: In landscapes, focusing at the hyperfocal distance puts everything from H/2 to infinity within the depth of field. In portraits, the aperture is opened to blur the background. Stopping down too far to gain depth, however, makes the diffraction blur (about 21 µm in diameter at f/16) approach the circle of confusion and softens the whole image, so the F-number is chosen to balance depth and resolution. In microscopes the depth is extremely shallow, on the order of λ/NA², and when viewing three-dimensional specimens at high magnification, focus stacking, combining images taken at different focus positions, is widely used.

faq.q: What is the difference between depth of field and depth of focus?
faq.a: Depth of field is the range of object-side distances that look in focus. Depth of focus is the image-side range over which the sensor can shift and the image still looks in focus, about ±Nc (N is the F-number, c the circle of confusion). Both deepen when stopping down.

faq.q: How can depth of field be increased?
faq.a: The basics are stopping down to a larger F-number, moving farther from the subject, and, at the same distance, using a shorter focal length. Stopping down too far softens the whole image through diffraction, so choose a balance between depth and resolution.

faq.q: What value should the circle of confusion have?
faq.a: There is no fixed value; it is a convention based on how large and from how far the image is viewed. For 35 mm format about 0.03 mm is common, and smaller sensors use smaller values. When high-resolution images are viewed enlarged, an even smaller value is used.

ストレール比.desc: The peak intensity of the point image of an aberrated system divided by that of an aberration-free, diffraction-limited system. A value of 0.8 or more is commonly taken as diffraction-limited.

about.h: Measuring performance by the point-image peak
about.p: The Strehl ratio is the peak intensity of the point image of an aberrated system divided by that of an aberration-free, diffraction-limited system with the same aperture. Aberrations spread light from the center of the point image to its surroundings, lowering the peak. The ideal value is 1, and it falls as aberrations grow. Because it is a single number, it is widely used to evaluate high-performance systems with small aberrations. The peak intensity of the point image also equals the optical transfer function (OTF) integrated over spatial frequency, so the Strehl ratio can also be written as the ratio of the integrated OTFs of the aberrated and aberration-free systems.

about.h: Estimating it from RMS wavefront error
about.p: For small aberrations, the Maréchal approximation S ≈ exp[−(2πσ/λ)²], with RMS wavefront error σ, gives an estimate: about 0.91 at σ = λ/20 and about 0.67 at λ/10. The criterion S ≥ 0.8 for diffraction-limited performance corresponds to σ ≤ λ/14. For the same σ, the ratio is lower at shorter wavelengths: a system with σ = 50 nm has about 0.96 at 1550 nm but about 0.67 at 500 nm. Because the approximation fails for larger aberrations, it should be treated as a formula for judgments around 0.8.

about.h: Relation to P-V values and the Rayleigh criterion
about.p: Rayleigh's criterion, which allows a peak-to-valley (P-V) wavefront error of λ/4, corresponds to about λ/14 RMS for defocus alone. For defocus the ratio of P-V to RMS is √12 ≈ 3.46, so λ/4 P-V is about λ/13.9 RMS, with a Strehl ratio of about 0.81. The P-V to RMS ratio differs with the type of aberration, however, and even a small local error can give a large P-V. For predicting image quality, the RMS value is therefore more suitable than the P-V value.

The Strehl ratio is used to evaluate astronomical telescopes and adaptive optics (which corrects wavefronts distorted by atmospheric turbulence with deformable mirrors), laser focusing optics, microscope objectives, and optical components measured with interferometers. In laser processing and optical communication, a lower Strehl ratio means lower peak intensity in the spot and lower coupling efficiency into fiber. In a mirror, the wavefront error is twice the surface figure error, so the surface accuracy must be half of the wavefront requirement. When the point image is measured directly, it must be normalized correctly by total power.

faq.q: What does a Strehl ratio of 0.8 mean?
faq.a: The peak intensity of the point image is 80% of that of an ideal aberration-free system. It corresponds to an RMS wavefront error of about λ/14 and is widely used as the practical threshold for diffraction-limited performance (the Maréchal criterion).

faq.q: How is the Strehl ratio calculated?
faq.a: For small aberrations, use the Maréchal approximation S ≈ exp[−(2πσ/λ)²] with RMS wavefront error σ: about 0.67 for λ/10 and about 0.91 for λ/20. More precisely, compute the point image from the wavefront, or measure it and compare with the ideal value.

faq.q: Should wavefront error be given as a P-V or an RMS value?
faq.a: RMS is better for predicting image quality. A P-V value is easily dominated by one large local error, and the same P-V can give very different Strehl ratios depending on the shape of the aberration. Specifications often state both.

比視感度.desc: A function V(λ) expressing how the brightness perceived by the human eye varies with wavelength, normalized to 1 at its peak. It peaks near 555 nm for photopic vision and near 507 nm for scotopic vision.

about.p: In bright surroundings the cones are active, and the photopic luminous efficiency function V(λ) peaks at about 555 nm (yellow-green), falling off steeply toward 400 nm and 700 nm. For example, it is about 0.11 at 650 nm and about 0.04 at 450 nm. In dim surroundings the rods are active, and the peak of the scotopic function V′(λ) shifts to about 507 nm. The Purkinje effect, in which red flowers look dark and blue flowers relatively bright at dusk, comes from this shift. Both are standard functions defined by the CIE as averages over many observers.

A photometric quantity is found by multiplying the spectrum of the radiometric quantity by V(λ), integrating, and multiplying by the maximum luminous efficacy Km = 683 lm/W. For luminous flux, Φv = 683 ∫ Φe(λ) V(λ) dλ. 1 W of monochromatic light at 555 nm is 683 lm, at 532 nm (V ≈ 0.88) about 600 lm, and in the infrared or ultraviolet, where V ≈ 0, nearly 0 lm. The value 683 comes from the definition of the candela (1 cd for monochromatic light at 540 THz with a radiant intensity of 1/683 W/sr). For scotopic vision, the maximum luminous efficacy is about 1700 lm/W.

Illuminance meters and luminance meters need the spectral responsivity of their sensors matched to V(λ). A silicon photodiode's responsivity peaks around 900 nm, so correction filters made of colored glass or interference coatings are combined with it to approximate V(λ). If the correction is imperfect, errors arise when measuring white LEDs or single-color LEDs whose spectra differ from the source used for calibration (usually standard illuminant A at about 2856 K). To reduce such errors, another approach is to measure the spectrum with a spectroradiometer and then apply V(λ) by calculation.

faq.q: Why does it peak at 555 nm?
faq.a: Because the sum of the sensitivities of the L and M cones, which contribute most to brightness, is largest around yellow-green. It is also thought to be related to the strength of the solar spectrum in the visible range and to the evolution of the eye.

faq.q: How many lumens is an infrared laser?
faq.a: Outside the visible range, in the infrared or ultraviolet, V(λ) is nearly 0, so the luminous flux is nearly 0 lm. Even though the eye perceives no brightness, energy still reaches the retina and skin, so safety is assessed with radiometric quantities (W).

faq.q: What should be used to compare how bright lights are?
faq.a: To compare visible brightness, use photometric quantities such as luminous flux (lm) or illuminance (lx). Even at the same wattage, light looks dimmer the farther its wavelength is from 555 nm, and the more infrared a source contains.

光束.desc: A photometric quantity expressing the amount of light leaving a source or passing through a surface, weighted by the luminous efficiency function. Its unit is the lumen (lm); its radiometric counterpart is radiant flux (W).

about.h: Light weighted by the eye's sensitivity
about.p: Luminous flux is the power of light (radiant flux) weighted by the sensitivity of the human eye, and its unit is the lumen (lm). It is found by multiplying the radiant flux spectrum Φe(λ) by the luminous efficiency function V(λ), integrating, and multiplying by 683 lm/W: Φv = 683∫Φe(λ)V(λ)dλ. One watt of monochromatic light at 555 nm is 683 lm, so 1 lm at that wavelength is about 1.46 mW. Infrared and ultraviolet have V(λ) of almost 0, so however strong they are, their luminous flux is almost 0. Luminous flux is the basic photometric quantity for how much visible light a source emits in total.

A source's efficiency is expressed as luminous flux per watt of electrical power (lm/W). Incandescent lamps radiate mostly infrared, giving only about 10 to 15 lm/W, while LED lighting commonly exceeds 100 lm/W. Under Japanese labeling for LED bulbs, the equivalent of a 60-type incandescent lamp is 810 lm; 810 lm from 7.3 W is about 111 lm/W, whereas a 60 W incandescent lamp gives about 13.5 lm/W. The "luminous efficacy of a source" (per electrical watt) and the "luminous efficacy of radiation" (per watt of light) have different denominators and are different quantities, so care is needed when comparing them.

about.h: Relation to luminous intensity, illuminance and luminance
about.p: Luminous flux is the total light from a source; dividing it by direction or area gives other photometric quantities. Per unit solid angle it becomes luminous intensity (cd = lm/sr), per unit area of a receiving surface illuminance (lx = lm/m²), and further per unit solid angle in the viewing direction luminance (cd/m²). Even for the same 1000 lm source, concentrating the light into a narrow range with a reflector raises the luminous intensity in that direction and the illuminance of the lit surface, but not the luminous flux. It is important to know which quantity a comparison of "brightness" is using.

The total luminous flux of a source is found by lighting it inside an integrating sphere with a white diffusing inner surface and measuring the light, made uniform by many reflections off the wall, with a detector matched to V(λ). The value is usually determined by comparison with a reference lamp. Large luminaires are measured with a goniophotometer, which moves a detector around the source to measure the luminous intensity in each direction and integrates over all directions to obtain the total flux. For sources whose spectra differ from lamp to lamp, such as white LEDs, a spectroradiometer measures the spectrum and the flux is calculated.

faq.q: What is the difference between lumens and watts?
faq.a: Watts measure the power of light (radiant flux) or electrical consumption; lumens measure light weighted by the eye's sensitivity V(λ). The same 1 W is 683 lm at 555 nm but almost 0 lm in the infrared. Lighting brightness is compared in lumens.

faq.q: What is the difference between lumens and lux?
faq.a: Lumens (lm) are the total light from a source; lux (lx) is luminous flux per unit area reaching a surface, with 1 lx = 1 lm/m². With the same source, the farther or larger the lit surface, the lower the lux.

faq.q: How bright is an LED bulb?
faq.a: Under Japanese labeling, the equivalent of a 60-type incandescent bulb is 810 lm. Power depends on the product, but an LED with an efficacy of around 100 lm/W needs about 8 W, roughly 1/7 to 1/8 the power of a 60 W incandescent bulb for the same flux.

光度.desc: The luminous flux per unit solid angle that a point source emits in a given direction. Its unit is the candela (cd = lm/sr). For a source uniform in all directions, it is the total luminous flux divided by 4π.

about.h: The strength of light in one direction
about.p: Luminous intensity is the luminous flux per unit solid angle that a point source emits in a given direction, and its unit is the candela (cd = lm/sr). The candela is one of the seven SI base units. In 1979 it was defined as the luminous intensity, in a given direction, of monochromatic light at 540×10¹² Hz (about 555 nm) whose radiant intensity in that direction is 1/683 W/sr, and the 2019 revision kept this value of 683 as a fixed defining constant. The name comes from the candle, and one candle has a luminous intensity of roughly 1 cd.

For a point source emitting uniformly in all directions, the luminous intensity is the total flux divided by 4π, so 810 lm gives about 64 cd. For a source like a Lambertian surface, with I₀ straight ahead and I₀cosθ at angle θ, the total flux is πI₀, so a 100 lm surface source has a forward intensity of about 31.8 cd. Concentrating light into a cone with a 10° half-angle (about 0.0955 sr), on the other hand, makes even 1 lm about 10.5 cd in that direction. Because the same flux gives very different intensities depending on the distribution, luminaires show intensity versus direction in luminous intensity distribution curves.

about.h: Relation to illuminance, and the distance condition
about.p: The illuminance on a surface at distance r from a source is E = I cosθ/r², with θ the angle of incidence, so it can be found from the luminous intensity. This inverse-square law holds far enough away that the source can be treated as a point; a rule of thumb (the five-times rule) says the error is small beyond about five times the source size. Measuring a large surface source up close departs from the inverse-square law. Luminous intensity is a property of the source, independent of distance, whereas illuminance depends on where the receiving surface is. Intensity is basically measured by measuring illuminance far enough from the source and computing E × r².

about.h: Use for LEDs and signal lights
about.p: Specifications of bullet-type LEDs give luminous intensity in mcd (millicandelas) together with a viewing angle. The narrower the viewing angle, the higher the forward intensity for the same flux, so intensity values alone cannot compare the overall brightness of sources. Standards for traffic signals, automobile headlamps and lamps, and aviation and marine lights specify the luminous intensity required in defined directions. Looking at both the center intensity (cd) and the luminous flux (lm) of a spotlight shows how narrowly it concentrates its light into a beam.

faq.q: What is the difference between candelas and lumens?
faq.a: Lumens are the total light from a source (luminous flux); candelas are luminous flux per unit solid angle in a given direction (luminous intensity), with 1 cd = 1 lm/sr. For a source uniform in all directions, the intensity is the total flux divided by 4π.

faq.q: How is illuminance found from luminous intensity?
faq.a: At distances where the source can be treated as a point, E = I cosθ/r². If the intensity in that direction is 200 cd, a surface facing the source 2 m away receives 50 lx, and at 4 m 12.5 lx. If the surface is tilted 30° to the light, cos30° ≈ 0.87 multiplies in, giving about 43 lx at 2 m.

faq.q: What does mcd mean for LEDs?
faq.a: Millicandelas (1/1000 cd), expressing an LED's luminous intensity in the forward direction. The narrower the viewing angle, the larger the value for the same flux, so compare the overall brightness of LEDs together with their viewing angles, or by luminous flux (lm).

照度.desc: The luminous flux incident on a surface per unit area. Its unit is the lux (lx = lm/m²). The illuminance from a point source is inversely proportional to the square of the distance and proportional to the cosine of the angle of incidence.

about.h: How much light reaches a surface
about.p: Illuminance is the luminous flux incident on a surface per unit area, with the unit lux (lx = lm/m²). It is irradiance (W/m²) weighted by the luminous efficiency function. Even with the same source, moving the surface away or tilting it changes the illuminance: from a point source E = I cosθ/r², inversely proportional to the square of the distance and proportional to the cosine of the angle of incidence. On a floor away from the point below a ceiling lamp, both distance and tilt act, so illuminance falls as cos³θ and becomes uneven. One foot-candle (lm/ft²) is about 10.76 lx.

Illuminance values differ by orders of magnitude. Direct sunlight on a clear day is about 100,000 lx, outdoors on a cloudy day several thousand to tens of thousands of lux, an office desk a few hundred to about a thousand lux, and the ground on a full-moon night less than 1 lx. Because the eye adapts across this wide range, the differences are hard to sense and become clear only when measured. Lighting standards set target illuminances for different tasks, with finer work requiring higher levels. Camera exposure meters and the automatic brightness adjustment of smartphones also use illuminance sensors.

An illuminance meter must satisfy two requirements: V(λ) correction, matching the detector's spectral sensitivity to V(λ), and cosine correction, receiving oblique light in proportion to the cosine of its angle. If the corrections are imperfect, errors arise with white LEDs whose spectra differ from the calibration source, and with light arriving obliquely. Place the detector facing the same way as the surface to be measured, and keep your shadow out. Illuminance is the light reaching a surface, so at the same illuminance the visible brightness (luminance) differs greatly depending on whether the lit object is white or black.

The average illuminance of a room is often estimated by the lumen method, E = ΦUM/A, from the total flux Φ of the sources, the utilization factor U (the fraction of light reaching the work plane), the maintenance factor M (allowing for dirt and aging) and the floor area A. To get 500 lx in a 10 m² room with U = 0.6 and M = 0.8, about 10,400 lm of total flux is needed. Illuminance at individual points is calculated by the point-by-point method from each source's intensity and distance, and the contributions are summed. Uniformity of illuminance (the ratio of minimum to average) is also an important measure of how easy the work is.

faq.q: What is the difference between lux and lumens?
faq.a: Lumens are the total light from a source; lux is the luminous flux reaching each square meter of a surface. If 1000 lm falls uniformly on 1 m², that is 1000 lx; spread over 10 m², it is 100 lx.

faq.q: How does illuminance change with distance?
faq.a: Illuminance from a point source is inversely proportional to the square of the distance, so doubling the distance cuts it to a quarter. If the surface tilts relative to the light, the cosine of the angle of incidence multiplies in as well. Large, nearby sources depart from the inverse-square law.

faq.q: What is the difference between illuminance and luminance?
faq.a: Illuminance is the light reaching a surface (lx); luminance is how bright that surface looks from a viewing direction (cd/m²). At the same illuminance, white paper has higher luminance than black paper. For a perfect diffuser, luminance = reflectance × illuminance/π.

輝度.desc: The brightness of a surface seen from a given direction, expressed as luminous flux per unit area per unit solid angle. Its unit is cd/m². It does not depend on viewing distance and is used for the brightness of displays.

about.p: Luminance is the light leaving a point of a surface in the viewing direction, divided by the area seen from that direction (the projected area) and by solid angle; its unit is cd/m². The "nit" often used for display brightness is a common name for the same unit. Luminance is the photometric quantity that corresponds most directly to visible brightness: under the same lighting, white paper looks brighter than black paper because its luminance is higher. Thinking of illuminance as light "entering a surface" and luminance as light "going from the surface toward the eye" makes them easy to distinguish. Its radiometric counterpart is radiance, W/(m²·sr).

about.h: Converting from illuminance, and familiar values
about.p: A perfect diffuser (Lambertian surface) with reflectance ρ under illuminance E has luminance L = ρE/π, the same from every viewing direction. White paper with reflectance 0.9 under 300 lx is about 86 cd/m². For displays, the sRGB reference white is 80 cd/m², ordinary monitors reach a few hundred cd/m², and some HDR displays produce peaks of 1000 cd/m² or more. The HDR signal standard (PQ) covers up to 10,000 cd/m². The midday sun, by comparison, has a luminance of about 1.6×10⁹ cd/m².

about.h: Why it does not depend on distance
about.p: Moving away from a surface reduces the light entering the eye in inverse proportion to the square of the distance, but the area of the image on the retina shrinks in the same proportion, so the retinal illuminance stays the same and the surface looks just as bright. This is why luminance does not depend on viewing distance. In passive optical systems such as lenses, the luminance of an image cannot exceed that of the object and, without loss, is equal within the same medium (conservation of luminance). Focusing sunlight with a magnifying glass cannot make an image of higher luminance than the sun's surface; focusing raises illuminance, not luminance.
