Perceived brightness is not proportional to luminance but changes roughly logarithmically or as a cube root. In CIE lightness, L* = 116(Y/Yn)^(1/3) − 16, a gray with 18% of white's luminance has L* ≈ 49.5, almost midway. The light reaching the retina is expressed in trolands (Td), luminance times pupil area; viewing 100 cd/m² through a 3 mm pupil gives about 707 Td. A luminance meter forms an image of the surface with a lens and measures light from part of it with a detector matched to V(λ). It is used to measure display screens and to evaluate glare.

faq.q: Are cd/m² and nits the same?
faq.a: Yes. The nit is a common name for cd/m²; it is not an official SI unit name, but it is widely used for display brightness. A 1000-nit display has a peak luminance of 1000 cd/m².

faq.q: How is luminance found from illuminance?
faq.a: For a perfect diffuser, L = ρE/π, with ρ the reflectance. A surface with reflectance 0.5 under 400 lx has about 64 cd/m². Dividing by π reflects how light from a diffuser spreads over the hemisphere with a cosθ distribution.

faq.q: Why does luminance stay the same when viewed from far away?
faq.a: Moving away reduces the light entering the eye, but the retinal image shrinks in the same proportion, so the light per unit area does not change. Without atmospheric attenuation, a surface's luminance does not depend on viewing distance.

等色関数.desc: Functions giving the amounts of three primaries needed to match the color of monochromatic light at each wavelength. Weighting a spectrum with the CIE x̄, ȳ and z̄ gives the tristimulus values XYZ.

about.p: Human color vision is determined by the responses of three types of cones, so any color can be matched by a combination of amounts of three primaries (for example, red, green and blue monochromatic lights). The color-matching functions express, as functions of wavelength, the amounts of the primaries needed to match monochromatic light at each wavelength. The three values obtained by multiplying a light's spectrum S(λ) by the color-matching functions and integrating are called the tristimulus values, and lights with the same tristimulus values look the same color even if their spectra differ (metamerism). This property is also why a display can represent many colors with only red, green and blue light.

With real red, green and blue primaries, parts of the color-matching functions become negative (because a primary must be added to the side of the monochromatic light to achieve a match). In 1931 the CIE linearly transformed these into color-matching functions x̄(λ), ȳ(λ) and z̄(λ) based on imaginary primaries that are positive everywhere. In doing so it made ȳ(λ) the same as the photopic luminous efficiency function V(λ), so the tristimulus value Y is proportional to photometric quantities such as luminance. X = k∫S x̄ dλ, and Y and Z are found in the same form.

about.h: Chromaticity coordinates and the chromaticity diagram
about.p: Dividing the tristimulus values by their sum gives the chromaticity coordinates x = X/(X + Y + Z) and y = Y/(X + Y + Z), which express the properties of a color apart from its brightness. The chromaticities of monochromatic light trace the horseshoe-shaped spectral locus; a mixture of two lights lies on the line joining them, and a mixture of three lies inside their triangle. A display's color gamut is shown by this triangle. For example, the white point of standard daylight D65 is (x, y) ≈ (0.313, 0.329). Distances on the xy chromaticity diagram are not proportional to perceived color differences, so color differences are evaluated in uniform color spaces such as CIELAB.

faq.q: Do color-matching functions differ between observers?
faq.a: There are individual differences, but the CIE color-matching functions are averages over many observers and are defined as a standard observer. Because appearance changes with field size, there are two versions: the 2° field (1931) and the 10° field (1964).

faq.q: What does the tristimulus value Y represent?
faq.a: Because ȳ(λ) has the same shape as the luminous efficiency function V(λ), Y is a quantity proportional to brightness (luminance or luminous flux). The color information is carried mainly by the chromaticity coordinates x and y, which are ratios that include X and Z.

faq.q: How do RGB values differ from XYZ?
faq.a: XYZ is a device-independent color system that expresses every color with positive values. RGB spaces such as sRGB are representations based on specific three primaries and a white point, obtained from XYZ by a 3×3 matrix and a gamma conversion. Colors outside the gamut become negative or greater than 1 in RGB.

色温度.desc: The color of light expressed as the temperature (K) of the blackbody that looks that color. For sources off the blackbody locus, the temperature of the closest blackbody (correlated color temperature) is used. Higher values are bluer white.

about.h: Describing light color by blackbody temperature
about.p: As a blackbody (an ideal object that absorbs all light) gets hotter, the share of short-wavelength radiation increases and its color moves from red through orange and white to bluish white. Using this relation, color temperature expresses the color of light as the temperature (K) of the blackbody that looks the same color. A candle flame is about 1900 K, incandescent lamps about 2700 to 2800 K, midday sunlight about 5000 to 5500 K, and the standard daylight D65 about 6500 K. Lower color temperatures are reddish, warm colors and higher ones bluish white, the opposite of the physical sense of heat.

about.h: Correlated color temperature and departure from the locus
about.p: The chromaticities of LEDs and fluorescent lamps do not lie exactly on the line of blackbody colors (the blackbody locus). The temperature of the nearest blackbody on a chromaticity diagram (CIE 1960 UCS u, v) is therefore used as the correlated color temperature (CCT), and the distance from the locus is expressed as Duv. The CIE asks that CCT not be used for light far from the locus, with |Duv| ≤ 0.05 as a guide. At the same 5000 K, positive Duv looks greenish and negative Duv pinkish-purple. D65 itself lies slightly above the locus (Duv ≈ +0.003).

about.h: Mireds and how color differences are perceived
about.p: Perceived differences in color temperature follow differences in the reciprocal more closely than in the temperature itself. The mired (micro reciprocal degree), 10⁶/T, is therefore used. The difference between 3000 K and 3200 K is about 20.8 mireds, but between 6000 K and 6500 K, though 500 K apart, it is only about 12.8 mireds, so at high color temperatures the same temperature difference looks smaller. Color conversion filters for photography and video, and LED color tuning, express their amounts in mireds. By Wien's displacement law, the peak wavelength is about 446 nm at 6500 K and about 1073 nm at 2700 K.

Japanese lighting classifies light colors as incandescent-like (about 2700 to 3000 K), warm white, white, neutral white (about 5000 K) and daylight (about 6500 K). Low color temperatures are often chosen for relaxing spaces and high ones for detailed work or places where colors are checked. Color temperature is an index of the light's color, not the temperature of the lamp or the LED chip itself. A higher color temperature also does not mean brighter light, nor that object colors look correct. How object colors look is evaluated separately by the color rendering index.

faq.q: What color is light with a high color temperature?
faq.a: Bluish white. Lower values are warmer, reddish or yellowish colors. Incandescent-like lighting is about 2700 to 3000 K, neutral white about 5000 K and daylight about 6500 K. Note that the direction is opposite to the sense of heat.

faq.q: What is correlated color temperature?
faq.a: The color of LED or fluorescent light lying slightly off the blackbody locus, expressed as the temperature of the nearest blackbody on a chromaticity diagram. The departure from the locus is given by Duv, and CCT is not used for light far off it (a guide is |Duv| > 0.05).

faq.q: What is a mired?
faq.a: The reciprocal of color temperature multiplied by 10⁶ (10⁶/T). Perceived color differences follow reciprocal differences more closely than temperature differences, so mireds express the strength of color conversion filters and color tuning. 3000 K is about 333 mireds and 6500 K about 154.

演色評価数.desc: An index of how close the colors of objects lit by a source are to how they look under a reference light of the same color temperature. The average over eight test colors is the general color rendering index Ra, with a maximum of 100.

about.h: Putting a number on how object colors look
about.p: The color rendering index expresses how closely the colors of objects lit by a source match their appearance under a reference light of the same correlated color temperature. The reference is blackbody radiation below 5000 K and CIE daylight at 5000 K and above. For each specified test color, the color difference ΔE under the two lights is found and scored as Ri = 100 − 4.6ΔE. No difference gives 100, and a ΔE of 5 gives 77. The average over eight test colors of medium saturation is the general color rendering index Ra.

Incandescent and halogen lamps are close to blackbody radiation, so their Ra is almost 100. Common white LEDs using a blue LED and yellow phosphor score about 70 to 80, and high-CRI LEDs with added red phosphor 90 or more. Sources close to monochromatic, such as low-pressure sodium lamps, have negative calculated Ra. Many standards for offices and similar spaces require Ra of 80 or more, and 90 or more is commonly chosen where colors must be judged correctly, as in museums, printing and medicine.

about.h: R9 and the limits of Ra
about.p: Because Ra is an average of eight colors, a source weak in a particular color can still score high. In particular, the saturated red test color R9 is not included in Ra, and white LEDs can have low or even negative R9 while Ra is 80 or above, making meat and skin look dull. Products advertised as high color rendering therefore increasingly state R9 as well. Because the method uses few test colors and an outdated color space, newer methods are also used, such as the CIE color fidelity index Rf and IES TM-30 (Rf with the gamut index Rg).

about.h: Difference from color temperature, and misconceptions
about.p: The color rendering index and color temperature are entirely separate indices. A 2800 K incandescent lamp has a low color temperature but an Ra of almost 100, while a 6500 K white LED can have an Ra in the 70s. Ra 100 also does not mean "looks the same as sunlight"; it means "looks the same as a reference light of the same correlated color temperature". Even with Ra 100, an incandescent lamp makes colors look different from daylight. There is also a trade-off with efficiency: adding long-wavelength red, where the eye is less sensitive, raises color rendering but tends to lower luminous efficacy.

faq.q: What is the general color rendering index Ra?
faq.a: The average of the indices R1 to R8, found from the color differences of eight medium-saturation test colors compared with a reference light. The maximum is 100; larger differences lower it, and sources close to monochromatic can even go negative.

faq.q: What is R9?
faq.a: The special color rendering index for a saturated red test color. It is not among the eight colors in Ra, so some sources have high Ra but low R9. It affects how meat, skin and red objects look, so R9 is also checked for high color rendering lighting.

faq.q: What is the difference between color rendering and color temperature?
faq.a: Color temperature describes the color of the light itself (reddish or bluish); color rendering describes how closely objects lit by it look as they do under the reference light. Incandescent lamps have low color temperature but almost the best color rendering.

波長分解能.desc: A spectrometer's ability to separate close wavelengths, given by the smallest separable wavelength difference Δλ or by the ratio R = λ/Δλ (the resolving power). For a diffraction grating, the upper limit of R is mN, the product of the number of illuminated grooves and the order.

about.h: Two ways of stating it: Δλ and R
about.p: Resolving power is expressed either as the smallest wavelength difference Δλ that a spectrometer can show as two separate lines, or as the ratio R = λ/Δλ, and because both are loosely called resolution, care is needed. A smaller Δλ and a larger R both mean better performance. Separating the sodium D lines (589.0 nm and 589.6 nm), for example, needs R ≈ 1000. The criterion for two lines being separated may be the Rayleigh criterion, where the maximum of one falls on the first minimum of the other, or the full width at half maximum of the instrument function, so align the definitions before comparing numbers.

The theoretical resolving power of a diffraction grating is the product of the number of illuminated grooves N and the order m, R = mN. Illuminating a grating with 1200 grooves per 1 mm over a width of 50 mm gives R = 60000 in first order, or Δλ ≈ 0.008 nm at 500 nm. Using the grating equation, mN = W(sinα + sinβ)/λ, where W is the illuminated width, so once the angles are fixed it depends only on W, not on groove density or order, and its upper limit is 2W/λ. For a prism, the resolving power is the product of the base length b filled by the beam and |dn/dλ|.

The resolution of a real spectrometer is almost always far below mN, because the bandpass given by the width of the slit image on the detector times the reciprocal linear dispersion, the pixel size and the aberrations of the optics take effect first. To record a line shape correctly, as a guide you also need to sample with at least 2–3 pixels per full width at half maximum of the line. Resolution is also a different property from wavelength accuracy, which describes how correct the wavelength scale is: even with high resolution, a calibration error means line positions are read wrongly.

The resolution needed varies widely with the application. A compact spectrometer measuring broad bands in the absorption spectrum of a solution can manage with a Δλ of several nm, while separating atomic emission lines or Raman lines may need 0.1 nm or better. In Fourier transform spectroscopy the resolution is stated in wavenumber as Δσ ≈ 1/δmax, where δmax is the maximum path difference, and is set by how far the moving mirror travels. A Fabry–Perot interferometer reaches resolving powers above 10⁵ through the product of order and finesse, R = mF, but its free spectral range is narrow, so it is combined with a pre-dispersing spectrometer.

faq.q: What is the difference between R and Δλ for resolution?
faq.a: Δλ is the smallest wavelength difference that can be separated, and smaller is better. R = λ/Δλ turns it into a dimensionless ratio, and larger is better. For the same R, Δλ is larger at longer wavelengths.

faq.q: How do you raise the resolution of a grating spectrometer?
faq.a: Increase mN by illuminating more grooves or using a higher order. In practice you also need to reduce the bandpass set by the slit image, by narrowing the slit or using a longer focal length, balancing this against the light throughput.

faq.q: How is a spectrometer's resolution measured?
faq.a: The usual method is to measure an emission line much narrower than the instrument, such as from a low-pressure mercury or neon lamp, and take the full width at half maximum of the recorded line as the instrument resolution. Checking whether two close lines appear separated is another method.

逆線分散.desc: The wavelength range spread over a unit length in a spectrometer's focal plane, dλ/dx (nm/mm). For a grating it is d cosβ/(mf); multiplying by the width of the slit image gives the bandwidth.

about.h: How wavelengths spread over the focal plane
about.p: The reciprocal linear dispersion dλ/dx expresses how many nm of wavelength are spread over 1 mm of a spectrometer's focal plane (the detector surface). Its inverse, dx/dλ (mm/nm), is called the linear dispersion, and because the names are similar the units are used to tell them apart. For a diffraction grating, dλ/dx = d cosβ/(mf), which becomes smaller as the groove spacing d gets smaller and as the order m and the focal length f get larger. The smaller the reciprocal linear dispersion, the more the wavelengths are stretched out and the finer the differences that can be separated, but the narrower the range that fits on the detector at once.

The reciprocal linear dispersion is used to estimate a spectrometer's bandpass. Using a grating with 600 grooves per mm in first order with a focal length of 500 mm and a diffraction angle of 10° gives dλ/dx ≈ 3.3 nm/mm. A slit image 100 µm wide then gives a bandpass of about 0.33 nm, a pixel 26 µm wide covers about 0.085 nm, and a detector 25 mm wide takes in a range of about 82 nm at once. In a spectrometer whose magnification between entrance and exit is not 1, use the image width, the entrance slit width multiplied by the magnification.

Because the diffraction angle β appears in the formula, the reciprocal linear dispersion differs slightly from one end of the detector to the other, so the wavelength scale is not strictly evenly spaced. Over a range where β is small, cosβ changes little and the scale of a grating spectrometer is nearly uniform. In a prism spectrometer, by contrast, dn/dλ changes greatly with wavelength, so the reciprocal linear dispersion is smaller at short wavelengths and larger at long ones. In either case, known emission lines such as those of mercury or neon are measured and a calibration formula relates pixels to wavelength.

about.h: Using it to choose a spectrometer
about.p: Spectrometer catalogs often give the reciprocal linear dispersion at the center wavelength in nm/mm, which serves as a guide for choosing the grating and focal length from the resolution and wavelength range you need. For high resolution, choose a grating with high groove density or a long focal length; to measure a wide range at once, choose a combination with a large reciprocal linear dispersion. The same spectrometer can be used in different ways by exchanging or rotating the grating. Performance is not set by reciprocal linear dispersion alone, though: aberrations, stray light and slit width must be considered as well.

faq.q: What is the difference between reciprocal linear dispersion and linear dispersion?
faq.a: Reciprocal linear dispersion is the wavelength range per 1 mm of the focal plane, dλ/dx (nm/mm), and linear dispersion is its inverse, dx/dλ (mm/nm). The smaller the former, or the larger the latter, the more the wavelengths are spread out.

faq.q: How do you find the bandpass from the reciprocal linear dispersion?
faq.a: Multiply the width of the slit image at the detector by the reciprocal linear dispersion. At 3.3 nm/mm with a slit image 50 µm wide, the bandpass is about 0.16 nm.

faq.q: How do you make the reciprocal linear dispersion smaller?
faq.a: Use a grating with a higher groove density, a spectrometer with a longer focal length, or a higher order. In exchange, the wavelength range that can be measured at once becomes narrower.

ブレーズド回折格子.desc: A diffraction grating whose grooves have a sawtooth cross-section, with the direction of specular reflection from the facets matched to a particular order. The diffraction efficiency of that order is high near the blaze wavelength.

about.h: Concentrating light into one order with the groove facets
about.p: In a grating with flat-bottomed or sinusoidal grooves, the incoming light is divided among the zero order and several other orders, and only a small fraction reaches the order you use. A blazed grating gives the grooves a sawtooth cross-section and aligns the direction of specular reflection from the facets with the diffraction direction of the order in use, concentrating light in that order. Blaze means to shine brightly, from the way the grating lights up when viewed from that direction. Changing the groove shape does not change the grating equation, so the diffraction angles and resolving power stay the same; only the distribution of efficiency among orders changes.

In the Littrow configuration, where the diffracted light returns along the incident direction, the blaze wavelength is λB = 2d sinθB/m, with θB the blaze angle. A grating with 1800 grooves per 1 mm and a blaze angle of 26.7° has a first-order blaze wavelength of about 500 nm. A grating blazed at λB in first order also has high efficiency near λB/2 in second order. The efficiency curve also differs in shape for polarization parallel and perpendicular to the grooves, and sudden changes (Wood's anomalies) can appear, so when using light of fixed polarization, check the efficiency plot for each polarization.

A grating with a large blaze angle and low groove density, used in high orders, is called an echelle. Gratings at about 63.4°, where tanθB = 2 (R2), are common; with 79 grooves per mm, a wavelength of 500 nm falls in about order 45. Because it works in high orders, even a small grating gives high resolving power, but the free spectral range is narrow, λ/m ≈ 11 nm. A cross-disperser, a prism or second grating dispersing in the perpendicular direction, is therefore added so that the orders are stacked one above another on a two-dimensional detector, covering a wide range at once.

about.h: Choosing one and points to watch
about.p: For gratings whose groove spacing is at least about twice the wavelength, a rough rule of thumb says first-order efficiency falls to about half its maximum at about 2/3 and about 1.5 times the blaze wavelength. The efficient range thus extends further on the long side, but real efficiency curves vary with polarization and groove shape, so choose the blaze wavelength by checking the manufacturer's efficiency plots. Ruled gratings cut mechanically are easy to blaze, while holographic gratings made by interference exposure have less stray light but grooves close to sinusoidal, and some are blazed by ion etching. Blazing does not remove order overlap, so an order-sorting filter is needed over a wide range.

faq.q: What is the blaze wavelength?
faq.a: It is the wavelength at which the direction of specular reflection from the groove facets coincides with the diffraction direction of a given order, a guide to where that order's diffraction efficiency is highest. In the Littrow configuration it is found from λB = 2d sinθB/m.

faq.q: Does a blazed grating have higher resolving power?
faq.a: No. Resolving power is set by mN, the product of the number of illuminated grooves and the order, and does not depend on the groove profile. Blazing changes only the efficiency, that is, how much light is sent into which order.

faq.q: What happens at half the blaze wavelength?
faq.a: A grating blazed in first order is also efficient near λB/2 in second order. Because λB in first order and λB/2 in second order leave at the same angle, they are separated with an order-sorting filter that removes the shorter wavelengths.

フーリエ変換分光法.desc: A spectroscopic method that obtains a spectrum by Fourier transforming the interferogram recorded while varying the path difference of a Michelson interferometer. Infrared FTIR is the representative example.

about.p: When light is sent into a Michelson interferometer and the movable mirror is moved, monochromatic light of wavenumber σ = 1/λ gives an intensity that varies as cos(2πσδ) with the path difference δ. For light containing many wavenumbers, the result is an interferogram I(δ) in which the cosine waves of each component overlap, and Fourier transforming it recovers the spectrum B(σ). Two close lines produce a beat, and its period 1/Δσ gives the difference in wavenumber. The instrument widely used in infrared spectroscopy is the FTIR (Fourier transform infrared spectrometer).

The interferogram can be measured only up to a finite path difference δmax, so the spectrum is broadened by the instrument function, and the wavenumber resolution is roughly Δσ ≈ 1/δmax. Moving the mirror by x changes the path difference by 2x, so a resolution of 0.5 cm⁻¹ requires about 1 cm of travel to one side. Sampling is triggered at even intervals by the fringes of a He-Ne laser (632.8 nm) sent along the same path. With one point per fringe cycle, the Nyquist condition gives a maximum measurable wavenumber of about 7900 cm⁻¹.

Because FTIR measures all wavelengths at once, in the infrared, where detector noise dominates, the signal-to-noise ratio improves by roughly √M for M spectral points (the Fellgett advantage). Other strengths are that no narrow slit is needed so much light can be collected (the Jacquinot advantage), and that the wavenumber scale is set accurately by the laser wavelength (the Connes advantage). In the visible and ultraviolet, on the other hand, where shot noise dominates, the multiplex advantage nearly disappears, and dispersive spectrometers with array detectors are commonly used.

faq.q: What determines the resolution of an FTIR?
faq.a: It is determined by the maximum path difference δmax, roughly Δσ ≈ 1/δmax. The mirror travel is half of that. Applying apodization to suppress truncation sidelobes widens the instrument function.

faq.q: Why is it so widely used for infrared spectroscopy?
faq.a: Because infrared detectors are noisy, so the multiplex advantage of measuring all wavelengths at once counts for a lot. Even with weak infrared sources, spectra with high signal-to-noise ratio can be obtained quickly, and wavenumber accuracy can also be high.

faq.q: What is the He-Ne laser used for?
faq.a: To mark the movable mirror's position with He-Ne fringes every 632.8 nm of path difference. This allows evenly spaced sampling even if the mirror speed fluctuates, and makes the wavenumber scale accurate.

インターフェログラム.desc: A record of how the detected light intensity changes as the path difference of an interferometer is varied. Fourier transforming it gives the spectrum of the light.

about.h: Intensity as a function of path difference
about.p: When the moving mirror of a Michelson interferometer changes the path difference δ between the two arms, the detected intensity varies as I(δ) = ∫B(σ)[1 + cos(2πσδ)]dσ, where σ is the wavenumber and B(σ) the spectrum. For monochromatic light this is a cosine wave completing one cycle for each wavelength of path difference. When many wavenumbers are mixed, their cosines line up and reinforce one another only at zero path difference and cancel away from it, so the interferogram has a sharp peak at zero path difference (the centerburst) with small oscillations on either side.

about.h: Relation to the spectrum and resolution
about.p: Once the constant part is removed, the interferogram is the cosine transform of the spectrum B(σ), so a Fourier transform recovers the spectrum. The farther the path difference is measured, the finer the structure that can be separated, and the resolution is Δσ ≈ 1/δmax, where δmax is the maximum path difference. Two lines 0.5 cm⁻¹ apart, for example, appear as a beat whose amplitude rises and falls with a period of 2 cm of path difference, so you must measure out to at least about that far. The sampling interval, on the other hand, is chosen to satisfy the Nyquist condition at the highest wavenumber of interest.

about.h: How it looks as a signal in time
about.p: When the moving mirror travels at a constant speed v, the path difference changes at 2v and a component of wavenumber σ becomes an electrical signal at frequency 2vσ. With a mirror speed of about 0.32 cm/s, the He-Ne laser (632.8 nm) fringes give a signal of about 10 kHz and infrared light at 1000 cm⁻¹ about 630 Hz. Because the detector only has to respond over this frequency range, the mirror speed is chosen to suit the detector: it is common to scan slowly with slow-responding pyroelectric detectors and quickly with fast MCT detectors, keeping the signal frequencies within each detector's useful bandwidth.

Because the interferogram is cut off at a finite path difference, transforming it directly gives a sinc-shaped broadening with negative side lobes on both sides of each line. Apodization suppresses this by multiplying the interferogram by a function that falls smoothly toward the ends of the path-difference range; the side lobes become smaller at the cost of broader lines. Delays in the optics and electronics also break the left–right symmetry, so in methods that measure one side much farther than the other, the phase is found from the two-sided data near the centerburst and used for correction (the Mertz method and others).

faq.q: What is the sharp peak in the middle of an interferogram?
faq.a: It is the centerburst at zero path difference (ZPD), formed because all wavenumber components reinforce one another in phase there. It is used for aligning the interferometer and for fixing the origin of the path difference.

faq.q: How is the spectrum obtained from an interferogram?
faq.a: The mean component is removed, an apodization function is applied, the phase is corrected if needed, and the result is Fourier transformed with respect to path difference. Transmittance is found from the ratio of this spectrum to the one measured without a sample.

faq.q: What does the interferogram of monochromatic light look like?
faq.a: It is a cosine wave of constant amplitude that repeats one cycle for each wavelength of path difference. There is no centerburst, and the amplitude does not decrease however far the mirror moves, so it can serve as a ruler for path difference.

自由スペクトル領域.desc: The wavelength (or frequency) range that can be used without transmission peaks or diffracted light of adjacent orders overlapping. It is λ²/(2nL) for a Fabry–Perot and about λ/m for order m of a grating.

about.h: A range set by repeating orders
about.p: Both diffraction gratings and Fabry–Perot interferometers satisfy the same condition again and again as the order m changes, so one wavelength in order m and a different wavelength in order m + 1 can appear at the same position. The free spectral range (FSR) is the range of wavelength (or frequency) that can be used without such overlap with the adjacent order. If the incoming light has a bandwidth wider than the FSR, it can no longer be told apart from the peaks of another order, so the FSR sets the upper limit on the range handled at once. Higher-resolution elements are often used in higher orders and tend to have narrower FSRs.

about.h: Formulas for the Fabry–Perot and the grating
about.p: For a Fabry–Perot with index n and spacing L, the transmission peaks are spaced by c/(2nL) in frequency and λ²/(2nL) in wavelength. A fused silica plate 1 mm thick (n ≈ 1.444) used at 1550 nm gives about 104 GHz, or about 0.83 nm. The peaks are evenly spaced in frequency, but their wavelength spacing changes in proportion to λ². When the medium is dispersive, strictly the group index should be used instead of n; here a group index of about 1.463 gives about 102 GHz. For order m of a diffraction grating, the FSR is about λ/m; this is why the second-order 400 nm light overlaps the position where 800 nm is measured in first order.

For a Fabry–Perot, the FSR divided by the full width at half maximum of the transmission peaks is the finesse F. At constant F, making the spacing L longer narrows both the FSR and the peak width in the same proportion. To raise resolution while keeping a wide FSR, therefore, you must increase F by raising the mirror reflectivity rather than changing the spacing. Ring resonators follow the same idea, using FSR = λ²/(n_g L) with L the circumference, and the ratio of FSR to linewidth is called the finesse. In silicon wire waveguides the group index and effective index differ greatly, so take care not to confuse them.

When an element has a narrow FSR, it is combined with another element that restricts the range. An echelle spectrometer working in high orders separates the orders with a cross-disperser, and a Fabry–Perot interferometer admits only light narrower than its FSR through a pre-dispersing spectrometer or bandpass filter. Conversely, the FSR's role as an evenly spaced frequency ruler is exploited: it serves as a scale when sweeping a laser's frequency, and etalons whose FSR is matched to the channel spacing of optical communication (for example 100 GHz) are used to manage wavelengths.

faq.q: How do you calculate the free spectral range?
faq.a: For a Fabry–Perot it is c/(2nL) in frequency and λ²/(2nL) in wavelength. With an air spacing of 5 mm it is about 30 GHz. For order m of a diffraction grating it is about λ/m.

faq.q: How are FSR and finesse related?
faq.a: The finesse is the FSR divided by the full width at half maximum of the transmission peaks. With an FSR of 30 GHz and a finesse of 100, the peak width is about 300 MHz.

faq.q: Why is the FSR often stated in frequency?
faq.a: Because the transmission peaks of a Fabry–Perot and the longitudinal modes of a laser are evenly spaced in frequency, whereas in wavelength their spacing changes in proportion to λ². When dealing with a wide range, frequency or wavenumber makes comparison easier.

フィネス.desc: The free spectral range of a Fabry–Perot interferometer divided by the full width at half maximum of its transmission peaks. For lossless mirrors it is π√R/(1 − R), increasing with reflectance.

about.p: The transmission peaks of a Fabry–Perot interferometer are spaced by the free spectral range (FSR), and their sharpness is expressed by the finesse F = FSR/δν (δν is the full width at half maximum). For two identical mirrors without absorption, F = π√R/(1 − R): about 30 for R = 0.90, about 103 for 0.97, and about 313 for 0.99. The quantity 4R/(1 − R)² that appears in the transmission formula T = 1/[1 + (4R/(1 − R)²) sin²(δ/2)] is a different quantity called the coefficient of finesse, so take care not to confuse them.

The resolving power of a Fabry–Perot interferometer is the product of the interference order m = 2nL/λ and the finesse, R = mF. With a mirror spacing of 5 mm, a wavelength of 500 nm and a finesse of 30, m = 20000 and R = 6×10⁵, more than an order of magnitude higher than a grating spectrometer. But the FSR, λ²/(2nL) = 0.025 nm, is narrow, so measuring a wide wavelength range requires first narrowing the range with a grating spectrometer or filter. The finesse can also be described as roughly how many resolvable peaks fit within the FSR.

Real interferometers have a lower finesse than the value set by reflectance alone. Surface irregularities of the mirrors (flatness) or a deviation from parallelism between the two shift the resonant wavelength from place to place, broadening the peaks. Obliquely incident light, beam divergence, and absorption or scattering in the mirrors do the same. As a guide, the overall finesse is found by adding the inverse squares of the finesses due to each factor, and it is set by the lowest one. High-finesse resonators use ultra-low-loss dielectric multilayer mirrors and reach values above 100,000.

faq.q: How is finesse calculated?
faq.a: In measurement, it is found by dividing the FSR by the full width at half maximum of a transmission peak. From the reflectance R of lossless mirrors, it can be estimated as F ≈ π√R/(1 − R). For R = 0.97 it is about 103.

faq.q: How do finesse and Q factor differ?
faq.a: Finesse is the ratio of the FSR to the peak width, and the Q factor is the ratio of the resonant frequency to the peak width. A longer resonator has a higher order, so for the same finesse the Q factor is larger, with the relation Q = mF.

faq.q: Does raising the finesse raise the resolving power without limit?
faq.a: Since the resolving power is mF, it does rise, but mirror flatness, parallelism and absorption cap the actual finesse. Also, the sharper the transmission peaks, the more strongly they are affected by fluctuations in the light frequency or the mirror spacing.

アッベ数.desc: A number expressing how small the dispersion of an optical material is, Vd = (nd − 1)/(nF − nC). The larger it is, the smaller the difference in index between wavelengths and the less chromatic aberration arises.

about.p: The Abbe number is found from the index nd at the d line (587.6 nm) and the index difference nF − nC between the F line (486.1 nm) and C line (656.3 nm), as Vd = (nd − 1)/(nF − nC). The denominator expresses the dispersion and the numerator the refracting power, so the Abbe number shows how little the colors separate relative to how strongly the material refracts. BK7-type glass is about 64, calcium fluoride about 95, and dense flint glasses around 20–30. Ve, referenced to the e line (546.1 nm), is also used.

Optical glasses are classified on a diagram (the Abbe diagram) with the index nd on the vertical axis and the Abbe number on the horizontal axis. As a guide, glasses with an Abbe number above about 50 are crown glasses and those below are flint glasses. Flint glasses contain heavy elements such as lead or titanium, giving a higher index at the cost of larger dispersion. In recent years they have been replaced by lead-free glasses for environmental reasons, but the classification works the same way.

The condition for two cemented lenses to bring two wavelengths to the same focus is φ₁/V₁ + φ₂/V₂ = 0, using the powers φ and Abbe numbers V. A positive lens of high-Abbe-number crown is combined with a negative lens of low-Abbe-number flint; the larger the difference in Abbe numbers, the weaker each lens can be, making aberration correction easier. Apochromats, which also bring a third wavelength to the same focus, use fluorite or special low-dispersion glasses with anomalous partial dispersion.

faq.q: What does a large Abbe number mean?
faq.a: The difference in index between wavelengths is small, so chromatic aberration is small even in a single lens. Calcium fluoride (about 95) and special low-dispersion glasses are used in telephoto lenses and high-performance microscope objectives to suppress color fringing.

faq.q: How is the Abbe number calculated?
faq.a: Using the indices at the d, F and C lines, Vd = (nd − 1)/(nF − nC). With nd = 1.5168 and nF − nC = 0.00806 it is about 64. Take care not to swap the numerator and denominator.

faq.q: Do higher-index glasses have lower Abbe numbers?
faq.a: As a tendency, yes: higher-index glasses have their ultraviolet absorption shifted to longer wavelengths and tend to have larger dispersion. But some materials, such as lanthanum-containing glasses, have a relatively large Abbe number despite a high index.

セルマイヤーの式.desc: An equation expressing the wavelength dependence of the refractive index as n²(λ) = 1 + Σ Bᵢλ²/(λ² − Cᵢ). Each term corresponds to an ultraviolet or infrared absorption resonance, and it represents dispersion in the transparent range accurately.

about.h: Refractive index as a sum of oscillators
about.p: The Sellmeier equation, n²(λ) = 1 + Σ Bᵢλ²/(λ² − Cᵢ), treats the electrons and lattice vibrations in a material as oscillators with fixed resonance wavelengths and adds up their contributions. Bᵢ is the strength of each oscillator and √Cᵢ its resonance wavelength; each term diverges as λ approaches √Cᵢ. For optical glasses the standard form has three terms, two for ultraviolet and one for infrared resonances, and glass catalogs list B₁–B₃ and C₁–C₃. Because it contains no damping from absorption, it is meant for the transparent range away from the resonances.

about.h: Units of the coefficients and a worked example
about.p: Catalog coefficients normally take λ in µm and give Cᵢ in µm². Mistaking Cᵢ for the resonance wavelength itself (in µm) gives completely wrong values. With representative coefficients for fused silica (the Malitson formula), n ≈ 1.4585 at 587.6 nm and n ≈ 1.4440 at 1550 nm. Because the equation can be differentiated analytically, it is also well suited to finding the group index n − λ dn/dλ and, from the second derivative, the group velocity dispersion. In fused silica the material zero-dispersion wavelength, where the second derivative vanishes, lies at about 1.27 µm.

about.h: How it differs from the Cauchy equation
about.p: A formula with a similar purpose is the Cauchy equation, which uses powers of the inverse wavelength, such as n = A + B/λ² + C/λ⁴. It is accurate enough over a narrow visible range but has no term for infrared absorption, so it fails at wavelengths beyond the near infrared. The Sellmeier equation, being based on oscillators, is accurate over a wide range, but neither is guaranteed outside the range it was fitted to. The coefficients are found by fitting to measured data, so note also that Bᵢ and Cᵢ do not necessarily match the actual strengths and wavelengths of absorptions exactly.

about.h: How it is used in design
about.p: Optical design software calculates the refractive index at any wavelength from each glass's Sellmeier coefficients and evaluates chromatic aberration. The Abbe number and partial dispersion ratios can also be computed from indices obtained with the equation. In lasers and optical communications, the group index and group velocity dispersion are found to estimate pulse broadening and fiber dispersion, and for nonlinear optical crystals, separate coefficients are given for the ordinary and extraordinary rays to calculate phase-matching angles and wavelengths. Temperature dependence is handled separately, with temperature-dependent coefficients or the thermo-optic coefficient dn/dT.

faq.q: What does Cᵢ in the Sellmeier equation represent?
faq.a: It is the square of a resonance wavelength, so √Cᵢ is the resonance wavelength. Catalogs normally take λ in µm and give Cᵢ in µm², and confusing the units throws the refractive index far off.

faq.q: Should I use the Sellmeier or the Cauchy equation?
faq.a: For a wide wavelength range or wavelengths beyond the near infrared, the Sellmeier equation, which includes infrared resonance terms, is the right choice. For an approximation over a narrow visible range, the simple Cauchy equation may be enough.

faq.q: Can group velocity dispersion be found from the Sellmeier equation?
faq.a: Yes. Compute GVD = λ³/(2πc²)·d²n/dλ² from the second derivative of the index with respect to wavelength. With the fused silica coefficients, this gives about 36 fs²/mm at 800 nm.

正常分散.desc: The property that the refractive index decreases as the wavelength gets longer. It is seen in the transmission range of transparent materials; inside absorption bands it reverses into anomalous dispersion.

about.p: Normal dispersion is the property that the refractive index becomes smaller at longer wavelengths, that is, dn/dλ < 0. The transmission range of a transparent material lies between the ultraviolet electronic resonances and the infrared lattice-vibration resonances, and at shorter wavelengths, closer to the ultraviolet resonances, the index is higher and changes more steeply. In N-BK7, dn/dλ is about −0.050 µm⁻¹ at 550 nm and about −0.014 µm⁻¹ at 1 µm. White light splitting in a prism with blue bent most, and the chromatic aberration of a single lens, both come from this normal dispersion.

Inside an absorption band, anomalous dispersion occurs, with the index increasing at longer wavelengths. Refractive index and absorption are linked by the Kramers–Kronig relations, which follow from causality, so a strong absorption brings large changes in index on either side of it. Normal dispersion is a historical name reflecting what is ordinarily seen in transparent materials; it does not mean that anomalous dispersion is a physically exceptional phenomenon. Near an absorption band the group velocity can exceed c or even become negative, but this does not mean that a signal travels faster than c.

about.h: A different usage for pulse dispersion
about.p: In ultrashort pulses and optical fibers, normal dispersion is used to mean group velocity dispersion β₂ > 0 (D < 0 in terms of the fiber dispersion parameter), the state in which longer wavelengths travel at higher group velocity. This is a different condition from dn/dλ < 0 and corresponds to the second derivative d²n/dλ² > 0. Fused silica has dn/dλ < 0 throughout its transparent range, yet at wavelengths longer than about 1.27 µm its group velocity dispersion becomes negative, and the 1.55 µm band is called anomalous dispersion. Which meaning is intended must be judged from context.

about.h: Dealing with normal dispersion in design
about.p: Since normal dispersion itself cannot be avoided, optical systems correct it with combinations that cancel each other. An achromatic lens combines a positive lens of low-dispersion crown glass with a negative lens of high-dispersion flint glass so that two wavelengths come to the same focus. In femtosecond lasers, pulses broadened by the positive group velocity dispersion of glass are compressed by applying negative dispersion with prism pairs, grating pairs or chirped mirrors. In optical fibers, waveguide dispersion is added to shift the zero-dispersion wavelength, and fibers with small dispersion in the communication band have been made.

faq.q: What is the difference between normal and anomalous dispersion?
faq.a: Normal dispersion is the property that the index becomes smaller at longer wavelengths, seen in the transparent range. Anomalous dispersion is the opposite, with the index becoming larger at longer wavelengths, and occurs inside absorption bands.

faq.q: What happens to the group index with normal dispersion?
faq.a: Because dn/dλ < 0, the group index ng = n − λ dn/dλ is larger than the index n. The envelope of a pulse or modulation travels at c/ng, slower than the phase velocity c/n.

faq.q: Is the 1.55 µm band of fiber normal dispersion?
faq.a: In terms of the refractive index it is normal dispersion, with dn/dλ < 0, but in terms of group velocity dispersion standard single-mode fiber has D > 0 there and it is called anomalous dispersion. When discussing dispersion, check which definition is meant.

誘電体多層膜ミラー.desc: A mirror made by alternately stacking λ/4 layers of dielectrics with different indices so that the reflections at each boundary add up. It has almost no absorption and can exceed 99.9% reflectance.

about.p: When films of high index nH and low index nL are stacked alternately, each with an optical thickness of λ₀/4, the light reflected at successive boundaries is shifted by a half wave on the round trip, and together with the phase reversal at the reflections they all add in phase. For an (HL)ᴺH structure the reflectance is R = [(1 − Y)/(1 + Y)]², Y = (nH/nL)^(2N)·nH²/ns, and each additional pair multiplies Y by (nH/nL)². Eleven layers of TiO₂ (2.35) and SiO₂ (1.45) give about 99.1%.

about.h: Width of the high-reflectance band and higher-order bands
about.p: The relative width of the band with high reflectance is Δλ/λ₀ ≈ (4/π) arcsin[(nH − nL)/(nH + nL)], set only by the index ratio; it is about 0.30 for TiO₂ and SiO₂. Adding pairs barely widens it, but increases the reflectance and sharpens the band edges. High-reflectance bands also appear at λ₀/3 and λ₀/5, where each layer is an odd multiple of λ/4, while at λ₀/2 each layer becomes a half-wave absentee layer and there is almost no reflection.

about.h: Differences from metal mirrors and uses
about.p: Aluminum and silver mirrors reflect over a wide range of wavelengths, but their absorption limits reflectance to about 90–98% and they heat up at high power. Dielectric mirrors have almost no absorption, so they are used as laser resonator mirrors and in high-finesse cavities with reflectances above 99.99%. In exchange, their reflection band is limited, and at oblique incidence the band shifts to shorter wavelengths and splits by polarization, so they are designed for a set angle and polarization.

faq.q: How does the reflectance change as pairs are added?
faq.a: Each added pair multiplies Y by (nH/nL)², and the reflectance approaches 100%. For TiO₂ and SiO₂ that is about 2.6 times per pair. The band width barely changes, however, and film stress and scattering loss grow with the number of layers.

faq.q: What happens at oblique incidence?
faq.a: The phase thickness in the films shrinks by the factor cosθ, so the reflection band shifts to shorter wavelengths. The effective indices also differ for s- and p-polarization, and the p-polarization band is narrower. Mirrors used at 45° are designed for that angle.

faq.q: Can a mirror reflect two wavelengths at once?
faq.a: A plain λ/4 stack has high-reflectance bands only at odd fractions of the design wavelength, so it cannot reflect 1064 nm and 532 nm together. This is achieved with designs whose thicknesses depart from λ/4, or by combining two stacks.

フッ化カルシウム.desc: Crystalline CaF₂. It transmits from about 0.13 µm in the vacuum ultraviolet to about 10 µm in the infrared and has low dispersion. Used in ultraviolet laser optics, infrared windows and apochromatic objectives.

about.h: A crystal transparent from vacuum UV to infrared
about.p: Calcium fluoride (CaF₂) is a cubic crystal that occurs naturally as fluorite; for optics, artificially grown single crystals are used. Its large band gap puts the ultraviolet absorption edge at short wavelengths and its lattice-vibration absorption lies at long wavelengths, so it transmits from about 0.13 µm to about 10 µm. Being cubic, it has almost no birefringence in the visible and infrared and disturbs polarization little. Its index is low, about 1.434 at the d line, so the reflection from one surface at normal incidence is about 3.2%, less than the roughly 4.2% of BK7.

about.h: Low dispersion and unusual partial dispersion
about.p: The Abbe number of CaF₂ is large, about 95, so its dispersion is small, and its partial dispersion ratio also departs from the line followed by ordinary optical glasses. Combined with glasses, it therefore makes it easier to bring not just two wavelengths but a third to the same focus, and it is used in apochromatic microscope objectives and in the fluorite lenses that suppress color fringing in telephoto lenses. Fluorine-containing special low-dispersion glasses have similar properties and are widely used because they are easier to work than CaF₂, but there remain situations where crystalline CaF₂ has the edge in correcting chromatic aberration.

CaF₂ has high deep-ultraviolet transmission and its absorption increases little under intense ultraviolet light, so it has been used together with fused silica in ArF excimer laser (193 nm) optics and in the projection lenses of semiconductor lithography tools. For the 157 nm F₂ laser, ordinary fused silica does not transmit enough, so CaF₂ was considered as the main material. It turned out, however, that at such short wavelengths even a cubic crystal shows a slight birefringence that depends on the propagation direction (intrinsic birefringence), and designs that cancel it by combining crystal orientations became necessary.

CaF₂ is soft, with a Knoop hardness a fraction of that of BK7, so it scratches easily and takes effort to polish. Its thermal expansion coefficient is about 19×10⁻⁶/K, more than 30 times that of fused silica, so it cracks easily under rapid temperature changes, and it also cleaves readily along {111} planes. It is very slightly soluble in water, but not enough to be a problem in normal environments. In the infrared it is used for windows and lenses for thermography in the 3–5 µm band, but absorption increases in the 8–12 µm band, where germanium or zinc selenide is used instead.

faq.q: At what wavelengths can calcium fluoride be used?
faq.a: A few mm thick, it transmits from about 0.13 µm in the vacuum ultraviolet to about 10 µm in the infrared. One material covers ultraviolet laser optics, infrared windows and lenses for the 3–5 µm band, and visible achromatic optics.

faq.q: What is a fluorite lens?
faq.a: A lens made of crystalline calcium fluoride. Its large Abbe number of about 95 and unusual partial dispersion let it correct chromatic aberration well, so it is used in microscope objectives and telephoto lenses to suppress color fringing.

faq.q: What precautions are needed when handling calcium fluoride?
faq.a: It is soft and scratches easily, and its large thermal expansion makes it prone to cracking under rapid temperature changes. When cleaning, bonding or heating it in vacuum equipment, change the temperature slowly and avoid rubbing hard.

レーザー損傷しきい値.desc: The fluence (J/cm²) or intensity at which laser light begins to damage an optical component or coating. It varies with wavelength, pulse width and beam size, so it is quoted together with those conditions.

about.h: A value that only means something with its conditions
about.p: The laser-induced damage threshold (LIDT) is the fluence (J/cm²) or intensity at which an optical component or coating begins to be damaged, and it varies greatly with wavelength, pulse width, repetition rate, beam size and the number of shots. Thresholds expressed as fluence are normally lower for shorter pulses. LIDT is therefore quoted with its conditions, as in so many J/cm² at 1064 nm, 10 ns and 10 Hz, and values for different conditions cannot be compared directly. For continuous-wave light, where thermal damage dominates, it may also be given in W/cm (power per beam diameter) as well as W/cm².

The damage mechanism changes with pulse width. With continuous light or long pulses, thermal damage dominates: defects and contamination in coatings or on surfaces absorb light, heat up, and melt or crack. With ns pulses, the distance heat spreads during the pulse scales with the square root of the pulse width, so as a guide the threshold fluence also scales with the square root of the pulse width, becoming lower for shorter pulses. For pulses shorter than a ps, mechanisms in which the material itself is ionized by multiphoton absorption and avalanche ionization take over, and damage approaches a deterministic process that depends little on defects. Materials with large band gaps are therefore favored for short pulses.

A common mistake when comparing values is the treatment of beam size. For a Gaussian beam with 1/e² radius w, the fluence at the center is 2E/(πw²), twice the average value obtained by dividing the pulse energy E by the area πw². A 10 mJ pulse at w = 1 mm gives an average of about 0.32 J/cm² and a center value of about 0.64 J/cm². Smaller beams are also less likely to hit a weak defect within the illuminated area, so they tend to give higher thresholds, and it is safer to use values obtained with a beam the same size as or larger than in the application.

Test methods for LIDT are specified in ISO 21254, including 1-on-1, with one shot per site, and S-on-1, with many shots on the same site. Many sites are irradiated at different fluences, the fraction of sites damaged is plotted against fluence, and the threshold is taken as the value extrapolated to zero damage probability. With repeated irradiation, damage often occurs at lower values than with a single shot, and surface contamination also lowers the threshold substantially. In design, catalog values are converted to the conditions of use and then an additional safety margin is taken.

faq.q: What are the units of laser-induced damage threshold?
faq.a: For pulsed light it is given as fluence (J/cm²), and for continuous light as intensity (W/cm²) or power per diameter (W/cm). In every case it is quoted together with the test conditions, such as wavelength and pulse width.

faq.q: How do you scale thresholds between pulse widths?
faq.a: In the ns range where heating is the main cause, a rule of thumb that fluence scales with the square root of pulse width is used. It does not apply to pulses shorter than a ps or to widely different pulse widths, so check measured values for those conditions.

faq.q: Why does the threshold change with beam size?
faq.a: Most damage starts at defects in coatings or surfaces, so a smaller illuminated area is less likely to hit a defect and gives a higher threshold. Values measured with a beam smaller than in actual use tend to be optimistic.

応力複屈折.desc: Birefringence induced by stress in an isotropic material. The path difference is Δ = Kσd (K is the photoelastic coefficient), and residual stress in glass is expressed as path difference per cm of thickness (nm/cm).

about.h: Stress makes an isotropic material anisotropic
about.p: Even isotropic materials such as glass and plastic develop a slight difference in refractive index between the stress direction and the direction perpendicular to it when stressed. This is stress birefringence (photoelasticity): the index difference between the two polarizations is Δn = Kσ, and the path difference after thickness d is Δ = Kσd. K is the photoelastic coefficient, expressed in Pa⁻¹, and 10⁻¹² Pa⁻¹ is called 1 brewster. Most optical glasses are a few brewsters; for a glass with K = 2.8×10⁻¹² Pa⁻¹, a stress of about 0.18 MPa gives a path difference of 5 nm per 1 cm of thickness.

As glass cools, stress is left behind by the difference in cooling between surface and interior. To reduce it, optical glass is annealed by cooling slowly from around the annealing point, and specifications state the birefringence from residual stress as path difference per 1 cm of thickness (nm/cm). In ISO 10110 drawing notation the maximum permitted value is specified in nm/cm, as in 0/5. Instruments using polarization and interferometers choose precision-annealed glass of a few nm/cm or less, while illumination optics normally do not demand much. Values often differ between the center and edge of a blank, so check them in the part actually used.

about.h: When unintended birefringence becomes a problem
about.p: Stress birefringence also arises during use. Clamping a lens tightly in its cell, or adhesive shrinking as it cures, disturbs polarization through local stress. In high-power lasers, the temperature distribution from absorption creates thermal stress, causing thermally induced birefringence that degrades polarization along with thermal lensing. Injection-molded plastic lenses and containers can have large birefringence from molding stress and molecular orientation. On the other hand, some flint glasses with a high lead content (such as SF57) have K close to zero and are used in elements that must preserve polarization.

Stress birefringence also provides a way to see stress. Placing a specimen between two crossed polarizers makes only the birefringent regions bright, and in white light, fringes of interference colors appear according to the path difference. Photoelastic experiments use this, loading transparent resin models to study the stress distribution inside structures. In glass inspection, compensator methods such as the Sénarmont method measure the path difference in nm. The mottled pattern seen when looking at a tempered glass window through polarized sunglasses is also birefringence from the stress left by tempering.

faq.q: How do you calculate the path difference from stress birefringence?
faq.a: Use Δ = Kσd with the photoelastic coefficient K, stress σ and thickness d. With K = 2.8×10⁻¹² Pa⁻¹, a stress of 1 MPa and a thickness of 10 mm, it is about 28 nm.

faq.q: What does the unit nm/cm mean?
faq.a: It is the path difference between the two polarizations per 1 cm of thickness, expressing the birefringence caused by residual stress in glass. A path difference of 25 nm through 5 cm of thickness is 5 nm/cm.

faq.q: How can stress birefringence be reduced?
faq.a: Reduce stress by choosing well-annealed glass, not overtightening mounts, and using adhesives that shrink little on curing or compliant mounting. For elements where polarization matters, another option is to choose a glass with a small photoelastic coefficient.

ファイバブラッググレーティング.desc: A periodic index structure written into a fiber core that reflects only light at the Bragg wavelength λB = 2n_effΛ. Used as strain and temperature sensors and as wavelength filters.

about.h: How it reflects, and how it is written
about.p: In an FBG the core index varies slightly with period Λ, and the weak reflections from each plane add in phase at the wavelength for which the round-trip path difference 2n_effΛ is exactly one wavelength. For n_eff = 1.447 and Λ = 535.6 nm, λB ≈ 1550 nm. The reflection bandwidth is about 0.1–1 nm, and other wavelengths pass almost untouched. A common writing method changes the index of a germanium-doped core with ultraviolet laser light made to interfere through a phase mask.

Stretching the fiber lengthens the period, and the photoelastic effect slightly lowers the effective index, so the Bragg wavelength increases by ΔλB = (1 − pe)ελB. With pe ≈ 0.22 this is about 1.2 pm/µε in the 1550 nm band. A rise in temperature lengthens it by about 10 pm/K through the thermo-optic effect and thermal expansion. Since a 1 K change corresponds to about 8 µε, strain measurements subtract the temperature contribution using a strain-free reference FBG.

Because an FBG measures through changes in wavelength, it is largely immune to fluctuations in light intensity and connection losses, and it also resists electromagnetic noise. Dozens of FBGs with different Bragg wavelengths can be placed on one fiber and read out by their reflection wavelengths, measuring strain or temperature at many points simultaneously. Besides monitoring bridges, tunnels, aircraft wings and power equipment, in optical communications they also serve as wavelength filters, dispersion compensators and fiber-laser resonator mirrors.

faq.q: How sensitive is an FBG to strain?
faq.a: About 1.2 pm/µε in the 1550 nm band. A strain of 500 µε shifts the wavelength by about 0.60 nm. If the interrogator's wavelength resolution is 1 pm, strains of about 1 µε can be resolved.

faq.q: How are temperature and strain distinguished?
faq.a: The basic approach is to place nearby a reference FBG fixed so that no strain reaches it, and subtract its wavelength change as the temperature contribution. Another approach combines two kinds of FBG with different temperature sensitivities and solves the two equations for both quantities.

faq.q: How do FBGs differ from distributed sensors?
faq.a: An FBG is a point sensor that measures only where it is written (quasi-distributed when many are lined up). Raman and Brillouin distributed sensors can measure the full length of an unmodified fiber continuously, but fall short of FBGs in spatial resolution and measurement time.

分布型光ファイバセンサ.desc: A sensor that measures the backscatter in a fiber position by position, using the round-trip time, so that the whole length of the fiber acts as a continuous sensor. Raman, Brillouin and Rayleigh scattering are used for different quantities.

about.p: In distributed sensing, a light pulse is launched into the fiber and the scattered light returning is recorded over time. Light returning a time t after launch was scattered at position z = ct/(2n) (n is the group index), so information at each position is obtained in the same way as with an OTDR. The spatial resolution is set by the pulse width, about 1 m for 10 ns. A single instrument can monitor tens of km of fiber, and the sensing part needs no electricity.

about.h: Using the three kinds of scattering
about.p: In Raman scattering the anti-Stokes intensity depends strongly on temperature, so temperature is measured from its ratio to the Stokes light (DTS). In Brillouin scattering the frequency shift of about 10.8 GHz in the 1550 nm band changes with strain and temperature, so strain distributions in structures are measured (BOTDR and BOTDA). Rayleigh scattering is elastic scattering with no frequency change, and with a narrow-linewidth laser the phase of the scattered light captures vibration and sound (DAS).

Each pulse must wait until the scattered light from the previous one has returned from the far end of the fiber, so the repetition rate is limited to c/(2nL), about 2 kHz for 50 km. Because the scattered light is weak, finding temperature or strain accurately requires many averages, and measurements take longer the longer the distance and the finer the spatial resolution. Pulse width, number of averages and method are therefore chosen to suit the application.

faq.q: What distances can be measured?
faq.a: It depends on the method, but 10 to several tens of km is typical for Raman DTS, and tens of km for Brillouin methods. Fiber loss weakens the scattered light, so temperature and strain accuracy drop as the distance grows.

faq.q: Can ordinary telecom fiber be used?
faq.a: Yes. Brillouin methods and DAS can often use already-installed telecom single-mode fiber as is, while Raman DTS commonly uses multimode fiber. How the fiber is fixed changes how strain and vibration are transferred to it.

faq.q: Which is better, distributed sensing or a line of FBGs?
faq.a: FBGs suit measuring fixed points with high accuracy and speed, while distributed sensing suits finding anomalies over long sections where the location is not known in advance. The two are also used in combination.

分布型温度センサ.desc: A technique that finds the temperature at each position along a fiber from the intensity ratio of anti-Stokes to Stokes Raman scattering. Used to monitor the temperature of power cables, pipelines and wells.

about.h: Measuring temperature from a Raman intensity ratio
about.p: Distributed temperature sensing (DTS) sends light pulses into a fiber and finds the temperature from the Raman-scattered light returning backward. Raman scattering in silica appears about 13 THz (about 440 cm⁻¹) away from the incident light, with the Stokes light on the long-wavelength side and the anti-Stokes light on the short-wavelength side. Anti-Stokes light arises from molecules whose vibrations are already excited, so it depends strongly on temperature through the Boltzmann factor exp(−hΔν/kT) that gives their number. Taking the ratio of the two cancels, to a degree, changes in source power and in losses from fiber bending.

The temperature coefficient of the intensity ratio is hΔν/(kT²); for Δν = 13.2 THz it is about 0.7%/K at 300 K and about 0.45%/K at 100 °C, becoming smaller at high temperature. Raman-scattered light is much weaker than Rayleigh-scattered light, so many measurements are averaged to reduce noise, and a single reading often takes from seconds to minutes. Position is found from the round-trip time as in OTDR, and a pulse width of 10 ns gives a distance resolution of about 1 m. Over relatively short distances, multimode fiber, which collects more light, is widely used; for longer distances, lower-loss single-mode fiber is used.

Distributed temperature can also be measured from the frequency shift of Brillouin scattering. The Brillouin approach suits long distances and can also measure strain, but because both strain and temperature change the frequency, the effect of strain must be separated when only temperature is wanted. Raman DTS has the strength of measuring temperature almost without influence from strain. On the other hand, the Stokes and anti-Stokes wavelengths lie far apart (about 200 nm with 1550 nm excitation) and suffer different fiber losses, so to correct changes in this difference, a method that loops the fiber and measures from both ends is used.

Because DTS can continuously measure the temperature distribution over several km to tens of km with a single fiber, it is used where placing many point thermometers would be difficult. On buried power cables, temperature is used to judge how much more current can be carried, and in tunnels and large buildings it is used for fire detection. In oil and geothermal wells, the temperature distribution along the depth reveals where fluids enter and leave, and in dams and levees temperature changes from leakage are sought. Another advantage is that fiber does not conduct electricity, so it can be used where there is high voltage or a risk of explosion.

faq.q: Why does DTS use the ratio of anti-Stokes to Stokes light?
faq.a: Anti-Stokes light depends strongly on temperature while Stokes light depends on it only weakly, so taking the ratio keeps the temperature information while canceling fluctuations in source power and fiber loss.

faq.q: What sets the spatial resolution of DTS?
faq.a: It is set mainly by the pulse width and the receiver bandwidth, with a distance resolution of about cτ/(2ng). With a 10 ns pulse and a group index of 1.468 it is about 1 m; shorter pulses improve resolution but return less light.

faq.q: How can the temperature precision of DTS be improved?
faq.a: The basic approach is more averaging: noise is inversely proportional to the square root of the number of averages, so making the measurement time 4 times longer roughly halves it. Coarsening the spatial resolution to gather more light per point is another option.

ブリルアン散乱.desc: Scattering of light by sound waves in a medium. The frequency shift is 2nVa/λ, about 11 GHz in silica fiber in the 1550 nm band, and it changes with strain and temperature.

about.p: Brillouin scattering is the scattering of light by sound waves (acoustic phonons) traveling through a material. The sound wave creates a periodic variation in refractive index that reflects light like a moving diffraction grating, and because this grating moves at the speed of sound, the scattered light is shifted in frequency by the Doppler effect. The shift is 2nVa sin(θ/2)/λ for scattering angle θ, reaching its maximum of 2nVa/λ for backscattering (θ = 180°). In silica fiber in the 1550 nm band it is about 11 GHz, far smaller than the shift of Raman scattering by optical phonons (about 13 THz).

When the light is strong, the beat between the incident and backscattered light reinforces the sound wave through electrostriction, and that sound wave scatters still more light, a positive feedback. This is stimulated Brillouin scattering (SBS). The Brillouin gain bandwidth of silica fiber is narrow, tens of MHz, so it occurs especially readily with narrow-linewidth light. Putting A_eff = 80 µm², g_B = 5×10⁻¹¹ m/W and an effective length L_eff ≈ 20 km for a 50 km fiber into the threshold estimate 21A_eff/(g_B L_eff) gives about 1.7 mW. Actual thresholds can be higher, depending on factors such as the polarization state, but above threshold the backscattered light rises sharply and the power reaching the far end levels off.

about.h: As a strain and temperature sensor
about.p: The frequency shift is set by the speed of sound and the refractive index, both of which change with strain and temperature, so in silica fiber in the 1550 nm band it changes by about 0.05 MHz/µε with strain and about 1 MHz/K with temperature. A temperature change of 1 K thus shifts the frequency as much as a strain of about 20 µε. Methods include BOTDR, which measures spontaneous scattering, and BOTDA, which injects light from both ends and uses stimulated scattering; strain distributions can be measured over tens of km. To separate the temperature contribution, a fiber laid so that it carries no strain, or a Raman temperature sensor, is used alongside.

about.h: Also used for material characterization and light sources
about.p: Because the Brillouin frequency shift directly reflects the speed of sound, Brillouin spectroscopy is used to measure elastic moduli of materials optically without contact, and research using it in microscopes to examine the stiffness of cells and tissues is advancing. In optical communications, SBS is a nuisance that limits the power that can be sent, and it is suppressed by modulating the phase or frequency of the transmitted light to broaden its linewidth. Conversely, the narrow gain bandwidth is exploited in Brillouin lasers with extremely narrow linewidths and in narrowband filters that process microwave signals optically.

faq.q: What is the difference between Brillouin and Raman scattering?
faq.a: Brillouin scattering is caused by sound waves (acoustic phonons), with a shift of about 11 GHz in silica fiber in the 1550 nm band. Raman scattering is caused by molecular or crystal vibrations (optical phonons), with a shift of about 13 THz in silica, more than 1000 times larger.

faq.q: How is stimulated Brillouin scattering suppressed?
faq.a: By applying phase or frequency modulation to the laser to broaden its linewidth beyond the Brillouin gain bandwidth, shortening the fiber, or lowering the launched power. In optical communication transmitters, broadening the linewidth by modulation is commonly used.

faq.q: How are strain and temperature separated in a Brillouin sensor?
faq.a: The same frequency shift can come from either strain or temperature, so a single measurement cannot separate them. They are separated by laying a strain-free fiber alongside to measure only the temperature part, or by using a Raman DTS as well.

分布型音響センシング.desc: A method that detects vibration and sound along a fiber position by position, from changes in the phase of Rayleigh backscatter of narrow-linewidth light pulses. Used for seismic monitoring and intrusion detection.

about.h: Turning a fiber into a row of vibration sensors
about.p: Distributed acoustic sensing (DAS) sends pulses from a narrow-linewidth laser into a fiber and detects vibration and sound position by position from changes in the phase of the Rayleigh-scattered light returning backward. Light from the many scatterers within the pulse interferes, producing a waveform with a fixed pattern along the fiber. When the fiber stretches or contracts slightly, the optical path length of that section changes and so does the phase, so by repeatedly sending pulses and tracking the phase at each position, tens of km of fiber act as thousands of vibration sensors. A major feature is that fiber already laid for communication can be used as it is.

Because the phase reads changes in optical path length in units of the wavelength, it is extremely sensitive. With a section length over which phases are compared (the gauge length) of 10 m at a wavelength of 1550 nm, a strain of 1 nε (10⁻⁹) changes the phase by about 0.09 rad, including the photoelastic correction. The measurable vibration frequency is set by the pulse repetition rate. Each pulse is sent only after the scattered light from the previous one has returned, so for a 10 km fiber (group index 1.468) the repetition rate is at most about 10 kHz, and vibrations up to half that, about 5 kHz, can be measured. Longer fibers lower this upper limit.

about.h: How it differs from a microphone
about.p: What DAS senses is strain along the fiber axis (or its rate of change), not the sound pressure in air itself. It is therefore sensitive to waves that stretch and compress the fiber along its length, but responds hardly at all to longitudinal waves arriving perpendicular to the fiber. In addition, the Rayleigh-scattered intensity becomes randomly weak at some positions (fading), where the phase cannot be read correctly, so measures such as using several pulses at different frequencies are taken. A longer gauge length raises sensitivity but coarsens the spatial resolution.

DAS is used for earthquake observation and for surveys of underground structure using wells (VSP), and research using submarine telecommunication cables to observe earthquakes and waves on the seafloor is advancing. On land, it is also used to detect intrusion or digging around pipelines and facilities and to monitor road and rail traffic. Whereas Raman DTS measures temperature and Brillouin methods measure slowly varying distributions of strain and temperature, DAS measures rapidly changing vibrations, and the methods are sometimes combined on the same fiber so that temperature, strain and vibration are all monitored along one cable.

faq.q: What is the difference between DAS and DTS?
faq.a: DAS measures vibration and sound along a fiber from changes in the phase of Rayleigh-scattered light, while DTS measures temperature from the intensity ratio of Raman-scattered light. DAS suits fast changes from Hz to kHz, and DTS suits temperatures that change slowly over seconds to minutes.

faq.q: How long a fiber can DAS measure?
faq.a: Tens of km is typical, and in research, distances beyond 100 km have been measured using optical amplification. The longer the fiber, the slower the pulse repetition and the lower the upper limit of measurable vibration frequency.

faq.q: What sets the spatial resolution of DAS?
faq.a: It is set by the pulse width and the length of the section over which phases are compared (the gauge length), typically from a few m to tens of m. A longer gauge length raises sensitivity but makes fine positional differences harder to separate.

FMCW.desc: A method that transmits continuous light with a linearly swept frequency and finds range from the beat frequency with the returning light and velocity from the Doppler shift. The range resolution is c/(2B).

about.h: Turning time into frequency by sweeping
about.p: FMCW (frequency-modulated continuous wave) transmits continuous light whose frequency is swept linearly in time and interferes the returning light with part of the transmitted light. The returning light carries the frequency from a round-trip time τ = 2R/c earlier, so with a sweep slope S the beat frequency is f_b = Sτ, proportional to the range R. For example, sweeping 4 GHz in 20 µs gives a beat of about 200 MHz from an object 150 m away. A key feature is that range can be found by measuring a beat frequency of order MHz, without measuring times of order ps.

Range resolution is set by the sweep bandwidth B as ΔR = c/(2B). A 4 GHz sweep gives about 3.7 cm, independent of the sweep time. In practice, deviations of the sweep from linearity spread the beat frequency and degrade resolution, so techniques for correcting sweep linearity are important. Also, as the round-trip time approaches the laser's coherence time, the beat linewidth broadens, so the measurable range is also limited by the laser linewidth. For a laser with a Lorentzian linewidth of 100 kHz, the coherence length c/(πΔν) is about 950 m.

about.h: Measuring velocity at the same time
about.p: If the object is moving, a Doppler shift f_D = 2v/λ, where v is the line-of-sight velocity, is added to the returning light; at 1550 nm it is about 12.9 MHz for 10 m/s. A common method alternates up-sweeps and down-sweeps and separates range from the average of the two beat frequencies and velocity from their difference. To know velocity with the ToF approach, which measures pulse round-trip times, the change in position must be differentiated over time, but FMCW gives the line-of-sight velocity directly in a single measurement, which helps automotive LiDAR distinguish moving objects.

The idea of sweeping frequency and finding range from the beat was long used widely in radar; done with light, it is easier to take a wide sweep bandwidth, giving high resolution. In testing optical fibers and components, OFDR (optical frequency domain reflectometry), based on the same principle, measures reflection positions with sub-mm resolution. OCT using a wavelength-swept source is also the same mechanism as FMCW in that it finds depth from the interference of swept light. Optical FMCW uses coherent detection and so is robust against background light, but it needs a narrow-linewidth source and a precise sweep.

faq.q: How do you calculate the range resolution of FMCW?
faq.a: From the sweep bandwidth B, ΔR = c/(2B). With B = 4 GHz it is about 3.7 cm, and doubling the bandwidth halves it. It does not depend on how long the sweep takes.

faq.q: What is the difference between FMCW and ToF?
faq.a: ToF sends pulses and measures the round-trip time directly, while FMCW finds range from the beat frequency of continuous light with a swept frequency.
