FMCW detects by interference, so it resists background light and also measures velocity, but it needs a narrow-linewidth laser that can be swept.

faq.q: How do you find range from the beat frequency?
faq.a: With sweep slope S (bandwidth divided by sweep time), R = c f_b/(2S). When sweeping 4 GHz in 20 µs, a beat of 200 MHz means a range of about 150 m.

光学式エンコーダ.desc: A sensor that measures position or rotation angle by reading a graduated grating with light. A- and B-phase signals offset by 90° determine direction, and ×4 decoding or interpolation raises the resolution.

about.p: An optical encoder reads a scale or disk marked with bright and dark graduations using a light source and photodetectors, and finds position or rotation angle from the pattern. Transmissive types receive light passing through the graduations, and reflective types light reflected from them. Incremental types count a periodic signal produced by motion to find relative position, while absolute types write a code representing position onto the scale so that the absolute position is known immediately after power-up. They are widely used in machine tools, semiconductor manufacturing equipment and motor control.

about.h: A and B phases and interpolation
about.p: In an incremental type, two detector sections offset by a quarter period produce A- and B-phase signals 90° apart in phase. Which one changes first gives the direction, and counting the rising and falling edges of both divides each period into four (×4 decoding). In encoders with near-sinusoidal output, the A and B phases are treated as sine and cosine, the phase is found by arctangent, and each period is finely subdivided by interpolation. Dividing a 20 µm period by 1000 gives a resolution of 20 nm. The accuracy of interpolation, however, depends on errors in signal amplitude, offset and phase difference.

The resolution in a catalog is the size of one count, which is different from accuracy, describing how correct the position is. Accuracy is affected by errors in graduation spacing, mounting tilt and eccentricity, and interpolation error, and temperature changes also have a large effect. If a glass scale has a thermal expansion coefficient of 8×10⁻⁶/K, for example, a 1 m length grows by about 8 µm for each 1 K change. Precision machines therefore choose scales of a material whose expansion matches the machine, or control the temperature. In rotary types, eccentricity of the disk is a major source of angle error.

about.h: Response speed and ways to measure finer
about.p: The signal frequency is set by the product of the number of graduations and the speed of motion. A disk with 2500 lines per revolution turning at 3000 rpm gives an A phase of 125 kHz, and the detectors and circuits need enough bandwidth to follow it. To measure more finely, interferential encoders interfere beams diffracted by the grating, combining gratings with periods of order µm with interpolation to reach sub-nm resolution. Because the optical path is short and little affected by air fluctuations, they are also used instead of laser interferometers, for example for positioning the stages of lithography tools.

faq.q: What is the difference between incremental and absolute encoders?
faq.a: An incremental encoder counts pulses produced by motion to find position relative to a reference, so the reference must be re-established after power-up. An absolute encoder reads position directly from a code on the scale, so the position is known right after power-up.

faq.q: What is ×4 decoding in an encoder?
faq.a: It means counting all rising and falling edges of the A and B phases, offset by 90°, to divide each period into four counts. A disk with 1000 lines per revolution then gives 4000 counts per revolution, or 0.09° per count.

faq.q: What is the Z phase?
faq.a: It is a reference signal output only once per revolution, or once at a fixed position. In incremental encoders it is used to set the reference after power-up and to check that no counts have been missed.

レーザードップラー速度計.desc: A technique that measures velocities such as those of flows without contact, from the frequency v/d of light scattered by particles crossing the interference fringes formed where two laser beams cross.

about.h: Particles flickering as they cross fringes
about.p: A differential laser Doppler velocimeter (LDV) splits a laser beam in two and crosses the beams at an angle θ, forming interference fringes with spacing d = λ/(2 sin(θ/2)) where they cross. When a particle carried by the flow crosses the fringes, its scattered light flickers, and from the frequency f = v/d the velocity component perpendicular to the fringes is found. At a wavelength of 633 nm and a crossing angle of 6°, the fringe spacing is about 6.05 µm, and a particle at 10 m/s gives a signal of about 1.65 MHz. Calculating it as the difference between the Doppler shifts of the two beams gives the same result.

Only the small region where the two beams intersect (the measurement volume) is measured. Its size is set by the focused beam diameter and the crossing angle; a region 100 µm wide with a fringe spacing of 6 µm contains about 16 fringes. Each passing particle gives a short signal (a burst) with a Gaussian envelope, whose frequency is found by FFT or similar. In flow measurement, small particles of order µm are added to the flow, on the assumption that they follow it well. Particles that are too large lag behind rapidly changing flows.

In an arrangement without a frequency shift, the signal frequency depends only on the magnitude of the velocity, so the direction is unknown. One beam is therefore shifted by tens of MHz with an acousto-optic device so that the fringes move, allowing the direction, and the velocity of nearly stationary particles, to be measured. One pair of beams measures only one velocity component, so to measure two or three components, several beam pairs of different wavelengths are crossed in different orientations. Phase Doppler anemometry (PDA) also measures particle size at the same time from the phase difference of the scattered light.

about.h: From flow measurement to vibration measurement
about.p: Because LDV measures without disturbing the flow, it is used to measure velocities where probes cannot be inserted, such as in wind tunnels and water tanks, engine combustion chambers and flows inside pipes. Since velocity is found from a fringe spacing set by the wavelength and crossing angle, a wide range from slow to supersonic flows can be measured without calibration. A laser vibrometer, which measures the vibration of an object's surface, is a different arrangement that directs a single beam at the surface and measures the Doppler shift 2v/λ of the reflected light by interference, and is distinguished from the differential velocimeter. In medicine, there are also methods that assess skin blood flow from the frequency broadening of scattered light.

faq.q: How is velocity calculated with LDV?
faq.a: Multiply the fringe spacing d = λ/(2 sin(θ/2)) by the signal frequency f, so v = fd. With a fringe spacing of 6.05 µm and a signal of 1.65 MHz, the velocity is about 10 m/s.

faq.q: Does LDV need calibration?
faq.a: Velocity is found from the fringe spacing, which depends only on wavelength and crossing angle, so in principle no velocity calibration of the kind needed for a hot-wire anemometer is required. You do need to measure the crossing angle accurately and confirm that the two beams overlap well in the measurement volume.

faq.q: What is the difference between LDV and a laser vibrometer?
faq.a: A differential LDV measures flow velocity from the frequency at which particles cross the interference fringes of two beams. A laser vibrometer directs one beam at an object and measures the Doppler shift of the reflected light by interference with a reference beam to find the surface vibration velocity.

空間周波数.desc: The number of times bright and dark fringes repeat per unit length, the reciprocal of the period. Expressed in cycles/mm, it is used to compare the fineness of images and the performance of lenses.

about.h: Thinking of images as sums of fringes
about.p: Spatial frequency is the number of times bright and dark fringes repeat per unit length, the reciprocal of the period. Fourier optics treats any image as a superposition of sinusoidal fringes with various spatial frequencies and orientations. Low spatial frequencies carry the overall brightness distribution and large shapes, and high spatial frequencies carry edges and fine patterns. In the same way that a time signal is broken into frequency components, lenses and image sensors can then be evaluated as filters, in terms of how much of each spatial frequency they pass.

Spatial frequency is expressed in cycles/mm; lp/mm (line pairs per mm), which counts one bright and one dark line as one cycle, means the same thing. TV lines, used in video, count bright and dark lines separately and are stated per picture height, so they are easy to confuse. When thinking in angles, as for the performance of the eye, cycles/degree is used: fringes 1 arcminute wide, which an eye with 1.0 visual acuity can just distinguish, have a period of 2 arcminutes and so correspond to 30 cycles/degree. It is also important not to confuse spatial frequency with angular spatial frequency (rad/mm), multiplied by 2π.

When collimated coherent light falls on a sinusoidal grating of spatial frequency ν, the light is diffracted in the direction sinθ = λν. Finer structures bend light to larger angles, so the range of angles a lens can collect, that is, its numerical aperture, determines up to which spatial frequency it can carry into the image. In the back focal plane of a lens with focal length f, the component ν gathers at a distance λfν from the axis; with f = 100 mm, a wavelength of 633 nm and 50 cycles/mm, that is about 3.2 mm. Selecting or blocking components in this plane lets you manipulate the spatial frequencies of the image directly.

The MTF, which describes lens performance, shows how contrast is transferred at each spatial frequency. Under incoherent illumination, the contrast from an aberration-free lens falls to zero at 1/(λN) on the image side, where N is the f-number; for F2.8 at a wavelength of 0.55 µm this is about 650 cycles/mm. An image sensor cannot represent components above the Nyquist frequency 1/(2p) set by its pixel pitch p, and components beyond it fold back as moiré. When comparing camera resolution, consider the lens MTF and the sensor's Nyquist frequency side by side on the same spatial-frequency axis.

faq.q: What are the units of spatial frequency?
faq.a: Cycles/mm (lp/mm) is common. Fringes with a period of 10 µm are 100 cycles/mm. For eye performance or wide-field systems, cycles/degree is used, and in Fourier optics formulas it may also be written in mm⁻¹ or µm⁻¹.

faq.q: What is the difference between lp/mm and TV lines?
faq.a: lp/mm counts one bright and one dark line together as one, whereas TV lines count bright and dark lines separately. The TV-line value for the same fringes is therefore about twice as large, and it is also counted per picture height.

faq.q: How is spatial frequency related to resolution?
faq.a: Resolution is set by the highest spatial frequency that can be carried into the image. An optical system cannot pass frequencies above the cutoff set by its numerical aperture, so finer structures do not appear in the image.

4f系.desc: An imaging system with two lenses of focal lengths f₁ and f₂ separated by f₁ + f₂, with a total length of 2f₁ + 2f₂. A Fourier plane forms between them, and the magnification is −f₂/f₁.

about.p: A 4f system places an object in the front focal plane of a lens of focal length f₁ and a second lens of focal length f₂ at a spacing of f₁ + f₂. The first lens forms the Fourier transform of the object in its back focal plane, and the second lens transforms it once more, forming an image in its own back focal plane. Two Fourier transforms invert the coordinates, so the image is inverted and the magnification is −f₂/f₁. The name comes from the total length from object to image being 4f when f₁ = f₂ = f.

Placing a stop in the common focal plane of the two lenses puts it at infinity as seen from both the object and image sides, giving a doubly telecentric system in which the chief rays are parallel to the axis on both sides. As a result, the magnification does not change even if the object or image plane shifts slightly back and forth, which makes this the basic form of lenses for dimensional measurement by imaging. The system is also afocal, sending collimated light out as collimated light; it is the same arrangement as a Keplerian beam expander and changes the beam diameter by a factor of f₂/f₁.

about.h: The Fourier-plane aperture sets the resolution
about.p: In the common focal plane (the Fourier plane), the component of the object at spatial frequency ν lies at a distance λf₁ν from the axis. A stop of radius r here passes spatial frequencies up to r/(λf₁); with f₁ = 100 mm, a wavelength of 633 nm and r = 1 mm, that is about 16 cycles/mm. In other words, the size of the aperture in the Fourier plane directly sets the upper limit on image detail. Under coherent illumination, the frequency components of the image are the Fourier-plane amplitude multiplied by the filter transmittance, so stops, blocking masks and phase plates can process the image as designed.

4f systems have been used for image processing with spatial filters and in optical correlators that place a reference filter in the Fourier plane to test whether shapes match. In scanning microscopes, they serve as relay systems imaging the galvanometer mirror onto the objective's pupil, so that the beam stays centered in the pupil as the mirror swings. In ultrashort pulse shaping, a grating and lens spread the wavelength components across the Fourier plane, a spatial light modulator placed there changes their phase or amplitude, and the components are then recombined.

faq.q: How is the magnification of a 4f system determined?
faq.a: The lateral magnification is −f₂/f₁, the negative sign meaning the image is inverted. With f₁ = 50 mm and f₂ = 150 mm, the magnification is −3 and the total length is 2f₁ + 2f₂ = 400 mm.

faq.q: Why is the object placed in the front focal plane of a 4f system?
faq.a: Because then an exact Fourier transform, with no extra phase factor, forms in the back focal plane of the first lens. This makes it easier to manipulate spatial-frequency components, and the image then forms in the back focal plane of the second lens.

faq.q: What is the difference between a 4f system and a beam expander?
faq.a: The arrangement is the same: two positive lenses with coincident foci. A 4f system places an object in the front focal plane and uses the image and the Fourier plane, while a beam expander is used to change the diameter of a collimated beam by a factor of f₂/f₁.

空間フィルタ.desc: A method of removing particular spatial-frequency components by placing a stop or pinhole in the Fourier plane. Used to clean up laser beams and to enhance edges.

about.h: Selecting components in the Fourier plane
about.p: A spatial filter places a stop, pinhole, slit, phase plate or similar in the Fourier plane of a lens to select which spatial-frequency components of the object pass. Passing only the low frequencies at the center removes fine structure and gives a smooth image, while blocking the center brings out edges and fine scratches. Blocking only the components of a periodic pattern removes regular patterns such as halftone dots or scan lines from the image. Under coherent illumination, the image components are the Fourier-plane amplitude multiplied by the filter transmittance, so the effect can be predicted by calculation.

The most common use is the pinhole spatial filter that removes unevenness from a laser beam. Around the spot formed at the focus of a focusing lens, the disturbance components from dirt or scratches on lenses spread outward, and a pinhole somewhat larger than the spot blocks them. For a Gaussian beam, a pinhole with the same diameter as the spot's 1/e² diameter passes about 86% of the light, and one 1.5 times larger about 99%. With a focal length of 25 mm, a beam diameter of 1 mm and a wavelength of 633 nm, the spot's 1/e² diameter is about 20 µm.

about.h: How it differs from digital image processing
about.p: Image processing software also calls smoothing and edge enhancement spatial filtering, but an optical spatial filter differs in using the Fourier transform performed by a lens to process the whole image at once, as light. Mathematically both are multiplication in the frequency domain, that is, convolution of the image, but a coherent optical system acts on amplitude, so it can also handle negative values and phase changes. Under incoherent illumination, however, what acts on the intensity image is the OTF set by the autocorrelation of the pupil, so the effect of something placed in the Fourier plane is not as simple as in the coherent case.

The idea of spatial filtering underlies many observation methods. In the schlieren method, a knife edge in the Fourier plane turns light deflected by refractive-index gradients from air flow or heat into brightness differences. Darkfield illumination in a microscope corresponds to removing the zero-order light, and phase-contrast microscopy to shifting its phase. In inspecting semiconductor wafers and masks, methods are used that block the diffracted light from repeating patterns in the Fourier plane and pick out only the light scattered by foreign particles or defects that break the regularity of the pattern, making even small defects stand out against a dark background.

faq.q: How do you choose the pinhole size?
faq.a: Find the 1/e² diameter of the focused spot (about 4λf/(πD)) and use about 1.5 times that as a guide. Too small, and the central light is clipped, reducing the output; too large, and the disturbance components pass through.

faq.q: What is the difference between low-pass and high-pass spatial filters?
faq.a: A low-pass filter passes only the center of the Fourier plane, removing fine components to give a smooth image. A high-pass filter blocks the center, removing the uniform component and emphasizing edges and fine structure.

faq.q: How do you align the pinhole?
faq.a: Mount the pinhole on a three-axis translation stage, adjust the two directions perpendicular to the axis while watching the transmitted intensity, and then bring it to the focus along the axis. As it comes into alignment, the transmitted light grows stronger and unevenness and diffraction rings in the output beam disappear.

フラウンホーファー回折.desc: Diffraction observed far enough from an aperture, or in the focal plane of a lens. The amplitude of the diffraction pattern is the Fourier transform of the aperture's amplitude distribution.

about.p: When the distance L from an aperture is large enough, the difference in distance from each point of the aperture to the observation point can be approximated by an expression linear in the aperture position, and the diffraction pattern becomes a function only of the observation direction. This is Fraunhofer diffraction, in which the amplitude of the diffraction pattern is the Fourier transform of the aperture's amplitude distribution. As a guide, the condition is that the Fresnel number a²/(λL), with a the aperture radius, is much smaller than 1. In this region, changing the distance does not change the shape of the pattern; only its size grows in proportion to the distance.

The intensity of the diffraction pattern of a single slit of width a has a sinc² shape, with the first dark fringe in the direction sinθ = λ/a. For a width of 0.1 mm, a wavelength of 633 nm and a distance of 1 m, the first dark fringe is about 6.3 mm from the center and the bright central band is about 12.7 mm wide. A circular aperture of diameter D gives an Airy pattern, with the first dark ring at an angular radius of 1.22λ/D. That smaller apertures spread the pattern more is exactly the relation by which the Fourier transform of a narrow function is broad. Periodic apertures give sharp peaks in the directions set by the grating equation.

about.h: Viewing it in the focal plane of a lens
about.p: Arranging a distance of several m or more in the laboratory is awkward, but with a lens, light traveling in the same direction gathers at one point in the focal plane, so the diffraction pattern at infinity can be seen in the focal plane. With a lens of focal length f, light diffracted at angle θ gathers, in the paraxial case, at a distance fθ in the focal plane. That the point image of an aberration-free lens is an Airy disk is also Fraunhofer diffraction by the lens aperture. The resolution limits of telescopes and microscopes, and the size of a focused laser spot, are set by this diffraction.

The fact that the diffraction pattern is the Fourier transform of the aperture or object is used to work back from the pattern to the object's shape and size. Laser diffraction particle size analyzers measure the angular distribution of forward scattering from a group of particles and find the size distribution using the Fraunhofer approximation for large particles and Mie scattering theory for small ones. X-ray crystal structure analysis also relies on the diffraction intensity being the squared magnitude of the Fourier transform of the electron density. Because only intensity can be measured, however, the phase information is lost, and methods are needed to make up for it.

faq.q: What is the difference between Fraunhofer and Fresnel diffraction?
faq.a: Fraunhofer diffraction is diffraction far enough from the aperture: the pattern is the Fourier transform of the aperture and its shape does not change with distance. Fresnel diffraction occurs closer in, where a phase term proportional to the square of position within the aperture matters, so the pattern's shape changes with distance.

faq.q: How far away must you be for Fraunhofer diffraction?
faq.a: With a the aperture radius, the guide is that L is much larger than a²/λ. For a radius of 0.5 mm and a wavelength of 500 nm, a²/λ = 0.5 m, so view it several m away or in the focal plane of a lens.

faq.q: Why is the far-field pattern the Fourier transform of the aperture?
faq.a: Because far away, the path difference from each point of the aperture to the observation point reduces to a term linear in the position within the aperture. The integral adding up light from every point then takes the form of the aperture distribution multiplied by a phase proportional to position and integrated, which is a Fourier transform.

フレネル数.desc: The number NF = a²/(λL) formed from the aperture radius a, distance L and wavelength λ. When it is much smaller than 1 the diffraction is treated as Fraunhofer, and when it is around 1 as Fresnel diffraction.

about.h: The number of Fresnel zones in the aperture
about.p: The Fresnel number NF = a²/(λL) expresses how many Fresnel zones (concentric bands whose distances to the observation point differ in steps of half a wavelength) fit inside the aperture as seen from the observation point. When NF is much smaller than 1, the phase hardly changes across the aperture and the diffraction is Fraunhofer. With NF from about 1 to a few tens, the contributions of the zones reinforce or cancel one another in Fresnel diffraction, and for still larger NF the result approaches geometrical optics, with only fine fringes along the edge of the shadow.

about.h: Brightness at the center behind a circular aperture
about.p: When a plane wave falls on a circular aperture of radius a, the intensity on the central axis is 4I₀ sin²(πNF/2), where I₀ is the intensity without the aperture. At NF = 1 it is four times as bright as without the aperture, at NF = 2 it is completely dark, and changing the distance makes it alternate between bright and dark. This is because an odd number of Fresnel zones in the aperture reinforce, while with an even number neighboring zones cancel. A Fresnel zone plate, which blocks every other zone, uses this property to focus light like a lens and is also used to focus X-rays.

about.h: Definition conventions and its role as a guide
about.p: The Fresnel number is usually defined with the aperture radius, but some literature writes it with the diameter or side length, and using the diameter makes the value 4 times larger. NF is also a guide to which approximation can be used, not a strictly defined boundary, and the actual diffraction depends on which part of the observation plane is viewed and whether the illuminating light is converging. For Gaussian beams, a similar judgment is made with the beam radius and Rayleigh length, and positions well beyond the Rayleigh length correspond to the far field.

In a laser resonator, NF = a²/(λL) is formed from the mirror radius a and mirror spacing L. In a resonator with small NF, the loss from light diffracting past the mirror edges on each round trip is large, and because higher-order transverse modes lose more, low-order modes are favored. With large NF the diffraction loss is small, but many transverse modes oscillate easily. A resonator with a mirror radius of 1 mm, a spacing of 0.5 m and a wavelength of 1064 nm has NF ≈ 1.9. The size of an aperture for selecting transverse modes is also chosen with this reasoning.

faq.q: How do you calculate the Fresnel number?
faq.a: From the aperture radius a, the distance to the observation plane L and the wavelength λ, NF = a²/(λL). For a radius of 1 mm, a wavelength of 633 nm and a distance of 1 m it is about 1.6.

faq.q: What happens when the Fresnel number is greater than 1?
faq.a: It is the region treated as Fresnel diffraction: several Fresnel zones fit in the aperture, so the central brightness and the fringe shapes change greatly with distance. For even larger values the image approaches the geometrical shadow.

faq.q: How is the Fresnel number related to the condition for Fraunhofer diffraction?
faq.a: Fraunhofer diffraction holds when NF ≪ 1. The condition is met by making the distance much larger than a²/λ or by observing in the focal plane of a lens.

タルボ効果.desc: The phenomenon in which a grating of period d illuminated with coherent light produces, without a lens, images identical to the grating at every distance 2d²/λ. Also called self-imaging.

about.h: Grating images that appear without a lens
about.p: When a grating of period d is illuminated with collimated coherent light, images with the same bright and dark pattern as the grating appear without a lens at every distance zT = 2d²/λ from the grating. This is the Talbot effect (self-imaging), and zT is called the Talbot distance. Talbot observed it in 1836, and in 1881 Rayleigh derived the distance and explained it. Illuminating a grating with a period of 100 µm at 633 nm gives zT ≈ 32 mm, and moving a white card or camera behind the grating shows the grating image appearing and breaking up.

Light passing through the grating splits into a set of diffracted beams traveling at fixed angles. As they propagate, each order picks up a phase delay that, in the paraxial approximation, is proportional to the square of the order number. At the distance zT the phase differences of all orders become integer multiples of 2π, and the distribution returns to that just behind the grating. At zT/2 the odd orders are shifted by π, giving an image displaced sideways by half a period, and at fractional distances in between, images with finer periods and other patterns appear (the fractional Talbot effect). The same relation exists in the time domain, where an evenly spaced pulse train is known to return to its original shape through dispersion.

The Talbot effect appears clearly when the grating period is well above the wavelength so that the paraxial approximation holds, and the grating is illuminated with monochromatic, spatially coherent light. With a broad spectrum, zT differs by wavelength, so more distant images become blurred. With a grating of finite size, the diffracted beams travel at angles and overlap less from the edges inward, so the image stays clean only over the central part of the grating, shrinking at larger distances. When the period becomes as small as a few µm, departures from the paraxial approximation shift the distance at which images appear slightly away from 2d²/λ.

Because the Talbot effect forms images of periodic structures without a lens, it is used in several fields. In X-ray phase imaging, Talbot interferometers read the grating's self-image with a second grating to detect slight bending of the wavefront by a specimen. In lithography, methods that print periodic patterns using the self-image of a mask are under study. In testing optical systems, Talbot interferometry measures the collimation of a beam or the focal length of a lens from the moiré fringes produced by two gratings placed a suitable distance apart along the beam.

faq.q: How do you calculate the Talbot distance?
faq.a: From the grating period d and wavelength λ, zT = 2d²/λ. For a period of 50 µm and a wavelength of 500 nm it is 10 mm. At half that distance, a grating image shifted by half a period also appears.

faq.q: Does the Talbot effect occur with white light?
faq.a: Because the Talbot distance differs by wavelength, with white light the images of each color appear at different positions and overlap, so except near the grating no clear image forms. It appears clearly with monochromatic, spatially coherent illumination.

faq.q: How are the Talbot effect and moiré fringes related?
faq.a: Overlaying a second grating on the self-image produced by the Talbot effect magnifies slight differences in period or orientation between the two into visible moiré fringes. This combination is used to measure the tilt and curvature of wavefronts.

ホログラフィ.desc: A technique that records the interference fringes between an object wave and a reference wave and reconstructs the object wavefront by diffracting the reference wave. Because it records both amplitude and phase, it gives three-dimensional images.

about.h: Recording amplitude and phase as interference fringes
about.p: Recording materials and image sensors can record only the intensity of light, and an ordinary photograph loses the phase information. In holography, a coherent reference wave R, split from the same source, is superposed on the object wave O scattered by the object, and the intensity |O + R|² is recorded. The OR* and O*R terms in it form interference fringes, writing the phase of the object wave into the positions of the fringes and its amplitude into their contrast. Recording requires a source coherence length longer than the optical path difference between the two waves, and enough stability that the fringes do not move during exposure.

When the recorded hologram is illuminated with the reference wave R, diffraction by the fringes produces a component of the transmitted light proportional to the object wave O, reproducing the wavefront of the light that came from the original object. That is why a three-dimensional image with depth, whose appearance changes as the viewing position changes, is seen. At the same time a phase-reversed conjugate image (twin image) and zeroth-order light also appear. In Gabor's in-line type these overlapped on the same axis, but Leith and Upatnieks, with the off-axis type in which the reference wave enters at an angle, made it possible to separate and observe the images.

In a volume hologram recorded in a thick material, the fringes form layers inside the material, and only wavelengths and angles satisfying the Bragg condition are strongly diffracted. Reflection volume holograms can reconstruct images with little color smearing even under white light. The holograms most widely used against counterfeiting on banknotes and cards, however, are embossed holograms, whose fringes are mass-produced as surface relief by stamping. In digital holography, which records the hologram with an image sensor and reconstructs it by computing diffraction, the phase distribution of the object wave is obtained as numbers, so it is used to measure the thickness of transparent cells and the shape of surfaces. Because the pixels are large, the reference angle is limited to a few degrees or less.

faq.q: How does a hologram differ from an ordinary photograph?
faq.a: A photograph records only the intensity distribution of light imaged by a lens. A hologram records both the amplitude and phase of light as interference fringes with a reference wave, so on reconstruction the very wavefront from the object is reproduced, giving a three-dimensional image whose appearance changes with viewing direction.

faq.q: Why is a laser needed to record a hologram?
faq.a: For the object and reference waves to form stable interference fringes, a coherence length longer than the optical path difference is needed. The coherence length of white light is only on the order of µm, so the fringes quickly become invisible. Reflection volume holograms can be reconstructed with white light, but recording requires coherent light.

faq.q: How fine are the interference fringes?
faq.a: When two waves cross at an angle θ, the spacing is λ/(2 sin(θ/2)). At a wavelength of 633 nm and 30° it is about 1.22 µm (about 820 cycles/mm), so recording uses dedicated high-resolution plates or photopolymers, and vibration is suppressed.

計算機ホログラム.desc: A hologram whose fringe or phase distribution, designed to produce a desired wavefront, is created by computation. Realized with spatial light modulators or microfabrication, and used for beam shaping and optical tweezers.

about.p: An ordinary hologram is made by recording the interference fringes of object and reference beams in a photosensitive material. A computer-generated hologram (CGH) is made directly by computing, from the desired wavefront or light distribution, the amplitude or phase distribution that produces it, so it can create wavefronts of objects that do not exist or light distributions defined by equations. An early representative example is the binary detour-phase hologram shown by Brown and Lohmann in 1966, which represented phase by shifting the positions of apertures. Types that change only the phase without changing the amplitude are also called kinoforms.

about.h: Number of phase levels and diffraction efficiency
about.p: CGHs are often made by quantizing the phase into a number of steps rather than continuously, and the number of steps sets the efficiency. When a sawtooth phase is approximated by a staircase of N levels, the first-order diffraction efficiency is sinc²(1/N): about 40.5% for 2 levels, about 81% for 4, about 95% for 8 and about 99% for 16. With 2-level phase, equal amounts of light go to the +1 and −1 orders, a disadvantage for uses that need only one. In microfabrication, each extra mask doubles the number of levels, to 2, 4 and 8.

When only the intensity of the desired image is given, the phase distribution that produces it is not unique, so it is found by iterative calculation. A representative method is the Gerchberg–Saxton algorithm, which goes back and forth between the hologram plane and the image plane by Fourier transforms, replacing only the amplitude to match the constraint in each plane and updating the phase. After tens to hundreds of iterations, an image close to the target is often obtained. A phase-only hologram cannot, however, produce an arbitrary intensity perfectly, and speckle-like unevenness may remain in the image.

With a liquid-crystal spatial light modulator (SLM), a CGH can be rewritten like a display. The finest period that can be represented with pixel pitch p is 2p, so the maximum diffraction angle is about λ/(2p): about 3.8° for an 8 µm pitch at 1064 nm. Zero-order light that is not diffracted overlaps the image, so it is common to add a grating phase that shifts the image away from it. CGHs are used for beam shaping and multi-spot processing in laser machining, for optical tweezers that manipulate many particles at once, and in augmented-reality displays.

faq.q: How does a computer-generated hologram differ from an ordinary hologram?
faq.a: An ordinary hologram records the interference of light from a real object with a reference beam, whereas a computer-generated hologram is made by computing the required amplitude or phase from the desired wavefront. It can also reconstruct objects that do not exist or light distributions defined by equations.

faq.q: How high is the diffraction efficiency of a computer-generated hologram?
faq.a: It depends on the number of phase levels: about 40% into the first order with 2 levels and about 95% with 8. In liquid-crystal spatial light modulators, disturbances at pixel boundaries and leakage of zero-order light lower the actual efficiency.

faq.q: What is a kinoform?
faq.a: A computer-generated hologram that changes only the phase without changing the amplitude; because it absorbs no light, it is highly efficient. It is realized as a phase distribution wrapped into the range 0 to 2π, by surface-relief fabrication or with a spatial light modulator.

ケーラー照明.desc: An illumination method that images the light source onto the condenser aperture diaphragm and the field diaphragm onto the specimen plane. It lights the field evenly regardless of source unevenness and lets the illumination NA be adjusted.

about.p: Köhler illumination, devised by Köhler in 1893, is a microscope illumination method that images the light source onto the condenser aperture diaphragm (its front focal plane) and the field diaphragm onto the specimen plane. The microscope then contains two conjugate series: field diaphragm, specimen, intermediate image and sensor (or retina), which carry the shape of the image, and light source, aperture diaphragm, objective back focal plane and eyepoint, which carry the angles of the light. Because the shape of the source is not imaged onto the specimen, the field is evenly lit even if the filament or LED is uneven.

about.h: The roles of the two diaphragms
about.p: The field diaphragm sets the illuminated area and is opened to just beyond the field being observed. Limiting illumination to where it is needed reduces stray light and flare from unwanted light and, in fluorescence observation, also prevents photobleaching outside the field. The aperture diaphragm sets the range of illumination angles, that is, the numerical aperture of the condenser. Closing it increases image contrast and depth of field but lowers resolution. As a guide it is said to be often set to about 70–80% of the objective's numerical aperture, but it is adjusted to suit the specimen.

about.h: Do not set brightness with the aperture diaphragm
about.p: A common mistake is to adjust image brightness with the aperture diaphragm. Closing it does darken the image, but it also lowers the illumination numerical aperture, degrading resolution and producing an image with prominent diffraction fringes. Brightness should be changed with source output or ND filters, and the aperture diaphragm set by balancing resolution against contrast. With the resolution estimate 1.22λ/(NA_obj + NA_cond), λ = 550 nm and NA 0.65 for both objective and condenser give about 0.52 µm, but closing the condenser to NA 0.3 worsens it to about 0.71 µm.

about.h: Setting it up, and uses beyond the microscope
about.p: To set it up, first focus on the specimen, close the field diaphragm and adjust the condenser height until its edge is sharp, center it in the image, and then open it to just beyond the field. Finally, remove the eyepiece or use a centering telescope to view the back focal plane while adjusting the aperture diaphragm. This illumination is also the basis for phase-contrast and differential interference contrast microscopy. The idea of separating the image of the source from the illuminated plane is also widely used in the illumination optics of projectors and semiconductor lithography tools.

faq.q: What is the difference between Köhler and critical illumination?
faq.a: Critical illumination images the light source directly onto the specimen plane, so unevenness of the source is superimposed on the image. Köhler illumination images the source onto the aperture diaphragm and the field diaphragm onto the specimen, giving even illumination without unevenness.

faq.q: How far should the aperture diaphragm be closed?
faq.a: About 70–80% of the objective's numerical aperture is said to be a guide, but it depends on the specimen. Closing it increases contrast and depth of field but lowers resolution, so keep it fairly open when looking at fine structure.

faq.q: Why does the edge of the field diaphragm look blurred?
faq.a: Because the condenser height is not set correctly and the image of the field diaphragm is not formed in the specimen plane, so the illumination is not Köhler. Move the condenser up or down until the edge is sharp, and center it in the field with the centering screws.

暗視野照明.desc: A method that illuminates at angles larger than the objective's NA so that direct light does not enter the objective, forming the image only from light scattered or diffracted by the specimen. The background is dark and fine particles appear to glow.

about.h: Keeping direct light out of the objective
about.p: Darkfield illumination lights the specimen only at angles larger than the numerical aperture of the objective. In transmitted light, an annulus of light with the center of the condenser blocked, or a dedicated condenser with a paraboloidal or cardioid reflecting surface, is used. The direct light passes by without entering the objective, so the background is dark and only light scattered or diffracted by the specimen forms the image. In Fourier optics terms it is the image with all the zero-order light that would reach the objective's back focal plane removed, so only the edges and fine structures of the specimen shine brightly.

about.h: Why things smaller than the resolution can be seen
about.p: Because scattered light shines against a dark background, even particles smaller than the resolution can be detected as glowing points if their scattered light is strong enough to detect. What is recorded, though, is a point image broadened by diffraction, so particle size and shape cannot be measured correctly. Scattering from particles much smaller than the wavelength is proportional to the sixth power of the diameter, so halving the diameter reduces scattering to 1/64, and particles that are too small suddenly become invisible. Particles that scatter strongly through plasmon resonance, such as gold nanoparticles, look bright even at tens of nm.

The condition for darkfield is that the inner numerical aperture of the illumination exceeds that of the objective. High-NA oil-immersion objectives are therefore used with an iris built into the objective to lower their numerical aperture. Dust and bubbles in the specimen and scratches on the slide all glow too, so clean specimens and optics are essential. In thick or strongly scattering specimens, scattered light from outside the focus brightens the background and lowers contrast. Also, because the image is formed only from scattered light it tends to be dim, so a bright light source is needed.

Darkfield illumination is used to see unstained bacteria and their flagella and tiny particles, the observation of the syphilis pathogen being a long-standing example. In inspecting metals and semiconductors, reflected darkfield makes scratches, dust and steps on surfaces glow so they can be found, and wafer inspection tools count particles from the scattering of obliquely incident laser light. Rheinberg illumination, which combines color filters so that background and specimen appear in different colors, is a development of darkfield. In nanoparticle research, the scattering spectrum of a single particle is measured in darkfield.

faq.q: What is the difference between darkfield and brightfield illumination?
faq.a: In brightfield the direct illumination also enters the image, and differences in absorption by the specimen become differences in brightness. In darkfield the direct light is kept out of the objective and the image is formed only from scattered light, so the background is dark and transparent particles and fine structures glow.

faq.q: How small a particle can be seen in darkfield?
faq.a: It depends on the strength of the scattered light and the detection sensitivity; particles smaller than the resolution can still be seen as glowing points. Scattering weakens with the sixth power of the diameter, so the limit depends greatly on the particle material and the brightness of the source.

faq.q: Why is darkfield hard with high-NA objectives?
faq.a: The illumination angle must exceed the objective's numerical aperture, so if the objective's NA approaches the condenser's, direct light gets in. Objectives with a built-in iris are used to lower the numerical aperture.

位相差顕微鏡.desc: A microscope that shifts the phase of the direct light by about λ/4 with a phase plate and makes it interfere with the diffracted light, turning phase differences in transparent specimens into brightness differences. Devised by Zernike.

about.p: Transparent specimens such as living cells absorb almost no light and only slightly delay its phase. When the phase delay φ is small, the transmitted light is the sum of strong direct light and weak diffracted light shifted in phase by about π/2, and in brightfield the intensity change is only of order φ². At φ = 0.1 rad this is about 1%, almost invisible. Zernike devised a method that shifts the phase of the direct light by λ/4 so that it is in phase or in antiphase with the diffracted light, raising the intensity change to about 2φ, or about 20%, and received the 1953 Nobel Prize in Physics.

In a phase-contrast microscope, an annular stop in the front focal plane of the condenser illuminates the specimen with a hollow cone of light. The direct light gathers in a ring in the objective's back focal plane, and there a phase plate is placed whose optical path is changed only in the ring. The diffracted light spreads over the whole back focal plane, so most of it passes outside the ring. The ring of the phase plate also carries a film that attenuates the direct light, bringing the strengths of direct and diffracted light closer to raise contrast. The condenser annulus is chosen to match the ring size of each objective (Ph1, Ph2 and so on).

about.h: Halos, and specimens it suits or does not suit
about.p: Phase-contrast images show bright halos along the edges of structures, and the centers of large uniform structures approach the brightness of the background (shade-off). This is because the ring has a finite width, so some of the low-spatial-frequency diffracted light passes through the same ring as the direct light. The phase approximation also holds only for small phase shifts, and in thick specimens or ones with large index differences, contrast can reverse or the image can become disturbed. Thin specimens such as monolayer cultured cells suit it best, and it is not suited to thick tissue sections.

Phase-contrast microscopy does not use polarization, so it works directly with birefringent plastic culture dishes. For this reason inverted phase-contrast microscopes are widely used for routine checks of cultured cells. Differential interference contrast microscopy, on the other hand, has no halos and can use a large condenser numerical aperture, giving a shallow depth of field that makes it easier to view one plane inside a thick specimen. Both turn optical path differences into brightness, and they can be told apart by thinking of phase contrast as seeing the path difference itself and DIC as seeing its gradient.

faq.q: Why can transparent cells be seen with a phase-contrast microscope?
faq.a: Light passing through a cell is slightly delayed in phase relative to its surroundings. When a phase plate shifts the phase of the direct light by λ/4, interference with the diffracted light turns the phase difference into an intensity difference, so the cell appears darker (or brighter) than the background.

faq.q: What is the difference between positive and negative phase contrast?
faq.a: In positive (dark) contrast, structures of higher index appear darker than the background; in negative (bright) contrast they appear brighter. Which one results depends on whether the phase plate advances or retards the phase of the direct light.

faq.q: What is the halo in phase-contrast images?
faq.a: It is a bright (or dark) outline along the edges of structures, caused by part of the diffracted light also passing through the ring of the phase plate. It is an image artifact characteristic of phase contrast, so take care when reading the boundaries of shapes.

微分干渉顕微鏡.desc: A microscope that passes two beams of orthogonal polarization, shifted slightly sideways, through the specimen and shows the gradient of optical path difference as shaded brightness. Also called DIC.

about.h: Seeing the phase difference between two beams
about.p: In a differential interference contrast (DIC) microscope, light made linearly polarized by a polarizer is split into two beams of orthogonal polarization by a Nomarski prism, a modified Wollaston prism. The two beams are slightly displaced sideways at the specimen (the shear) and each passes through neighboring points. A second prism behind the objective recombines them and an analyzer makes them interfere, so the path difference between the two points, that is, the gradient of path difference along the shear direction, becomes brightness. The shear is usually chosen smaller than the objective's resolution, so resolution is hardly lost.

about.h: Why it looks three-dimensional, and the pitfall
about.p: Adding a constant phase difference (bias) between the two beams by the position of the second prism or a compensator makes one side bright and the other dark according to the sign of the gradient, giving an image with shading as if lit obliquely. This shading, however, represents the gradient of path difference, not height, so a part that looks raised is not necessarily higher. Gradients perpendicular to the shear direction also produce no contrast, so elongated structures look different depending on their orientation, and the specimen is sometimes rotated to check.

about.h: Shallow depth of field and strength with thick specimens
about.p: DIC microscopy can use a large condenser numerical aperture, so its depth of field is shallow and one plane inside a thick specimen can be seen sharply. There are no halos as in phase contrast, and fine edges and granules show cleanly even within large structures. It is therefore often used for observing embryos and thick tissue, and as the transmitted-light image overlaid on fluorescence to show cell outlines. On the other hand, because it uses polarization, the bottoms of plastic containers that are birefringent from molding stress interfere with observation, and glass-bottom containers are recommended.

Reflected-light DIC looks at the path difference between two beams reflected from a surface, so it emphasizes slight steps and slopes as shaded images. In reflection a step of height h gives a path difference of 2h over the round trip, so steps of order nm can sometimes be distinguished, and it is used for inspecting semiconductor wafers, polished surfaces and metal microstructures. Obtaining height as a number from the brightness, however, needs calibration, and when an accurate height is needed, instruments such as white-light interferometers or stylus profilers are used.

faq.q: What is the difference between DIC and phase-contrast microscopy?
faq.a: Both turn phase differences in transparent specimens into brightness. Phase contrast shows the phase difference itself and tends to produce halos, while DIC shows the phase gradient as shading; it has no halos and a shallow depth of field, but is hard to use with containers that disturb polarization.

faq.q: What is a Nomarski prism?
faq.a: It is a modified Wollaston prism, made of two cemented birefringent crystals, in which the plane where the two beams separate lies outside the prism. It can therefore be matched to the objective's back focal plane even when that plane lies inside the lens and cannot be reached.

faq.q: Does the shading in a DIC image represent height?
faq.a: No. The shading is the gradient of path difference along the shear direction and includes differences in refractive index. Something that looks raised is not necessarily higher, so check shapes with other methods as well.

ストークスシフト.desc: The shift of the fluorescence wavelength to longer than the excitation wavelength. It arises because an excited molecule loses energy through vibrational relaxation before emitting, and it allows filters to separate the excitation light from the fluorescence.

about.h: Why fluorescence comes out at longer wavelengths
about.p: A molecule that absorbs light rises to a high vibrational level of an excited electronic state, but within a short time of order ps it undergoes vibrational relaxation to the lowest vibrational level, and only then emits fluorescence with a lifetime of order ns. Fluorescence also often returns the molecule to a high vibrational level of the ground state, and at both stages part of the energy is lost as heat. The fluorescence photon therefore has less energy than the absorbed photon, and a longer wavelength. The name comes from Stokes's observation with a solution of quinine in 1852.

about.h: Compare in wavenumber rather than wavelength
about.p: The Stokes shift is expressed as the difference between the maxima of the absorption and fluorescence spectra; it is often written in nm, but wavenumber (cm⁻¹) is better for comparing energy differences. For a dye such as fluorescein, absorbing at about 490 nm and fluorescing at about 520 nm, the difference is 30 nm, about 1180 cm⁻¹ in wavenumber, or about 0.15 eV in energy. The same 1180 cm⁻¹ shift with excitation at 700 nm puts the fluorescence at about 763 nm, a difference of more than 60 nm. Note that for longer-wavelength dyes, the difference in nm looks larger.

about.h: How it differs from Raman Stokes lines
about.p: The same name Stokes is used for the Stokes lines of Raman scattering, but with a different meaning. In Raman scattering the shift is the vibrational energy of the molecule itself, and the shift in wavenumber does not change when the excitation wavelength changes. The fluorescence Stokes shift is the difference between the maxima of the absorption and emission spectra, and it also changes with factors such as solvent polarity. Also, in two-photon excitation and upconversion, light at a shorter wavelength than the excitation is emitted, but this uses the combined energy of two or more photons and does not violate conservation of energy.

In fluorescence microscopy and fluorescence measurement, the Stokes shift is what allows excitation light and fluorescence to be separated by wavelength. The excitation filter, dichroic mirror and emission filter divide the light within this shift, so with a dye whose shift is small, the filter bands must be narrowed and part of the fluorescence is discarded. Conversely, dyes with large shifts make it easier to remove leaked or scattered excitation light, and also suit multicolor observation combining dyes that are excited at one wavelength but fluoresce in different colors. Quantum dots absorb over a broad range extending to shorter wavelengths, so a single source can excite many colors.

faq.q: Why does the Stokes shift occur?
faq.a: Because an excited molecule loses part of its energy as heat through vibrational relaxation before fluorescing, and often returns to a high vibrational level of the ground state. The fluorescence photon has correspondingly less energy and a longer wavelength.

faq.q: How is the Stokes shift expressed?
faq.a: As the difference between the maxima of the absorption and fluorescence spectra. It is also written in nm, but to compare it as an energy difference, the difference of the reciprocals of the absorption and fluorescence wavelengths is found in wavenumber (cm⁻¹).

faq.q: What are the advantages of dyes with a large Stokes shift?
faq.a: The excitation and fluorescence wavelengths are far apart, so they are easy to separate with filters, reducing background from leaked or scattered excitation light. They also suit multicolor observation using dyes that fluoresce in different colors at the same time with one excitation wavelength.

共焦点顕微鏡.desc: A microscope that scans the specimen with light focused to a point and blocks light from outside the focal plane with a pinhole at a position conjugate to the focus, giving images of a thin layer along the optical axis (optical sections).

about.h: Selecting the focal plane with a pinhole
about.p: In a confocal microscope, the objective focuses laser light to a single point in the specimen, and the fluorescence or reflected light from there is collected by the same objective and detected through a pinhole placed at a position conjugate to the focus. Light from the focal plane is focused onto the pinhole and passes through, but light from above or below the focal plane is spread out at the pinhole and is mostly blocked. Even in thick specimens there is therefore little blur from outside the focal plane, and optical sections showing only a thin layer along the optical axis are obtained. Stacking sections while shifting the focus little by little lets you assemble a three-dimensional image.

The pinhole diameter is expressed in Airy units, with 1 Airy unit equal to the diameter of the Airy disk at the detection plane (1.22λ/NA at the specimen plane multiplied by the magnification). At around 1 Airy unit, the pinhole removes out-of-focus light well while passing most of the light from the focus. Making it smaller still improves the lateral resolution by up to about 1.4 times, because the image is set by the product of the illumination and detection point images, but the light passing through drops sharply and the signal-to-noise ratio falls. The axial resolution is several times worse than the lateral and is inversely proportional to the square of NA, so higher-NA objectives give thinner sections.

about.h: Scanning methods and differences from other techniques
about.p: The image is built by arranging point-by-point signals through scanning, most commonly by sweeping the beam with galvanometer mirrors. The spinning-disk type, using a rotating disk with many pinholes (a Nipkow disk), scans many points at once and images quickly, so it suits observing fast movements in living cells. A two-photon excitation microscope obtains optical sections without a pinhole by not emitting fluorescence outside the focus. The difference is that confocal selects the focal plane on the detection side and two-photon on the excitation side, and in deep, strongly scattering tissue two-photon has the advantage.

faq.q: How does a confocal microscope differ from an ordinary fluorescence microscope?
faq.a: An ordinary (widefield) fluorescence microscope illuminates the whole field and records out-of-focus fluorescence as it is, so in thick specimens the blur piles up. A confocal microscope illuminates and scans with a point and blocks light from outside the focal plane with a pinhole, giving sharp images of only a thin layer.

faq.q: How large should the pinhole be?
faq.a: About 1 Airy unit is commonly used. With 63× magnification, NA 1.4 and a fluorescence wavelength of 520 nm it is about 28.5 µm. Making it smaller thins the section but darkens the image; making it larger brightens it at the cost of mixing in out-of-focus light.

faq.q: Why is the depth resolution worse than the lateral resolution?
faq.a: Because the objective collects light only over a limited range of angles from one side of the specimen, the range of spatial frequencies it can capture along the optical axis is narrower than laterally. The axial resolution is inversely proportional to the square of NA, so it improves as higher-NA objectives are used.

二光子励起顕微鏡.desc: A microscope that excites fluorescence through simultaneous absorption of two photons. Because absorption is proportional to the square of the intensity, only the focus is excited, and near-infrared light allows deep observation in living tissue.

about.h: Exciting only the focus through the square of intensity
about.p: In two-photon excitation, a molecule absorbs two photons almost simultaneously and is excited by the sum of their energies. Göppert-Mayer predicted it theoretically in 1931, and Denk and colleagues demonstrated it as a microscope in 1990. Because the absorption probability is proportional to the square of the intensity, excitation is strong only near the focus and falls off quickly away from it. There is therefore almost no fluorescence or photobleaching outside the focus, and optical sections are obtained without a pinhole. For excitation equivalent to 488 nm with one photon, light near 976 nm, about twice the wavelength, is used.

Two-photon absorption is extremely unlikely, so femtosecond pulses that concentrate the intensity in time are used. At the same average power, a signal proportional to the square of intensity grows by the inverse of the fraction of time the pulses are on (the duty cycle). For pulses at an 80 MHz repetition rate and 100 fs width, the duty cycle is about 8×10⁻⁶, giving about 10⁵ times the signal of continuous light (apart from a factor depending on pulse shape). This makes observation possible with average powers at the specimen of a few mW to tens of mW, and titanium-sapphire lasers and fiber lasers are used as sources.

about.h: Why it is strong in deep tissue
about.p: Near-infrared light scatters less in biological tissue than visible light and reaches deeper. Moreover, because excitation occurs only at the focus, fluorescence scattered on its way back can all be used as signal, as having come from the focus. Large-area detectors placed near the specimen therefore collect fluorescence without sending it back through the scanning optics (non-descanned detection). In a confocal microscope, scattered fluorescence is blocked by the pinhole, so the deeper the location, the greater the advantage of two-photon excitation. In mouse brain, observation down to about 1 mm below the surface has been reported.

Because the excitation wavelength is about twice as long, the lateral resolution is slightly worse than that of a confocal microscope exciting the same dye with one photon. The squared intensity does narrow the excitation distribution, but not enough to cancel the effect of the longer wavelength. Also, the intensity at the focus is very high, so raising the power too far rapidly increases photobleaching at the focus and damage from higher-order absorption. To see still deeper, three-photon excitation using light near 1300 nm or 1700 nm is also being studied.

faq.q: What is the difference between two-photon and confocal microscopes?
faq.a: A confocal microscope forms sections by blocking out-of-focus light with a pinhole on the detection side, while a two-photon microscope forms sections by confining the excitation itself to the focus. In deep, strongly scattering tissue, two-photon excitation has the advantage because scattered fluorescence can also be used.

faq.q: What wavelengths are used for two-photon excitation?
faq.a: Near-infrared light at roughly twice the one-photon excitation wavelength is used. Green fluorescent protein (GFP), for example, is often excited with light at around 920 nm.

faq.q: Why is a femtosecond laser needed?
faq.a: Because two-photon absorption is proportional to the square of intensity, the signal grows the more the light is concentrated into short pulses, even at the same average power. With 80 MHz, 100 fs pulses, excitation is about 10⁵ times more efficient than with continuous light.

STED顕微鏡.desc: A super-resolution microscope that switches off fluorescence around the excited spot by stimulated emission with a doughnut-shaped beam, making the emitting region narrower than the diffraction limit.

about.h: Shrinking the emitting region beyond the diffraction limit
about.p: A STED (stimulated emission depletion) microscope excites fluorescent molecules with an excitation beam and immediately overlays a doughnut-shaped beam with zero intensity at its center (the STED beam), returning the surrounding molecules to the ground state by stimulated emission so that they do not fluoresce. Only molecules in a very small region at the center of the doughnut can fluoresce, so even though focusing remains diffraction-limited, the emitting region is smaller than the diffraction limit. Hell and colleagues proposed it in 1994, and Hell received the 2014 Nobel Prize in Chemistry together with researchers of single-molecule methods.

about.h: Resolution improves with the square root of intensity
about.p: A guide to the resolution is d ≈ d₀/√(1 + I/Is), where d₀ is the diffraction-limited resolution, I the STED beam intensity, and Is a saturation intensity indicating where suppression of fluorescence starts to take effect. With d₀ = 214 nm (wavelength 600 nm, NA 1.4), I/Is = 99 gives about 21 nm, and reaching 30 nm needs I/Is ≈ 50. Because resolution improves only with the square root of intensity, strong light is required. For biological specimens it is often used at resolutions of tens of nm, balancing against photobleaching and photodamage.

about.h: The doughnut beam and choice of wavelength
about.p: The doughnut-shaped beam is made by focusing light that has passed through a vortex phase plate, whose phase winds from 0 to 2π around the optical axis. How close the central intensity comes to zero affects the resolution, so control of polarization and aberrations is important. The STED wavelength is chosen in the long-wavelength tail of the fluorescence spectrum so that it does not itself excite the molecules, and sources such as 592 nm and 775 nm are commonly used. To raise the axial resolution as well, a separate beam shaped to sandwich the focus from above and below is added.

about.h: How it differs from other super-resolution methods
about.p: Single-molecule localization methods such as PALM and STORM switch on only a few molecules at a time, estimate their positions and build up the image from many frames, so they achieve high resolution but take time to acquire and need computational reconstruction. STED narrows the emitting region itself while scanning, so the image is obtained directly as measured, and small areas can be imaged quickly. On the other hand, it uses intense light, so dyes resistant to photobleaching must be chosen. A method called RESOLFT applies the same idea with lower light intensity, using molecules that can be switched with weak light.

faq.q: What resolution does a STED microscope achieve?
faq.a: It depends on the STED beam intensity, and for biological specimens tens of nm is common. By the guide formula d ≈ d₀/√(1 + I/Is), larger I/Is gives finer resolution, but photobleaching and damage also increase.

faq.q: How is STED related to the confocal microscope?
faq.a: STED is a scanning confocal microscope with a doughnut-shaped STED beam added. Switching the STED beam off gives an ordinary confocal image, so resolution can be compared in the same field of view.

faq.q: Why does STED use a doughnut-shaped beam?
faq.a: Because its intensity is zero at the center, only the molecules at the center escape being switched off by stimulated emission and can fluoresce. Switching off only the surrounding molecules makes the emitting region narrower than the diffraction limit.

外部量子効率.desc: In an LED or similar device, the number of photons leaving the device per injected electron. It is the product of the injection efficiency, internal quantum efficiency and light-extraction efficiency.

about.p: Driving an LED with current I injects I/q electrons per second. The external quantum efficiency (EQE) is the fraction of these that leave the device as photons, found from the optical output P and wavelength λ as EQE = (Pλ/hc)/(I/q). With wavelength in nm, current in A and optical output in W, EQE ≈ Pλ/(1240 I). It differs from the wall-plug efficiency, a power ratio (optical output / electrical input); because the drive voltage exceeds the photon energy, the wall-plug efficiency is smaller than the external quantum efficiency by that margin.

The external quantum efficiency is the product of the injection efficiency with which electrons and holes reach the active layer, the internal quantum efficiency (the fraction of recombinations in the active layer that produce photons), and the light-extraction efficiency (the fraction of generated photons that escape). InGaN blue LEDs reach high internal quantum efficiencies, and the remaining challenge is extraction. From a crystal with an index of about 2.5, only about 4% of the light can leave through each flat face into air, so surface roughening, patterned substrates, resin encapsulation and reflective electrodes are combined to raise extraction.

The external quantum efficiency changes with current: at low current, defect-assisted nonradiative recombination is relatively large, and raising the current raises the efficiency. Raising the current density further increases Auger recombination and carrier leakage, and the efficiency falls, which is called efficiency droop. A hotter active layer also lowers the efficiency through more nonradiative recombination, so for lighting LEDs, enlarging the chip to lower the current density and good thermal design are keys to maintaining efficiency. The same definition of external quantum efficiency is used for OLEDs.

faq.q: What is the difference between external quantum efficiency and luminous efficacy (lm/W)?
faq.a: External quantum efficiency is the ratio of numbers of photons and electrons, a physical efficiency independent of the color of light. Luminous efficacy is the luminous flux (lm) per watt of power, weighted by the eye's sensitivity, so for the same external quantum efficiency it is larger for light closer to the green where the eye is most sensitive.

faq.q: How is the optical output found from the external quantum efficiency?
faq.a: The optical output is P = EQE × (I/q) × (hc/λ). For example, at 350 mA, 450 nm and an external quantum efficiency of 52%, using a photon energy of about 2.76 eV gives about 0.5 W.

faq.q: How is the internal quantum efficiency measured?
faq.a: It is hard to measure directly, so it is estimated by taking the ratio of emission intensity at room temperature to that at low temperature, where nonradiative recombination is assumed to stop, or by analyzing the current-output relation with a recombination model. The light-extraction efficiency is estimated by calculations such as ray tracing.

光取り出し効率.desc: The fraction of photons generated in the active layer that can escape the device. Inside a high-index semiconductor, light is trapped by total internal reflection, so it is raised by surface roughening and similar means.

効率ドループ.desc: The fall in an LED's external quantum efficiency at high currents after it peaks at some current. Auger recombination and carrier leakage are considered the main causes.

白色LED.desc: An LED that converts part of a blue LED's light to yellow or other colors with a phosphor and mixes them into white. Adding a red phosphor raises color rendering but tends to lower luminous efficacy.

有機EL.desc: A device that emits light when current flows through thin films of organic material. Its pixels emit by themselves, so displays can show deep black, and phosphorescent materials that also emit from triplets raise the efficiency.

液晶ディスプレイ.desc: A display that passes or blocks backlight pixel by pixel with two polarizers and a liquid crystal whose molecular orientation changes with voltage.

色域.desc: The range of colors a display or similar device can reproduce. On a chromaticity diagram it is the inside of the triangle with the three primaries' chromaticities as vertices; standards include sRGB and BT.2020.

about.p: A display makes colors by varying the intensities of red, green and blue primaries. The chromaticity of additively mixed light is a weighted average of the primaries' chromaticities, so reproducible colors are limited to the inside of the triangle on the xy chromaticity diagram whose vertices are the three primaries. This is the color gamut. Monochromatic light lies on the horseshoe-shaped spectral locus, and no colors exist outside it, so no choice of three primaries can reproduce every visible color. The triangle is drawn in chromaticity, which is independent of brightness, so high luminance has nothing to do with the width of the gamut.

about.h: Gamut standards and how to compare them
about.p: Standards such as sRGB for computers and the web, Adobe RGB for photography and printing, DCI-P3 for cinema and BT.2020 for ultra-high-definition television each define primary chromaticities and a white point. The BT.2020 primaries are monochromatic light on the spectral locus, giving a much larger triangle than sRGB. A display's gamut is expressed as its area ratio to a standard's triangle or as the fraction of the standard's triangle it covers (coverage). Distances on the xy diagram are not proportional to perceived color differences, so the u′v′ diagram is also used, and you need to check which diagram a figure was calculated on.

about.h: Technologies for wider gamut, and color management
about.p: The narrower the primaries' spectra, the closer their chromaticities move to the spectral locus and the wider the gamut. With white-LED backlights and color filters the primaries tend to be broad, so color conversion with quantum dots or narrow-band phosphors, or microcavities that narrow OLED emission, are used. Even on a wide-gamut display, however, sRGB images are shown oversaturated unless the values are converted from the image's color space to the display's. The color management of the operating system and applications performs this conversion.

faq.q: Is a wider color gamut always a better display?
faq.a: It is an advantage in that more colors can be shown, but seeing correct colors requires color management. Without it, sRGB images look too vivid and unnatural, so being able to switch to an sRGB mode for some uses also matters.

faq.q: What does "72% NTSC" mean?
faq.a: It usually expresses the area ratio of a display's triangle to the triangle of primaries of NTSC, an old television standard. The sRGB triangle has about 71% of the NTSC area on the xy diagram, so "72% NTSC" indicates a gamut roughly the size of sRGB.

faq.q: How are colors outside the gamut shown?
faq.a: A display cannot produce colors outside its triangle, so color management replaces them with nearby colors inside it (gamut mapping). Methods include reducing only saturation and compressing everything to keep the relations between colors, chosen according to the purpose.

量子ドット.desc: A semiconductor nanoparticle a few nm in size. Its emission wavelength changes with size and its spectrum is narrow, so it is used for color conversion that widens display color gamut.

CMOSイメージセンサ.desc: An image sensor with an amplifying transistor in each pixel, read out by selecting rows. Everything up to AD conversion can be integrated on the same chip, making it fast and low in power.

about.p: A typical four-transistor pixel consists of a photodiode that converts light to electrons and stores them, a transfer gate that moves the charge to the floating diffusion, a reset transistor that initializes the floating diffusion, an amplifying (source-follower) transistor that converts charge to voltage, and a row-select transistor. The floating diffusion's capacitance C sets the voltage per electron q/C (conversion gain), a few tens of µV per electron for a few fF. Correlated double sampling, which takes the difference between the voltage just after reset and after charge transfer, cancels the kTC noise that changes at every reset and holds the read noise to a few electrons or less.

about.h: Readout and the difference from CCDs
about.p: A CMOS image sensor selects one row at a time, amplifies the voltages of that row's pixels in parallel with per-column circuits, AD-converts them, and outputs digital values. It does not transfer charge over long distances as a CCD does, so no high transfer voltages are needed, power is low and readout is fast. Timing control, AD conversion and even image-processing circuits can be integrated in the same semiconductor process. Early devices suffered from larger pixel-to-pixel variation and noise than CCDs, but pinned photodiodes and correlated double sampling overcame this, and they are now used in most cameras.

As pixels shrink, the wiring above the photodiode blocks light, so backside-illuminated sensors, which thin the wafer and let light in from the back, are widely used. Stacked sensors go further, making the pixel layer and the signal-processing layer on separate wafers and bonding them, so the pixel area can be devoted to receiving light and the circuits can use a high-speed logic process. A rolling shutter that exposes rows in sequence is the basic mode, but there are also global-shutter sensors with a storage element in each pixel to hold the charge temporarily, used for imaging and measuring fast-moving objects.

faq.q: Which gives better image quality, a CMOS image sensor or a CCD?
faq.a: Today CMOS image sensors match or exceed CCDs in most uses, with read noise down to about 1 to 2 electrons. CCDs were used in some scientific measurements that benefit from low pixel-to-pixel variation and binning in the charge domain, but they are being replaced by scientific CMOS image sensors.

faq.q: What are the drawbacks of a small pixel pitch?
faq.a: Each pixel receives fewer photons, so the shot-noise-limited S/N falls, and the full-well capacity also shrinks, tending to narrow the dynamic range. Diffraction blur also easily exceeds the pixel size, so detail is lost at large f-numbers.

faq.q: What is conversion gain?
faq.a: It is the voltage in µV that one electron produces in the pixel, q/C for a floating-diffusion capacitance C. A larger value makes later-stage noise less significant but reduces the number of electrons that fit in the same voltage range.

CCDイメージセンサ.desc: An image sensor that transfers each pixel's charge step by step by switching electrode voltages and converts it to voltage with a few output amplifiers. Pixel-to-pixel variation is small.

フルウェル容量.desc: The maximum number of electrons a pixel can store. Beyond it the pixel saturates; it sets the bright end of the dynamic range and the maximum S/N obtainable (its square root).

読み出し雑音.desc: Noise added when a pixel's charge is converted to voltage and read out, expressed as an rms number of electrons. It sets the S/N in dark scenes and the dark end of the dynamic range.

ダイナミックレンジ.desc: The ratio of the largest signal a measurement or recording can handle to the smallest, set by noise. For image sensors, the ratio of full-well capacity to read noise is expressed in dB or stops.

about.h: The ratio of full-well capacity to read noise
about.p: An image sensor's pixel cannot hold more electrons than its full-well capacity, and brighter areas saturate to white. On the dark side, read noise and dark-current noise exist even without light, and smaller signals are buried in them. Dynamic range is the ratio of these two; for example, with a full-well capacity of 20000 electrons and read noise of 4 electrons, the ratio is 5000.
